Jude was one of those whom Jesus chose after spending a night in prayer.
Over the next three years he walked with Jesus, heard His teaching, and saw His miracles: the sick healed, the storm calmed, the crowd of thousands fed, and the dead raised.
He was also sent out with the others, two by two, to preach and heal.
The Bible does not say who his partner was.
But the promise Jesus gave them was clear: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”
Jude went on a mission with the authority of Jesus.
The last supper.
On the night before the crucifixion, Jesus ate the Passover meal with the twelve, washed their feet and gave them a long talk. It was a heavy evening.
Jesus said He would soon leave, that one of them would betray Him and that Peter would deny Him.
The disciples were confused and afraid.
He told them, “Let not your hearts be troubled.
Believe in God; believe also in me.
In my Father’s house are many rooms...
I go to prepare a place for you.”
He promised: “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.”
He said He would send the Helper, the Holy Spirit, who would teach them everything.
“Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me.”
The disciples did not fully understand.
Jude’s question.
In the middle of this teaching, “Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, ‘Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?’”
John takes care to say “not Iscariot,” to make it clear who was speaking.
Jude had picked up on something important.
Jesus had said that the world would not see Him, but the disciples would. He wondered why.
If Jesus was the Messiah, why not show Himself openly to everyone?
Many Jews of the time expected the Messiah to come in power and be seen by all.
Jesus’ answer is one of the most beautiful in the Gospels: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.”
God would not just visit His people. He would live in them.
Jude’s question gave Jesus a chance to explain that the Father and the Son would make their home in everyone who loves and obeys Him.
“Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.”
From the upper room to the world.
When Jesus was arrested, Jude fled with the others.
But after the resurrection, Jesus appeared to His disciples and restored them.
After the ascension, they returned to Jerusalem and went upstairs to the room where they were staying.
Acts lists them by name, and one of them is “Judas the son of James.”
They prayed together until Pentecost.
The promise Jude had asked about came true.
The Holy Spirit came on them all, and the apostles began to preach.
Jesus was now present in His people, as He had said.
The Bible does not say where Jude went to preach.
Traditions say he went to Mesopotamia, Syria, Persia and Armenia, and was martyred.
The Bible does not confirm them, but they match how the apostles spread out across the empire.
The letter of Jude.
One of the shortest books of the New Testament is the letter of Jude.
Its author calls himself “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James.”
Many scholars think this was Jude, the half-brother of Jesus, who along with James is named in the Gospels as one of Jesus’ brothers.
If so, he was not the apostle.
The Bible does not say clearly.
The letter was written to believers who were being threatened by false teachers.
“Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.”

It ends with one of the best-known blessings in the Bible: “Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Jude’s question teaches us that it is good to ask honest questions of Jesus.
He did not pretend to understand when he did not.
He asked, and the answer has encouraged believers for 2,000 years.
The answer itself is a promise: if we love Jesus and keep His word, the Father and the Son will make their home with us.
The God of the universe does not only visit. He moves in.
The closing words of the letter of Jude are a prayer for the end of a hard day, or a hard life: that the One who is able to keep us from stumbling will present us blameless with great joy.
We are not holding on to God alone. He is holding on to us.
Who Simon the Zealot was.
Simon the Zealot is one of the twelve apostles.
He appears in all four lists of the apostles in the New Testament, but the Bible records nothing he said and no individual event.
To tell his story, we have to look at who he was, who he was following, and what the Gospels show about the world he lived in.
He is called “the Zealot” in Luke and Acts.
In Matthew and Mark he is called “the Cananaean,” which is the Aramaic word for the same idea: someone who is zealous.
Why his story matters.
Simon’s nickname tells us something surprising about the group Jesus gathered.
Jesus put together people from opposite sides of the political world.
The story of Simon is about what happens when a person with fierce loyalties meets Jesus.
A zealous man.
In the first century, Israel was ruled by Rome.
Many Jews hated the occupation.
They paid heavy taxes and saw Roman soldiers and pagan symbols in their holy land.
Some groups wanted to rebel.
The Jewish historian Josephus describes an organized party known as the Zealots who led the revolt against Rome in AD 66.
That war ended with the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in AD 70.
The Bible does not say exactly what Simon’s nickname meant.

It may mean he was part of a resistance movement before he met Jesus, or it may simply describe his burning passion for God and the law, like the Old Testament’s Phinehas and Elijah, who were called “zealous for the Lord.”
Either way, Simon was a man of strong convictions who cared about God’s honor and about his people’s freedom.
An odd team.
Among the twelve disciples was Matthew, also called Levi, a tax collector.
Tax collectors worked for Rome, collected the hated taxes and often took more than they should.
Zealots saw such men as traitors.
A Zealot and a tax collector would normally have been bitter enemies.
Jesus put them on the same team.
Simon the Zealot walked, ate and slept alongside Matthew for three years. Peter was a fisherman.
Others were brothers who fought with each other over who was greatest.
The fact that they stayed together is itself a small miracle.
It shows that Jesus’ way of uniting people did not depend on politics.
What bound them was loyalty to Him.
A different kind of king.
Like many people, Simon probably hoped that Jesus would be the king who would throw off Rome.
The disciples’ questions show this.
Even after the resurrection they asked Jesus, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?”
Jesus’ teaching went in a different direction.
“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.”
“If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.”
When Jesus was arrested in the garden, one of His disciples drew a sword and cut off a man’s ear.
Jesus told him, “Put your sword back into its place.
For all who take the sword will perish by the sword.”
To Pilate, He said, “My kingdom is not of this world.
If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting.”
The Bible does not tell us what Simon thought.
But a man who had once put his hopes in a fight would have had to rethink everything he knew about how God would save His people.
In the upper room.
When Jesus was crucified, all the disciples ran away, including Simon.
Their dream of the kingdom seemed dead.
Then Jesus rose from the dead and appeared to them.
Before He ascended, He gave them their task: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations...
And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
After the ascension, the eleven went to the upper room in Jerusalem and the Bible lists their names.
Simon the Zealot is there, on the list, together with the rest.
Then at Pentecost the Holy Spirit came on them all.
Simon, like the others, was now part of the Spirit-filled church.
His zeal was now directed toward telling people about Jesus.
What happened to Simon.
The Bible does not say what Simon did after Pentecost.
Later church traditions give several versions: that he preached in Egypt, in North Africa, in Persia, or in Britain, and that he died as a martyr.
These traditions differ, and none of them can be confirmed.
The Bible’s silence is itself part of his story.
Many faithful people served God without leaving a record.
What we do know is that Jesus knew him by name, chose him, and gave him a place among the twelve.
In the book of Revelation, the wall of the New Jerusalem has twelve foundations carrying the names of the twelve apostles. His name is there.
What does this mean for us today?.
Simon was passionate.
He was probably someone who cared deeply about justice and about his country.
Jesus did not tell him to give up his passion. He redirected it.
A zealous person has energy, and in the hands of Jesus it can become a powerful gift.
His place in the group is also a lesson.
The church is the place where people of different backgrounds, parties and opinions can stand together because Jesus is their Lord.
If a Zealot and a tax collector can share a table, the people of Jesus can learn to love each other across differences.
And the quiet pages of the Bible are a comfort.
Simon’s name is written in the list four times and nothing else about him is told.
Not everyone who follows Jesus is in the spotlight.
But every one of them is known.
Who Judas was.
Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles.
“Iscariot” most likely means “man of Kerioth,” a town in southern Judea, which would make him the only one of the twelve not from Galilee.
His father was named Simon.
Every list of the apostles places him last and adds a note: “who betrayed Him.”
Judas was not an outsider who slipped in.
He was chosen by Jesus after a night of prayer, sent out with the others to preach and heal, and trusted to keep the group’s money bag.
Why Jesus chose Judas.
This is one of the hardest questions in the Bible, and the Bible doesn’t say exactly why.
John’s Gospel says Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray Him, and Jesus once said, “Have I not chosen you, the Twelve?
Yet one of you is a devil.”
Jesus fulfilled the Scriptures, including a psalm about a close friend who shared bread and then turned against Him.
Yet Jesus treated Judas as a friend to the very end: He washed his feet, shared bread with him at the Last Supper, and even greeted him in the garden by calling him “friend.”
Judas was given every opportunity.
Chosen too.
Judas son of Simon Iscariot was chosen by Jesus as one of the twelve apostles after Jesus prayed all night on a mountain.
He traveled with Jesus for about three years.
He saw the blind receive sight and the dead raised, heard the Sermon on the Mount, and watched Jesus feed thousands.
When Jesus sent the twelve out two by two to preach that the kingdom of heaven was near, heal the sick and drive out demons, Judas was among them.
Nothing in the Gospels suggests the other disciples suspected him of anything.
In fact, the group trusted him enough to make him the treasurer, keeping the common money bag used for their needs and for giving to the poor.
A thief.
Six days before Passover, Jesus was at a dinner in Bethany with Lazarus, Martha and Mary.
Mary took a pint of pure nard, an expensive perfume imported from India, poured it on Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair.
The whole house filled with the fragrance.
Judas objected loudly: “Why wasn’t this perfume sold and the money given to the poor?
It was worth a year’s wages.” It sounded generous.
But John, who knew him well, explains: “He did not say this because he cared about the poor but because he was a thief; as keeper of the money bag, he used to help himself to what was put into it.”
Jesus defended Mary: “Leave her alone.
It was intended that she should save this perfume for the day of My burial.”
Matthew and Mark place Judas’s visit to the chief priests right after this dinner.
The deal.

The chief priests and elders had already gathered at the palace of Caiaphas, the high priest, and agreed to arrest Jesus secretly and kill Him — but not during the festival, because they feared a riot among the crowds who loved Him.
Judas solved their problem.
He went to them and asked, “What are you willing to give me if I deliver Him over to you?”
They counted out 30 pieces of silver.
Under the law of Moses, that was the payment for a slave who was killed, and the prophet Zechariah had described being valued at that same insulting price.
Luke and John both say that Satan entered Judas.
From then on, Judas watched for an opportunity to hand Jesus over when no crowd was present.
The kiss.
At the Last Supper, Jesus washed all the disciples’ feet, including Judas’s.
Then He said, deeply troubled, “One of you is going to betray Me.”
The disciples were stunned and asked, “Surely you don’t mean me, Lord?”
Jesus said it was the one to whom He would give a piece of bread dipped in the dish, and He handed it to Judas.
In that culture, offering someone a choice morsel was a gesture of honor and friendship.
Jesus told him, “What you are about to do, do quickly.” Judas went out.
John adds: “And it was night.”
Hours later, Judas led a large crowd with swords, clubs, torches and lanterns into the garden of Gethsemane — a place he knew because Jesus often met there with His disciples.
He had given them a signal: “The one I kiss is the man; arrest Him.”
A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.
Judas walked up, said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him.
Jesus answered, “Do what you came for, friend,” and in Luke, “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?”
Then the soldiers seized Him.
How it ended.
Early Friday morning, the council decided to hand Jesus over to Pilate to be executed.
When Judas saw that Jesus was condemned, Matthew says he was seized with remorse.
He brought the 30 pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders and said, “I have sinned, for I have betrayed innocent blood.”
They answered coldly, “What is that to us?
That’s your responsibility.”
Judas threw the money into the Temple and went away and hanged himself.
The priests picked up the coins but said it was against the law to put blood money into the Temple treasury.
So they used it to buy a potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners, which became known as the Field of Blood.
Acts adds more details about how his body was found in that field.
Peter later said that Judas “was one of our number and shared in our ministry,” and the apostles chose Matthias to take his place.
Why Judas matters today.
Judas is a warning that it’s possible to be very close to Jesus — to see the miracles and hear the teaching — without truly following Him.
But his story also sits beside Peter’s.
Both failed Jesus on the same night.
The difference was what they did next: Peter came back to Jesus and was restored; Judas, filled with remorse, turned away in despair.
No failure is beyond Jesus’ forgiveness for anyone who returns to Him.
Who Matthias was.
Matthias is the man chosen to take the place of Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles.

He is mentioned only in the first chapter of the book of Acts, but the story of how he was chosen gives us a window into the first days of the church, just after Jesus rose from the dead and went up into heaven.

The Bible tells us only what is needed: he had been following Jesus from the beginning, from the time John the Baptist was baptizing in the Jordan, through the whole of Jesus’ ministry until the day He ascended.
Why his story matters.
Matthias reminds us that God’s work is done by many faithful people who are not famous.
It also shows how seriously the early church took the number twelve, and what an apostle was.
The twelve.
After a night of prayer on a mountain in Galilee, Jesus called His many disciples and chose twelve of them, “whom he named apostles.”
The number twelve was important: it matched the twelve tribes of Israel.
Jesus was building a renewed people of God.
He said they would “sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”
They were to be with Him, to learn from Him, and to be sent out to preach with authority.
One of the twelve was Judas Iscariot.
He kept the money bag and later betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver.
On the night of the Last Supper he led soldiers to arrest Jesus in the garden.
Overcome with guilt, Judas returned the money, then went and hanged himself.
The chief priests used the money to buy a potter’s field, which became known as the Field of Blood.
Forty days and a promise.
Jesus rose from the dead on the third day.
For forty days He appeared to His followers, spoke about the kingdom of God and proved He was alive.
On the Mount of Olives, He told the eleven to wait in Jerusalem for the gift the Father promised, the Holy Spirit.
“You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”
Then He rose into the sky, and a cloud took Him out of their sight.
Two angels said He would come back in the same way.
The eleven went back to Jerusalem and went to the upstairs room where they were staying.
There were Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas son of James.
“All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.”
A seat to fill.
About 120 believers were gathered.
Peter stood up and explained that Judas’ betrayal and death fulfilled Scripture.
He quoted from the Psalms: “Let another take his office.”
Peter set out the qualifications.

The replacement should be “one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.”
The main job of an apostle was to be an eyewitness of the risen Jesus.
That is what made the apostles’ message credible.
The church put forward two men: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
Both had been with Jesus for three years.
Both were qualified, and the Bible gives us no more details about either.
The lot falls.

The disciples prayed: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” Then they cast lots.
Casting lots was a way of asking God to decide, used in the Old Testament, for example in dividing the promised land.
“And the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.”
It is the last time in the Bible that lots were used to find God’s will.
Soon after, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit was poured out, and from then on the church was guided by the Spirit in a more direct way.
Some people have wondered whether Peter was right to hurry and whether Paul was God’s own choice for the twelfth place. The Bible does not say.
What it shows clearly is that the church wanted to be obedient and to pray first.
What came after.
After Acts 1, Matthias is not mentioned again by name.
But he was among the apostles on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came and 3,000 people believed.
When the book of Acts says, “Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice,” the eleven now included Matthias.
And in the book of Revelation, the foundations of the walls of the New Jerusalem bear “the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.”
Early church writers, such as Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius, say that Matthias was one of the seventy disciples Jesus sent out earlier.
The Bible does not say exactly, but tradition has said that he preached in Judea and then in other regions, and was martyred for his faith.
The details are unclear and differ from one account to another.
What does this mean for us today?.
Matthias is a name most people do not know, and he did not give famous speeches or write a book of the Bible.
What the Bible says about him is that he stayed.
He was with Jesus from the beginning to the end and was ready when God had a place for him.
Much of God’s work is done by people like that, who follow faithfully and never get a headline.
The way the church chose him is a lesson in making decisions: they used Scripture, they gave clear requirements, they prayed and they waited.
In an important decision it is good to pray, look at what the Bible says and seek wise counsel.
And Judas’ empty seat is a warning and a promise.
A person can walk with Jesus for three years and still turn away.
But Jesus’ plan did not fail.
God filled the seat, and the work went on.
Who Jesus is.
Jesus of Nazareth is the center of the whole Bible.
He is the eternal Son of God, the second person of the Trinity — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — who existed before creation and through whom all things were made.
About 2,000 years ago, He became a human being, born as a baby in Bethlehem.
He did not stop being God; He added a full human nature.
That’s why the Bible calls Him both “Son of God” and “Son of Man.”
He lived about 33 years in Roman-occupied Israel.
He spent most of them in Nazareth, a small village in Galilee, working as a craftsman like His legal father Joseph.

Around age 30 He began a public ministry of teaching, healing and calling disciples that lasted about three years, ending with His death by crucifixion in Jerusalem under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, His resurrection three days later, and His ascension into heaven.

Besides the four Gospels, Jesus is mentioned by ancient non-Christian writers, including the Jewish historian Josephus and the Roman historian Tacitus, who records that “Christus” was executed by Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius.
What the Old Testament promised.
For centuries before Jesus was born, the prophets described someone God would send.

He would be a descendant of Abraham through whom all nations would be blessed, a son of King David whose kingdom would last forever, a prophet like Moses, born in Bethlehem, coming to Jerusalem riding on a donkey, suffering and being “pierced for our transgressions,” and not being abandoned to the grave.
Jesus told His disciples after His resurrection that everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled.
The Word became flesh.
John’s Gospel opens: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.”
He is fully God and fully man — not half of each.
He was born a real baby, grew up, got hungry and tired, wept, and died a real death.
His name, Yeshua in Hebrew, means “the Lord saves.”
“Christ” is not a last name but a title — the Greek for Messiah, “the anointed one,” the King God had promised for centuries.
Born in Bethlehem.

A Roman census forced Joseph and Mary to travel about 90 miles from Nazareth to Bethlehem, Joseph’s ancestral town — fulfilling the prophet Micah, who said the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem.
There was no space in the guest room, so the newborn was laid in a feeding trough.
That night an angel appeared to shepherds outside town: “Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you; He is the Messiah, the Lord.”
A crowd of angels filled the sky praising God.
The shepherds hurried to find the baby and spread the news.
Wise men and a wicked king.
Magi — scholars who studied the stars — arrived in Jerusalem asking where the newborn King of the Jews was.
King Herod, paranoid about rivals, pretended he wanted to worship too.
The star led the Magi to the house in Bethlehem, where they gave gold, frankincense and myrrh.
Warned in a dream, they went home another way.
An angel warned Joseph to flee to Egypt.
Herod then ordered every boy two years old and under in Bethlehem killed.
After Herod died, the family returned and settled in Nazareth.
Twelve years old in the Temple.
It’s the only story we have of Jesus’ childhood.
His family traveled in a big group of relatives for Passover, so Mary and Joseph went a whole day before realizing He wasn’t with them.
After three days of searching they found Him sitting with the teachers, listening and asking questions.
Mary said, “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.”
He answered, “Didn’t you know I had to be in My Father’s house?”
Then He went home and obeyed them, and grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and people.
He worked as a carpenter until about age 30.
Baptized and tested.
As He came up out of the Jordan, the Spirit came down like a dove and the Father’s voice spoke — Father, Son and Spirit all present.
Then the Spirit led Him into the desert.
After 40 days without food, Satan tempted Him three times: turn stones into bread, jump from the Temple to prove God would catch Him, and bow down to get all the kingdoms of the world.
Each time Jesus answered with Scripture: “Man shall not live on bread alone,”
“Do not put the Lord your God to the test,”
“Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.”
Where Adam failed in a garden, Jesus held firm in a wilderness.
Water into wine.
When the wine ran out, Mary told Jesus, then told the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.”
He had them fill six stone jars used for ritual washing — each holding 20 to 30 gallons — with water.
When the master of the banquet tasted it, it was wine, and better than what had been served first.
John calls it the first of His signs, revealing His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.
Calling the twelve.
He called Peter, Andrew, James and John from their boats and Matthew from his tax booth.
He chose twelve — matching the twelve tribes of Israel — to be with Him, to preach and to drive out demons.
They were mostly ordinary, uneducated working men.
He trained them for about three years by living with them.
The Sermon on the Mount.
“Blessed are the poor in spirit… blessed are those who mourn… blessed are the meek… blessed are the peacemakers.”
He taught that anger is like murder in the heart and lust is like adultery.
Instead of revenge: turn the other cheek.
Pray for those who persecute you.
Don’t worry about tomorrow — look at the birds; your Father feeds them.
Do to others what you want them to do to you.
He ended with the wise man who built his house on the rock.
The crowds were amazed, because He taught as one with authority.
Healing the hurting.
He touched a man with leprosy — something no one did — and he was clean.
Four friends lowered a paralyzed man through a roof, and Jesus first said, “Your sins are forgiven,” then told him to walk.
A woman bleeding for twelve years touched His cloak and was healed.
He opened blind eyes and deaf ears.
He raised Jairus’s daughter, a widow’s only son at Nain, and His friend Lazarus after four days in the tomb.
The miracles showed His power and His compassion — and pointed to who He is.
Lord of the storm.
Jesus was asleep on a cushion in the back of the boat while it filled with water.
The terrified disciples woke Him: “Teacher, don’t You care if we drown?”
He got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a dead calm.
Then He asked, “Why are you so afraid?
Do you still have no faith?”
They were more terrified than before: “Who is this?
Even the wind and the waves obey Him!”
On another night He walked across the lake to them.
Feeding the 5,000.
The count was 5,000 men, besides women and children.
He had them sit on the green grass in groups, gave thanks, broke the bread and kept giving it to the disciples to hand out.
The next day He told the crowd, “I am the bread of life.
Whoever comes to Me will never go hungry.”
Many followers found that teaching too hard and left.
Jesus asked the twelve, “Do you want to leave too?”
Peter answered, “Lord, to whom would we go?
You have the words of eternal life.”
Stories that stick.
A parable is a short, everyday story with a deeper point.
When a lawyer asked “Who is my neighbor?”, Jesus told about a Samaritan — a despised outsider — who stopped to help a beaten man that religious leaders walked past.
He told about a shepherd who leaves 99 sheep to find one, and a father who runs to welcome home a son who wasted everything.
The kingdom of God, He said, is like a tiny mustard seed that grows into a tree, or like treasure hidden in a field worth selling everything for.
Friend of sinners.
He went to Zacchaeus’s house, let a sinful woman wash His feet with her tears, and said to a woman dragged before Him for adultery, “Neither do I condemn you. Go and sin no more.”
When disciples shooed children away, He said, “Let the little children come to Me.”
His critics called Him “a friend of tax collectors and sinners.”
He said, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
Who do you say I am?.
Jesus made claims no ordinary teacher would make: “I am the light of the world,”
“I am the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep,”
“I am the resurrection and the life,”
“Before Abraham was, I am” — using God’s own name.
He forgave sins, which only God can do.
Three times He predicted His death and resurrection.
The disciples didn’t understand.
Palm Sunday.
The prophet Zechariah had said Israel’s king would come “humble and riding on a donkey.”
Crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road.
Days later He overturned the tables of merchants and money changers in the Temple courts: “My house will be called a house of prayer, but you are making it a den of robbers.”
The chief priests began looking for a way to kill Him, but were afraid of the crowds.
The Last Supper.
He took bread: “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”
He took the cup: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, poured out for you.”
He gave them a new command: “Love one another as I have loved you.”
He promised to send the Holy Spirit and prayed for them and for all who would believe through them.
Gethsemane.
He was so distressed His sweat was like drops of blood.
Three times He found the disciples sleeping.
Judas identified Him with a kiss.
Peter swung a sword; Jesus healed the wounded servant and let Himself be arrested. All the disciples fled.
On trial.
False witnesses contradicted each other.
The high priest finally asked, “Are You the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?”
Jesus said, “I am,” and they condemned Him for blasphemy.
Since only Rome could execute, they took Him to Pilate, accusing Him of claiming to be a king.
Pilate said, “I find no basis for a charge.”
The crowd demanded the release of Barabbas, a murderer, instead, and shouted, “Crucify Him!”
Pilate had Jesus flogged, soldiers crowned Him with thorns, and Pilate handed Him over.
The cross.
Around nine in the morning they nailed Him to a cross on Golgotha.
Above Him was a sign: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.”
He prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
He promised a dying thief, “Today you will be with Me in paradise.”
Darkness covered the land from noon until three.
He cried, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” then, “It is finished,” and “Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit.”
The Temple curtain tore from top to bottom.
Isaiah had written: “He was pierced for our transgressions… by His wounds we are healed.”
He is risen.
Women came at dawn with spices and found the stone rolled away.
Angels said, “Why do you look for the living among the dead?
He is not here; He has risen!”
He appeared to Mary Magdalene in the garden, to two disciples walking to Emmaus, to the apostles behind locked doors, to Thomas, and to seven of them by the lake.
He ate with them and showed them His wounds.
Paul, writing about 25 years later, lists the witnesses — including over 500 at once, most of them still alive to be asked.
Ascended — and coming back.
“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.
Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit… and surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”
Then He was taken up before their eyes, and two angels said, “This same Jesus will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”
Ten days later the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost, and the church began.
Why Jesus came.
Jesus said, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,” and “to give His life as a ransom for many.”

The Bible teaches that every person has sinned and is separated from God, and that Jesus, who never sinned, died in our place and rose again so that anyone who trusts in Him is forgiven and receives eternal life.
“For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that whoever believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.”
Why Jesus matters today.
Jesus is not only a figure from history.
He is risen and alive, and He promised to return.
He invites everyone, as He invited Peter and Matthew: “Follow Me.”
He also said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.”
Who Mary was.
Mary was the mother of Jesus.
She was a young woman from Nazareth, a small village in Galilee, and she was engaged to a carpenter named Joseph, a descendant of King David.
The Bible does not give her age.
Most scholars think she was a teenager, as was usual for engagements at the time.
Luke says she was a relative of Elizabeth, who was married to a priest named Zechariah.
Nothing in the Bible says she was rich or famous.
She was an ordinary girl in an out-of-the-way village.
That is the point of her story: God chose someone no one would have noticed.
Why her story matters.
Mary’s “yes” to God, in the face of danger and gossip, is one of the great acts of faith in the Bible.
She is also the only person who is present at both the birth and the death of Jesus.
The angel Gabriel.
In the sixth month of Elizabeth’s pregnancy, God sent the angel Gabriel to Nazareth.
He said, “Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!”
Mary “was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.”
Gabriel said, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.
And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.
He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High.
And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”
Mary asked a plain question: “How will this be, since I am a virgin?”
Gabriel answered, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God.”
He added that Elizabeth, who was old, was also pregnant: “For nothing will be impossible with God.”
Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.”
She knew it could cost her everything.
An unmarried pregnant woman could be shamed or even stoned. She said yes anyway.
Joseph’s dream and Elizabeth’s house.
Mary went quickly to the hill country of Judea to visit Elizabeth.
When she greeted her, the baby in Elizabeth’s womb, the future John the Baptist, leaped.
Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cried out, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!
And why is this granted me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?...
Blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.”
Mary answered with a song, called the Magnificat: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant...
He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.”
She stayed about three months and then went home.
Back in Nazareth, Joseph learned that she was pregnant.
He was a righteous man and did not want to shame her publicly, so he planned to divorce her quietly.
Then an angel appeared to him in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.”
He woke up and did as the angel said.
Bethlehem and the shepherds.
The Roman emperor Augustus ordered a census, so Joseph and Mary, who was very pregnant, traveled about ninety miles from Nazareth to Bethlehem, Joseph’s ancestral town.
“And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth.
And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.”
That night, an angel appeared to shepherds in the fields: “Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people.
For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.”
The shepherds hurried to Bethlehem and found Mary, Joseph and the baby lying in a manger.
They told everyone what the angels had said.
“But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.”
She would keep doing that for the rest of her life.
Simeon’s warning, the wise men and Egypt.
Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the Temple in Jerusalem to be presented to the Lord.
They offered two young pigeons, the offering of the poor.
An old man named Simeon, who had been promised that he would see the Messiah before he died, took the baby in his arms and praised God.

Then he said to Mary, “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.”
An elderly prophetess named Anna also gave thanks.
Later, wise men from the East came to Jerusalem looking for the king of the Jews.
They found the child in a house with Mary his mother, bowed down and gave Him gold, frankincense and myrrh.
King Herod wanted to kill the child.
An angel warned Joseph in a dream, and they fled to Egypt that night.
They stayed until Herod died, then settled in Nazareth.
The boy in the Temple and the wedding at Cana.
When Jesus was twelve, the family went to Jerusalem for Passover.
On the way home, they discovered He was not with the group.
They searched for three days and found Him in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions.
Mary said, “Son, why have you treated us so?
Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.”
Jesus said, “Why were you looking for me?
Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?” They did not understand.
He went home with them and “was submissive to them.
And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart.”
At the beginning of His public ministry, Mary was at a wedding at Cana.
The wine ran out, which was a serious embarrassment for the hosts.
Mary told Jesus, “They have no wine.”
He answered, “Woman, what does this have to do with me?
My hour has not yet come.”
Mary turned to the servants: “Do whatever he tells you.”
Jesus had them fill six stone jars with water, and it became wine.
These are the last recorded words of Mary in the Gospels.
They are the best advice she could give.
At the cross and in the upper room.
Mary is mentioned a few times during Jesus’ ministry, and once when she and His brothers came to find Him and He said that those who do the will of God are His family.
Then she appears at the cross.
“Standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.”
The sword that Simeon had spoken about had arrived.
Even in His last hours, Jesus took care of her.

“When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, ‘Woman, behold, your son!’ Then he said to the disciple, ‘Behold, your mother!’ And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.”
After the resurrection and ascension, Acts 1 says the apostles were “devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.”
It is the last time the Bible mentions her.
The Bible does not say how or when she died.
She began as a young girl who said yes, and she ended up among the first believers praying in Jerusalem.
What does this mean for us today?.
Mary shows us what faith looks like.
She did not understand everything, and she asked honest questions.
But when God’s will became clear, she said, “Let it be to me according to your word.”
She trusted God with her reputation, her plans and her future.
She also shows us what faithful presence looks like.
She was at the manger, at Cana, at the cross and in the upper room.
She kept watching, listening and treasuring.
Following Jesus is not only a moment of decision but a lifetime of staying close to Him.
And her last words in the Gospels are a command we can all take to heart: “Do whatever he tells you.”
That is still the simplest summary of what it means to be a disciple.
Who Joseph was.
Joseph was a craftsman, or tekton in Greek, a word that can mean carpenter, builder or stonemason.
He lived in Nazareth, a small village in Galilee.
He was a descendant of King David through a family line that had once ruled in Jerusalem but was now living in modest circumstances.
Matthew’s Gospel calls him “a just man,” someone who cared about doing right.
He was engaged to Mary, a young woman of Nazareth.
A Jewish engagement was a legal commitment, usually lasting a year, before the husband took his wife home.
Why his story matters.
Joseph never speaks a word in the Bible.
But he was chosen to be the earthly father of the Son of God, and he protected Jesus and Mary through scandal, danger and exile.
His quiet obedience is a model of faith.
A hard discovery.
Joseph found out that Mary was expecting a child, and he knew he was not the father.
In that world, it was a grave matter.
The law allowed him to publicly shame her, and in some cases, much worse.
But the Bible says, “Joseph, her husband, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly.”
Think about the pain.
He had to believe that the woman he loved had been unfaithful, or else believe an astonishing story. He chose mercy.

Before he could act, he went to sleep, and an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.
She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”
The name Jesus means “the Lord saves.”
Obedience and Bethlehem.
“When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife.”
He chose to accept the scandal and the gossip of a small town.
That meant standing next to Mary in public.
Months later, the Roman emperor Augustus ordered a census.
Everyone had to register in their ancestral town.
For Joseph, a descendant of David, that meant Bethlehem, about 90 miles south of Nazareth.
Mary, who was about to give birth, went with him.
The town was crowded, and there was no place for them in the guest room.
Jesus was born in Bethlehem, in humble surroundings, and laid in a manger, a feeding trough.
Joseph gave Him the name Jesus on the eighth day, as the angel had said.
Shepherds came with news of angels, and Joseph listened to their story with Mary.
At the Temple.
According to the law of Moses, a mother was to present an offering after the birth of a child.
A lamb was the normal offering, but the poor could offer two doves or pigeons.
Joseph and Mary brought two birds, a sign that they did not have much.
At the Temple, an old man named Simeon, who had been promised he would see the Messiah, took Jesus in his arms and thanked God.
“My eyes have seen your salvation.”
He told Mary that a sword would pierce her own soul.
An elderly prophetess named Anna also thanked God and told everyone who was waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
“And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.” Joseph was amazed, too.
He was raising a child who was going to change the world.
Flight to Egypt.
Wise men from the East came to Jerusalem looking for the king of the Jews, and Herod heard of it.
Herod decided to kill the child.

“An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, ‘Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him.’ And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt.”
Notice that Joseph did not argue or ask for time.
He got up in the middle of the night.
They left behind home, work and family to live as refugees in a foreign country.
The wise men’s gold may have helped provide for the family.
They stayed until Herod died.
Then an angel appeared again: “Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel.”
Learning that Herod’s son Archelaus was ruling Judea, Joseph was afraid, and a dream directed him to the region of Galilee.
“And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth.”
A father at home.
In Nazareth, Joseph worked as a craftsman, and Jesus learned the trade.
Later, people in Nazareth said of Jesus, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?”
Joseph also saw to Jesus’ religious upbringing.
“Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover.”
Luke says that Jesus “grew and became strong, filled with wisdom.
And the favor of God was upon him.”
When Jesus was twelve, the family went to Jerusalem for Passover.
On the way back, they could not find Him.
After three days of searching, they found Him in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, asking and listening.
Mary said, “Son, why have you treated us so?
Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.”
“Why were you looking for me?
Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?”
Even so, “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them.”
This is the last scene in the Bible where Joseph appears.
He is not mentioned during Jesus’ ministry.
The Bible does not say exactly what happened to him, but because Jesus entrusted His mother to John at the cross, it seems likely that Joseph had died by then.
What does this mean for us today?.
Joseph never says a word in the Bible, but his actions say a great deal.
He chose mercy when he could have chosen shame.
He obeyed immediately each time God spoke.
He protected a child who was not biologically his.
He taught Jesus a trade and took Him to the Temple.
His story reminds us that God often works through quiet, ordinary faithfulness.
There were no crowds cheering for Joseph.
Most of what he did was daily work, being a husband and father, and doing it faithfully.
And he shows what fatherhood can look like.
The Bible says that Jesus was “submissive” to Joseph and Mary and grew in wisdom.
A father or any caregiver who is present, protects and teaches shapes a life.
Joseph’s name does not appear in a long speech, but the world has not forgotten him.
Who John the Baptist was.
John was the son of a priest named Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, a relative of Mary, the mother of Jesus.
He was born about six months before Jesus, in the hill country of Judea.
His parents were old and had never been able to have children.
The angel Gabriel announced his birth to Zechariah in the Temple in Jerusalem and said that John would be “great before the Lord” and “filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb.”
Zechariah did not believe the angel and was struck mute until the baby was born.
When John was eight days old and people expected the family name, Elizabeth said, “No; he shall be called John.”
Zechariah wrote, “His name is John,” and his tongue was loosed.
He praised God and prophesied that his son would be “the prophet of the Most High” and would “go before the Lord to prepare his ways.”
Why his story matters.
John is the last of the Old Testament-style prophets and the first witness to Jesus.
Jesus said, “Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist.”
His life shows what it means to point away from yourself and toward Jesus.
A voice in the wilderness.
The Bible tells us almost nothing about John’s childhood, except that he “grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.”
He appeared around AD 26, in the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius.
“Now John wore a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.”
It was the dress of the prophet Elijah.
He preached near the Jordan River: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
The prophet Isaiah had foretold him: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’”
People came from Jerusalem and all Judea and were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. John was blunt.
He told the religious leaders, “You brood of vipers!
Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bear fruit in keeping with repentance.”
What should we do?.
People asked, “What then shall we do?”
John said, “Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.”
Tax collectors asked what they should do: “Collect no more than you are authorized to do.”
Soldiers asked, “And we, what shall we do?”
“Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.”
He did not tell them to leave their jobs and live in the desert.
He told them to be honest and generous right where they were.
People wondered whether John himself was the Messiah.
He said, “I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.
He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”
He did not take any of the credit.
Baptizing Jesus.
One day Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. John tried to stop Him.
“I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?”
Jesus said, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”
When He came up out of the water, the heavens opened.
The Spirit of God descended like a dove and rested on Him, and a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
The next day, John saw Jesus walking toward him and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
Two of John’s disciples, Andrew and probably John the apostle, heard him and followed Jesus.
John did not hold them back.
As more people started going to Jesus, John’s disciples complained.
He said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.”
John described himself as the friend of the bridegroom, happy just to hear the groom’s voice.
Prison and doubt.
Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, had married Herodias, the wife of his own brother Philip.
John told him publicly, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” Herodias hated John.
Herod arrested him and put him in prison, according to the historian Josephus in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea.
Herod liked to listen to John, but his wife wanted him dead.
In prison, John heard about the things Jesus was doing.
He had expected a Messiah who would judge and set things right, but Jesus was healing and teaching, and John was in a cell.
He sent two disciples to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”

Jesus said, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them.
And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.”
Jesus did not scold John for doubting.
After the messengers left, He praised John in front of the crowd: “Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist.”
The death of John.
On Herod’s birthday, he held a banquet for his nobles and officers.

Herodias’ daughter danced for the guests, and Herod was so pleased that he promised, with an oath, to give her whatever she asked, up to half of his kingdom. She went to her mother. “What should I ask?”
“The head of John the Baptist.”
She went back and said, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.”
“And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.”
He sent an executioner, who beheaded John in the prison and brought his head on a platter to the girl, who gave it to her mother.
John’s disciples came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
Then they went and told Jesus.
Jesus withdrew to a quiet place by Himself.
John died young, probably in his early thirties, having fulfilled the work for which he was sent: he had prepared the way.
What does this mean for us today?.
John’s whole life was pointing to someone else.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
In a world that wants us to be the center of attention, John shows what it looks like to find joy in pointing people to Jesus.
He also shows courage.
He told the truth to ordinary people and to the king, and it cost him his life.
He did not have to be popular to be faithful.
And the story of his doubts is a comfort.
The greatest of the prophets had questions when he was in prison.
Jesus did not condemn him but gave him evidence and encouragement.
If you have doubts in a dark time, bring them to Jesus.
He knows how to answer honestly and gently.
Who Mary Magdalene was.
Mary Magdalene was a follower of Jesus from a town called Magdala, on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee.
She is named in the Gospels more than most of the other women who traveled with Jesus.
She is also named in every list of the women at the cross and the tomb, always near the front.
The Bible says that Jesus had driven seven demons out of her.
Luke says she and other women supported Jesus and the twelve “out of their means.”
That suggests she had some money and was willing to give it to Jesus’ work.
What the Bible does not say.
Many people think Mary Magdalene was a prostitute.
The Bible never says that.
That idea came from a sermon by Pope Gregory in the sixth century, which mixed her up with an unnamed sinful woman in another story.
The Bible’s own picture of her is a woman who was set free from a terrible oppression and followed Jesus faithfully, even to the cross and the tomb.
Set free.
Luke writes that Jesus went through cities and villages, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God.

“And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.”
The Bible does not describe how Jesus freed her.
But it says seven demons, a number that suggests severe suffering.
Whatever it was, her life was changed.
From that point, she was part of Jesus’ circle, traveling with Him and the twelve, helping to support the work.
She was one of several women, from different backgrounds, who were among the disciples, a remarkable thing in that time.
At the cross.
When Jesus was crucified, most of His male disciples were nowhere to be found.
But the Gospels say that several women stayed.
“Standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.”
They watched from a distance as He died, with other women who had followed from Galilee.
Roman crucifixion was horrible, and spectators could be arrested for being associated with the condemned. They stayed anyway.
After He died, Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus took His body down and laid it in a tomb.
“Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.”
The women watched so they would know where to return after the Sabbath to anoint His body properly.
The empty tomb.
“Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.”
She did not wait to see more.
She ran to Simon Peter and John and said, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”
Peter and John ran to the tomb.
John arrived first, looked in and saw the linen cloths.
Peter went in and saw the cloths lying there and the face cloth folded up by itself.
John then went in, “and he saw and believed.”
The two disciples went home.
Mary stayed outside the tomb weeping.
She did not know yet what had happened.
All she knew was that the body of the Lord she loved was gone.
“Mary”.
As she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb.
Two angels in white sat where Jesus’ body had been.
“Woman, why are you weeping?”
“Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”
Then she turned and saw a man standing there, but did not realize it was Jesus.
“Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?”
Thinking He was the gardener, she said, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus said, “Mary.” That was all.
“She turned and said to him in Aramaic, ‘Rabboni!’ (which means Teacher).”
The way He said her name was enough.
She had followed Him for years, and now He was alive.

She reached out for Him, and Jesus told her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”
The first witness.
“Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord’ — and that he had said these things to her.”
She was the first person to see the risen Jesus and the first to tell others.
In the first century, a woman’s testimony was not given much weight in a court.
Yet God chose to make a woman the first witness of the central event of history.
Mark’s Gospel confirms that Jesus “appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.”
Early Christian writers later called her “the apostle to the apostles,” since she was the one sent to tell the apostles.
The Gospels say that at first, the men did not believe her story.
“These words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.”
They believed only when Jesus appeared to them Himself.
The Bible does not tell us more about Mary’s later life.
But Jesus knew her by name, and she was there at the most important moment in history.
What does this mean for us today?.
Mary Magdalene’s story is about what Jesus does for a person who is broken.
She was a woman who had been tormented and Jesus gave her a new life.
Her response was loyal, grateful and costly.
Whatever might be tormenting you, the Bible shows that Jesus is stronger than it.
She also teaches us what faithfulness looks like.
She stayed at the cross when it was dangerous and went to the tomb when it seemed too late.
People who keep showing up, in love, are often the first to see what God is doing.
And the story shows how Jesus knows His people.
He did not announce Himself by a title.
He said her name, and she knew.
Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd... he calls his own sheep by name.” He knows your name, too.
Who Martha and Mary were.
Martha and Mary were sisters who lived in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, with their brother Lazarus.
Jesus was a close friend of the family and stayed with them when He was in the area.
The Gospel of John says, “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.”
The two sisters had very different personalities.
Martha was a hard-working organizer and host.
Mary was a quiet listener, someone who wanted to be close to Jesus.
The Gospels show them three times.
Why their story matters.
These two sisters show that there is more than one way to love Jesus, and that He values both service and listening.
They also show what faith looks like when it is tested by grief.
A busy house.
Luke tells that Jesus and His disciples were traveling and “a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house.”
The Bible says her sister Mary “sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his teaching.”
To sit at a rabbi’s feet was to be his student, a place usually given to men.
Jesus welcomed Mary there.
Martha was “distracted with much serving.”
There were probably thirteen or more guests to feed. She became frustrated.
She came to Jesus and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?
Tell her then to help me.”
She was not wrong to want help.
She was also criticizing both her sister and the Lord, whom she thought wasn’t paying attention.
“One thing is necessary”.
Jesus did not scold her.
He said her name twice, gently: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary.
Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”
Jesus was not saying that serving is bad.
Hospitality was important, and Jesus Himself fed people and washed feet.
He was pointing out that Martha had let her work push out the one thing that mattered most: being with Him.
Her problem was not the work but the worry.
And He also defended Mary’s choice to sit and listen, which was an unusual one for a woman of her time.
He was telling Martha that He did not need a big meal. He wanted her.
Martha’s confession.
Some time later, their brother Lazarus fell ill and died.
By the time Jesus arrived, he had been in the tomb four days.
Martha heard that Jesus was coming and went out to meet Him, while Mary stayed in the house.
She said, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”
Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life.
Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”
Martha answered with one of the greatest statements of faith in the Gospels: “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”
That is the same confession Peter made.
The practical, busy sister was also a woman of deep faith.
Then she went to call Mary quietly: “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”
Mary at His feet again.
Mary got up quickly and went to Jesus.
She fell at His feet, as she had done before, and said exactly what Martha had said: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
Her tears moved Jesus deeply. “Jesus wept.”
He went to the tomb, had the stone taken away and called, “Lazarus, come out!”
Lazarus came out, still wrapped in grave clothes.
Both sisters, with different temperaments, had the same grief and the same faith.
Each in her own way had brought her pain to Jesus.
And both of them saw the glory of God.
The same Jesus who said, “One thing is necessary,” gave them back their brother.
Dinner at Bethany.
Six days before Passover, Jesus came back to Bethany.
A dinner was held in His honor.
“Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.”
It is worth noticing: Martha is serving again, but there is no complaint this time.
She had learned to serve with peace.
Mary took a pound of expensive perfume made of pure nard, poured it on Jesus’ feet and wiped them with her hair.
The house was filled with the fragrance.
It was worth about a year’s wages.
Judas objected: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”
John adds that Judas did not care about the poor but was a thief.
Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.
For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”
Mary seems to have understood what the disciples did not: that Jesus was going to die.
Her act of love was remembered.
Another Gospel says, “Wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.”
What does this mean for us today?.
It is easy to see ourselves as Martha, busy with serving and worried about many things.
Jesus’ gentle words, “Martha, Martha,” are for everyone who feels too busy to rest at His feet.
The Bible is not saying that work does not matter.
It is saying that being with Jesus matters most, and that our work flows from it.
But Martha is also a model.
She was honest with Jesus.
When she was upset, she told Him.
When her brother died, she ran to Him.
And she gave one of the clearest statements of faith in the Bible.
Mary shows that love is often costly.
She poured out something precious without counting the cost.
Between them, the sisters show that Jesus welcomes both the doers and the listeners.
At the dinner in Bethany, Martha served with joy and Mary worshiped with love, and Jesus was pleased with both.
Who Lazarus was.
Lazarus lived in Bethany, a village about two miles east of Jerusalem on the road over the Mount of Olives.
He had two sisters, Martha and Mary.
Their home was a place Jesus often visited.
The Gospel of John says, “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.”
The sisters later called him “he whom you love.”
Lazarus himself never says a word in the Bible.
But what happened to him is one of the greatest miracles Jesus performed, and the event that pushed the leaders to decide to kill Jesus.
Why his story matters.
The raising of Lazarus is the last and greatest sign in John’s Gospel before the cross.
It shows who Jesus is, what He does with grief, and how He answers death itself.
“He whom you love is ill”.
When Lazarus became seriously ill, Martha and Mary sent a message to Jesus, who was across the Jordan, about a day’s journey away: “Lord, he whom you love is ill.”
They did not ask Him to come.
They trusted that He would know.
Jesus said, “This illness does not lead to death.
It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”
Then, surprisingly, “when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.”
John says plainly that Jesus loved them.
The delay was not because He did not care.
Then Jesus told His disciples, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.”
They thought He meant natural sleep.
“Lazarus has died, and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe.”
The disciples knew that Judea was dangerous since the leaders wanted to stone Jesus.
Thomas said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”
Martha and Mary.
When Jesus reached Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days.
Many people from Jerusalem had come to comfort the sisters.
Martha went out to meet Jesus.
“Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”
Jesus said, “Your brother will rise again.”
Martha: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”
Then Jesus said one of the great statements of the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life.
Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”
Martha answered, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”
She went and quietly called Mary, who came and fell at Jesus’ feet.
She said the same words: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
Jesus wept.
“When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.
And he said, ‘Where have you laid him?’ They said to him, ‘Lord, come and see.’ Jesus wept.”
It is the shortest verse in many English Bibles, and one of the most important.
Jesus knew in a few minutes He would raise Lazarus. Yet He wept.
He was not weeping because He had no hope, but because death is truly sorrowful, and because He loved His friends.
The people said, “See how he loved him!”
Some said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?”
The Son of God does not stand at a distance from our grief. He enters it.
“Lazarus, come out”.
The tomb was a cave with a stone across the opening.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.”
Martha, practical as ever, said, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”
Jesus answered, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”
They took away the stone.
Jesus looked up and prayed: “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.
I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”
Then He shouted, “Lazarus, come out!”
“The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth.
Jesus said to them, ‘Unbind him, and let him go.’”
Many of the Jews who had come to Mary believed in Him.
The plot.
Some of those who saw it reported to the Pharisees what Jesus had done.
The chief priests and Pharisees called a meeting of the council. “What are we to do?
For this man performs many signs.
If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”
Caiaphas, the high priest, said, “It is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”
John comments that Caiaphas was speaking more truly than he knew.
“So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.”
Six days before Passover, Jesus came back to Bethany.
They gave a dinner, with Martha serving and Lazarus reclining at the table with Jesus.
Mary took a pound of very expensive perfume and anointed Jesus’ feet, wiping them with her hair.
Large crowds came to see Jesus and also Lazarus.
“So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going over and believing in Jesus.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Lazarus’ story is for anyone who has prayed and not gotten the answer they wanted on the timetable they wanted.
Jesus stayed two days longer, and Martha and Mary were hurt. But He was not late.
He was working toward something greater than healing: raising a man who had been dead four days.
It also tells us what Jesus does with grief. He does not scold. He weeps.
If you are grieving, the Bible says Jesus knows what that is.
And it points to the greatest promise.
Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life.”
Lazarus’ rising was a sign of what Jesus would do Himself a few weeks later and what He will do for all who believe in Him.
Death is not the last word.
Who Nicodemus was.
Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council of seventy-one men.
He was one of the most respected religious men in Jerusalem.
Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel.” He lived about AD 30.
The Pharisees were known for their devotion to the law of Moses and its traditions.
Most of the Pharisees opposed Jesus, because He challenged their authority.
But Nicodemus was different.
He was curious and honest, and he kept returning.
Why his story matters.
Nicodemus appears three times in the Gospel of John, and each time we see a little more of his journey.
His story is about someone moving slowly from curiosity to faith, and how Jesus meets people where they are.
A visit at night.
Early in His ministry, Jesus came to Jerusalem for the Passover and cleared the merchants out of the Temple.
He also did signs that amazed people.
One night, Nicodemus came to see Him.
Perhaps he came at night so that no one would see him, or so they could talk without crowds.
John’s Gospel often uses night and day to mean spiritual darkness and light.
He started politely: “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.” Notice the “we.”
Other leaders had noticed too.
But Jesus skipped the small talk and went straight to the heart: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
Born again.
The Greek word for “again” can also mean “from above.”
Nicodemus took it literally: “How can a man be born when he is old?
Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”
Jesus explained: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.”
He used the wind as a picture: “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.
So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”
You cannot control it or explain it fully, but you can see what it does.
Nicodemus, the great teacher, was confused.
“How can these things be?”
Jesus said, “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?”
The snake and the most famous verse.
Jesus reminded Nicodemus of a story from the wilderness.
When the Israelites were bitten by poisonous snakes, Moses lifted up a bronze snake on a pole, and anyone who looked at it lived.
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.”
It was a hint of the cross.
Then comes what is probably the best-known verse in the Bible: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.
For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.”
The Bible does not tell us how Nicodemus responded that night.
The conversation just ends. But it was a seed.
Speaking up.
About two years later, at the Feast of Booths, many people were saying Jesus was the Prophet or the Christ.
The Pharisees sent officers to arrest Him, but they returned empty-handed.
“No one ever spoke like this man!”
The Pharisees were angry: “Have any of the authorities or of the Pharisees believed in him?
But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.”
Nicodemus spoke up, the first time he did so in public.
“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”
It was a cautious statement, based on the law, and not a confession of faith.
The others mocked him: “Are you from Galilee too?
Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”
Nicodemus said no more, but he had taken a stand.
At the cross.
Jesus was crucified on the day before the Sabbath of Passover week.
By evening, His body had to be taken down.
His disciples were gone, hiding.
Then two members of the Sanhedrin came forward.
One was Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, who asked Pilate for the body. The other was Nicodemus.
“Nicodemus, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.”
It was an enormous amount, the kind of burial spices fit for a king.
Together they took Jesus’ body, wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices, “as is the burial custom of the Jews,” and laid it in a new tomb in a garden, where no one had been laid.
It was a costly act.
These two men risked their positions, reputations and safety at the very moment when the disciples were hiding.
Nicodemus had come to Jesus at night and now at last stood in the light.
What does this mean for us today?.
Nicodemus shows that faith often grows slowly.
He came with questions at night, spoke up carefully, and finally acted at the cross.
Jesus did not turn him away at any stage.
If you are somewhere between curiosity and commitment, you are in good company.
His conversation with Jesus also gives us the heart of the Gospel.
We cannot earn our way into the kingdom, even if we are as respectable as Nicodemus.
We must be born again, from above, by the Spirit.
And the reason Jesus came was not to condemn but because God loved the world.
The last picture of him is a good one: a man who once hid in the dark, carrying seventy-five pounds of spices through the streets of Jerusalem in broad daylight to honor Jesus.
It is never too late to step forward.
Who Zacchaeus was.
Zacchaeus lived in Jericho, a busy trading city in the Jordan Valley, about 15 miles northeast of Jerusalem.
He was a chief tax collector, which means he supervised other tax collectors and was very rich.
He lived in the time of Jesus, about AD 30.
Jewish tax collectors worked for the Roman occupation.
They paid the Romans a set amount and kept whatever they could collect beyond that. Many cheated.
People hated them as traitors and thieves.
Zacchaeus, the boss of the local tax collectors in a rich trading town, was probably one of the most disliked men in Jericho.
Why his story matters.
Zacchaeus’ story is one of the best-loved in the Gospels.
It shows Jesus seeking out someone whom everyone else had written off, and what real change looks like.
A short man in a tree.
Jesus was passing through Jericho on His final journey to Jerusalem.
Just before, He had healed a blind beggar at the city gate, and crowds were thick along the road.
Zacchaeus “was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small of stature.”
He could have given up.
Or he could have sent a servant.
Instead, a rich official in a long robe ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree, a tree with low, wide branches.
It was an undignified thing for a grown man in his position to do.
He was curious, and perhaps lonely, and he was willing to look foolish to see Jesus.
Something in him was hungry.
“I must stay at your house”.
When Jesus came to that spot, He stopped and looked up.
“Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” Jesus knew his name.
He chose the least popular man in town.
He did not ask permission, and He did not say He would come after Zacchaeus changed.
He said, “I must stay,” as though it were a part of God’s plan.
“So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.” The crowd was upset.
“He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.”
In their world, eating with someone was a sign of friendship and acceptance.
Jesus was publicly choosing to be seen with the town’s worst cheat.
A changed heart.
The Bible does not tell us what was said at the meal. But something happened.
Zacchaeus stood up in front of the others and said, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor.
And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.”
That was a lot.
The law of Moses said that someone who stole should repay the amount plus one-fifth.
Four times was the penalty for stealing a sheep and slaughtering it.
Zacchaeus went far beyond what was required.
His giving was not demanded by Jesus, and it did not earn his salvation.
It was the fruit of a heart that had already been changed by being accepted.
Jesus had not lectured him.
Love had done what accusation could not.
Lost and found.
Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
