Even though the crowd saw Zacchaeus as a traitor, Jesus called him a son of Abraham, a true member of God’s people.
The last line sums up the whole mission of Jesus.
“To seek and to save the lost.”
Zacchaeus was looking for Jesus, but Jesus was also looking for him.
In the story it is hard to tell who found whom first.
Right after this, Luke tells the parable of the ten minas, to show that the kingdom of God was not about to appear immediately.
Jesus went on to Jerusalem, where in a few days He would be crucified.
Zacchaeus had met Him on the way.
What came after.
The Bible does not tell us what happened to Zacchaeus after that day.
A later tradition, written by early Christian writers, says he became a follower of Jesus and eventually a leader in the church in Caesarea.
The Bible does not confirm it.
But we can imagine the effect in Jericho.
People who had been cheated were suddenly repaid four times over.
The poor received half of his wealth.
Neighbors who had avoided him for years had to decide what to think.
A changed life is one of the strongest witnesses.
Zacchaeus’ name in Hebrew, Zakkai, means “pure” or “innocent.”
It is a name that his reputation did not match, until the day he met Jesus.
What does this mean for us today?.
Zacchaeus shows that no one is too far gone for Jesus.
The man everyone hated was the one Jesus chose to eat with.
If you have ever felt that you do not belong, this story says Jesus knows your name and wants to be with you.
It also shows what real repentance looks like.
Zacchaeus did not just feel sorry.
He changed how he used his money and made things right with the people he had wronged.
Faith in Jesus shows up in how we treat others.
And the story is about seeking.
Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus said that He had come to seek the lost.
If you are looking for Jesus, you are not alone in looking.
He is also looking for you.
Who Paul was.
Paul was born in Tarsus, a major city in what is now southern Turkey, around AD 5.
He was Jewish, from the tribe of Benjamin, and his parents named him Saul after Israel’s first king.
He was also born a Roman citizen, a valuable status that later saved his life more than once. Paul was his Roman name.
As a young man he moved to Jerusalem and studied under Gamaliel, one of the most respected rabbis of the day.
He became a Pharisee, and he says he was advancing beyond others his age in zeal for the traditions of his ancestors.
He also learned a trade, tentmaking, which he used to support himself throughout his ministry.
How Paul met Jesus.
Paul never met Jesus during His earthly ministry.
He was the church’s fiercest enemy: he approved Stephen’s execution and went from house to house dragging Christians to prison.
Then on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus appeared to him in a blinding light and spoke to him by name.
Paul later counted this as a true resurrection appearance — the last one — and it made him an apostle.
Why Jesus chose Paul.
Jesus told Ananias, the man sent to heal Paul’s blindness: “This man is My chosen instrument to proclaim My name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel.
I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.”
Paul himself said he was “the worst of sinners,” and that God showed him mercy so that he could be an example of Christ’s patience to everyone who would believe.
Saul of Tarsus.
He described himself as “a Hebrew of Hebrews… as for zeal, persecuting the church; as for righteousness based on the law, faultless.”
He made tents for a living.
Saul was his Hebrew name; Paul was his Roman one.
Hunting Christians.
He held the coats of the men who stoned Stephen.
Then he got letters from the high priest to arrest followers of “the Way” in Damascus and bring them back to Jerusalem in chains.
The Damascus road.
Saul was blind for three days and didn’t eat or drink.
God sent a disciple named Ananias — terrified, because of Saul’s reputation — to lay hands on him.
Something like scales fell from his eyes, he was baptized, and immediately began preaching in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.
His former allies plotted to kill him, and he escaped Damascus lowered in a basket through a window in the city wall.
Barnabas vouches for him.
Paul spent years in Arabia, Damascus and his hometown of Tarsus.
Later Barnabas went to find him and brought him to Antioch, where the believers were first called Christians.
Missionary journeys.
He usually started in the local synagogue, then reached Gentiles.
In Lystra he was stoned and left for dead, then got up and went back into the city.
In Athens he preached on Mars Hill about “the unknown god.”
In Ephesus a riot broke out because the silversmiths who made idols were losing business.
He worked making tents so he wouldn’t be a burden.
Singing in prison.
They had freed a slave girl from a spirit that let her owners make money telling fortunes.
The jailer woke, saw the doors open, and was about to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had escaped.
Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!”
The jailer asked, “What must I do to be saved?”
“Believe in the Lord Jesus.”
He and his whole household were baptized that night.
What he suffered.
He lists it himself: “in danger from rivers, bandits, my own people, Gentiles… I have known hunger and thirst… I have been cold and naked.”
He also had a “thorn in the flesh”
God didn’t remove, and heard God say, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is made perfect in weakness.”
His letters.
Romans explains salvation by grace through faith. 1 Corinthians 13 says, “Love is patient, love is kind.”
Philippians, written from prison, says, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” and “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.”
Galatians says, “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”
Arrested and shipwrecked.
A mob in the Temple nearly killed him.
He spent two years in custody in Caesarea, testifying before governors and King Agrippa.
As a Roman citizen he appealed to the emperor.
On the voyage a storm raged for two weeks; Paul told all 276 on board that an angel promised no one would die.
The ship broke apart off Malta, and everyone made it to shore.
A snake bit him and he was unharmed.
How it ended.
Acts ends with Paul in Rome “proclaiming the kingdom of God… with all boldness and without hindrance.”
His last letter, to Timothy, says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”
Clement of Rome and later writers record his martyrdom in Rome around AD 64–67.
As a citizen he would have been beheaded rather than crucified.
What made Paul extraordinary.

Paul traveled roughly 10,000 miles on foot and by ship, planted churches across modern-day Turkey and Greece, wrote 13 of the 27 books of the New Testament, and preached to synagogues, philosophers, governors and kings.
More than anyone, he carried the message of Jesus from a Jewish movement in Judea to the wider Roman world.
Why Paul matters today.
Paul’s life is the clearest example of God’s grace: the man who hunted Christians became the greatest missionary.
His letters still shape how Christians understand salvation, love and the church.
Near the end he wrote, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”
Who Stephen was.
Stephen was one of the first leaders of the church in Jerusalem, around AD 34.
He was probably a Greek-speaking Jew, one of the “Hellenists,” who had been born outside Israel and spoke Greek as their first language.
The Bible describes him as “a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit.”
He was chosen as one of seven men to take care of daily food for the widows in the church.
Then he became the first person to die for following Jesus.
Why his story matters.
Stephen’s death is the first martyrdom recorded in the Bible.
His story is the link between the early church in Jerusalem and the spread of the Gospel to the world.
It also introduces a young man named Saul, who would become Paul.
The seven.
The church in Jerusalem was growing fast, thousands of believers.
Some Greek-speaking Jewish widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food.
The apostles did not want to neglect prayer and the teaching of the Word to wait on tables.
So they asked the church to choose seven men “of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom.”
The people chose seven.
Every one has a Greek name, which suggests they were chosen from the group that had complained.
Stephen was first on the list.
The apostles prayed and laid hands on them.
It is a lovely picture of a church listening to a complaint and fixing it quickly, and of leaders giving real responsibility to others.
Full of grace and power.
Stephen did more than serve tables.
“And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.”
He also debated with Jews from several synagogues in Jerusalem, including the synagogue of the Freedmen, people from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia.
Among those from Cilicia was probably a young man named Saul from Tarsus.
“But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.”
Unable to win the argument, they paid some men to lie about him.
They said that Stephen spoke against Moses, against God, against the Temple and the law.
They stirred up the people and the elders and teachers of the law, seized Stephen and brought him to the council, the Sanhedrin.
“And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.”
The speech.
The high priest asked, “Are these things so?”
Stephen answered with the longest speech in the book of Acts.
He started with Abraham and went through Joseph, whose brothers sold him but whom God used to save them.
He talked about Moses, whom the people rejected at first when he tried to help them, though God sent him as their deliverer.
He pointed out that God was not limited to the Temple: “Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands.”
Then he turned to his audience: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit.
As your fathers did, so do you.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?
And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered.”
His point was that the same pattern was repeating: Israel had rejected God’s messengers again, this time Jesus Himself.
The vision.
“Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him.”
Stephen was completely calm.
“But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
And he said, ‘Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.’”
Elsewhere in the New Testament, Jesus is said to be seated at the right hand of God. Here, He is standing.
The Bible does not explain why.
Many have thought it shows Jesus rising to welcome His faithful servant, or to stand as a witness for him.
The members of the council covered their ears and shouted.
They rushed at him together, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him.
His last words.
The men who were stoning him took off their coats and laid them at the feet of a young man named Saul.
As the stones struck, Stephen called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
Then he knelt down and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”
“And when he had said this, he fell asleep.”
His final words echo Jesus’ words on the cross, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” and “Father, forgive them.”
In both cases, a man facing death offered forgiveness.
“Saul approved of his execution.”
Right after, a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem.
All but the apostles were scattered through Judea and Samaria.
“Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word.”
Persecution intended to stop the church only spread it.
The seed of Paul’s story.
Stephen’s death was not the end of his influence.
Saul, the young man who held the coats, was already leading the persecution, dragging believers out of their homes.
But on the road to Damascus he met the risen Jesus, who asked him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”
He became Paul, the apostle to the non-Jews and the author of much of the New Testament.
Many readers through the centuries have wondered whether Paul’s memory of Stephen’s face and prayer was part of what changed him.
The Bible does not say exactly.
But the story of Stephen is in the book of Acts right before the story of Saul’s conversion.
Meanwhile, another of the seven, Philip, went to Samaria and began preaching there, and it was Philip who later met the Ethiopian official on the desert road.
The scattering that began with Stephen’s death spread the message beyond Jerusalem.
What does this mean for us today?.
Stephen shows that serving others and speaking boldly can belong to the same person.
He started by waiting on tables and ended by standing before the council.
Faithfulness in small things prepares us for big ones.
His courage came from seeing Jesus.
While the crowd was grinding their teeth, Stephen was looking at heaven.
When we keep our eyes on Jesus, fear loses its grip.
And his last prayer is a model.
He did not curse the men who killed him.
He asked for forgiveness.
It is the hardest and most Christlike thing a person can do, and it may have been the seed that changed the life of the greatest missionary in history.
Forgiveness can accomplish more than revenge.
Who Barnabas was.
Barnabas was an early Christian leader, around AD 30 to 60.
His real name was Joseph, and he came from the island of Cyprus.
He was a Levite, from the tribe of priests.
The apostles gave him the nickname Barnabas, which means “son of encouragement.”
That nickname says a great deal about who he was.
He was a man of generosity, faith and courage.
The Bible says he was “a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.”
Why his story matters.
Barnabas is the man who believed in people others gave up on.
He was a bridge for Paul, for John Mark and for the church in Antioch.
His story shows how much one encourager can change.
A generous gift.
In the first months after Pentecost, thousands of people in Jerusalem believed.
Many had traveled from afar for the festival and stayed.
The believers shared what they had so that no one was in need.
“Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas, a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.”
That one verse introduces him.
Rather than keep his wealth, he put it to use for others.
Right after, the Bible tells of Ananias and Sapphira, who pretended to give everything but kept some back.
The contrast was clear: Barnabas gave honestly and freely.
Vouching for Saul.
Saul of Tarsus had been the church’s worst persecutor.
After he met Jesus on the road to Damascus, he began preaching in Damascus and then had to escape over the city wall in a basket.
When he got to Jerusalem, “he attempted to join the disciples.
And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple.”

“But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.” It was a risk.
If Saul was lying, it could have cost lives.
Barnabas trusted what he saw, and because of his word, Saul was welcomed.
The church in Antioch.
Believers who fled the persecution after Stephen’s death had spread out, and some in Antioch in Syria began telling Greeks, non-Jews, about Jesus. A large number believed.
When news reached Jerusalem, the church sent Barnabas to see what was going on.
“When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.
And a great many people were added to the Lord.”
The work was growing too large for one person, so Barnabas went to Tarsus, about 100 miles away, to find Saul and bring him to Antioch.
For a whole year they taught together.
It was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
When a famine hit, the church there collected money, and Barnabas and Saul carried it to Jerusalem.
The first mission.
While the leaders at Antioch were worshiping and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
They prayed, laid hands on them and sent them off.
Barnabas is named first, since at that time he was the senior leader.
They took Barnabas’ younger cousin, John Mark, as an assistant.
They sailed to Cyprus, Barnabas’ home island, then to what is now Turkey.
Gradually Saul, now called Paul, began to take the lead, and the Bible starts saying “Paul and his companions.”
In the town of Lystra, after Paul healed a lame man, the crowd decided Barnabas was Zeus and Paul was Hermes, and brought oxen to sacrifice.
Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes and rushed out: “Men, why are you doing these things?
We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news.”
A disagreement over Mark.
Some time later, Paul suggested they go back and visit the churches.
Barnabas wanted to take John Mark again.
But Mark had left them in the middle of the first journey and gone home.
Paul did not want to take him.
“And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other.
Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and set out.”
It was not a happy ending, but Barnabas stuck to his character.
He gave Mark a second chance.
Years later, Paul wrote from prison, “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry.”
Mark became a trusted helper of both Paul and Peter, and according to early tradition he wrote the Gospel of Mark.
Without Barnabas’ encouragement, it may never have happened.
The Bible does not say more about Barnabas’ later life.
Paul spoke of him warmly in his letters, as a fellow worker who, like him, supported himself with his own labor.
What does this mean for us today?.
Barnabas was never the star.
He introduced Paul to the apostles, then brought Paul to Antioch, then stepped aside as Paul took the lead.
He gave Mark a second chance when Paul would not.
The kingdom of God has room for people whose job is to lift others up.
His example is practical.
Encouragement is not just saying nice things.
It is being generous with money, with your reputation and with your time.
Barnabas put his own name on the line for Saul and Mark.
Whom could you encourage this week?
A new believer, a person who failed, someone who is overlooked.
The Bible says, “Therefore encourage one another and build one another up.”
Sometimes the most important people in a story are the ones who gave someone else a chance.
Who Timothy was.
Timothy was a young man from Lystra, a town in what is now central Turkey, who became Paul’s closest co-worker.
His mother, Eunice, was a Jewish believer, and his father was a Greek.
His grandmother Lois was also a woman of faith.
Paul wrote that the “sincere faith” that dwelt in them first now lived in Timothy too.
From childhood Timothy had been taught the Scriptures.
Paul later reminded him: “From childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.”
Why his story matters.
Timothy’s life shows how faith passes from one generation to the next, and how God uses younger people.
Paul’s two letters to him, 1 and 2 Timothy, are among the most personal in the New Testament.
Joining Paul.
On his first journey, about AD 47, Paul and Barnabas visited Lystra.
Paul healed a man who had been lame since birth, and the crowd wanted to worship them as gods.
A little later, Jews from other towns turned the crowd and stoned Paul, dragging him outside the city and leaving him for dead.
The disciples gathered around him, and he got up and went back into the city.
Timothy may have been among them.
A couple of years later, Paul came back on his second journey and found Timothy there.
“He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium.”
Paul wanted him to come along.
Because they would be going to Jewish communities, and Timothy’s father was a Greek, Paul had Timothy circumcised so that no one would object to him.
Church leaders laid their hands on him and gave a blessing, and Timothy left home to travel with Paul and Silas.
He was probably in his late teens or twenties.
A trusted partner.
Timothy was with Paul through some of his hardest years.
He was in Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth.
Paul sent him back to Thessalonica to encourage the new believers when he could not go himself.
He brought back good news that the church was standing firm.
Timothy’s name is on the greeting of several of Paul’s letters, including 1 and 2 Thessalonians, 2 Corinthians, Philippians and Colossians.
When Paul was in prison, he wrote to the church in Philippi that he hoped to send Timothy to them: “I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.
For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.
But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel.”
Paul often called him “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord.”
Leading in Ephesus.
Later, Paul left Timothy in Ephesus, a large and difficult city, to lead the church there.
Timothy faced false teachers, disorder in the church and, apparently, some who looked down on him because of his age.
In his first letter, Paul wrote: “Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.”
He also gave practical instructions about worship, church leaders, widows and money.
Paul also seemed to know Timothy’s health struggles.
“No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.”
Timothy was not a superhero.
He had weak spots, and Paul treated them kindly.
Paul’s last letter.
Around AD 66 or 67, Paul was in a Roman prison for the second time.
He knew he would soon die.
He wrote a final letter to Timothy: “I thank God... as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day.
As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.”
He told him, “I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.”
Timothy was probably timid by nature.
Paul urged him to preach the Word and endure suffering.
He wrote of his own end: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”
Then his plea: “Do your best to come to me soon...
Do your best to come before winter.”
The Bible does not tell us whether Timothy arrived in time.
The letter to the Hebrews says, “You should know that our brother Timothy has been released.” He was still serving.
What does this mean for us today?.
Timothy’s faith started at home.
His mother and grandmother taught him the Scriptures when he was small, and it shaped his whole life.
Whatever age you are, the faith you share with the young people around you may last further than you know.
His story also encourages anyone who feels too young, too shy or too weak.
Paul did not tell Timothy he had nothing to worry about.
He told him that God’s Spirit is “not of fear but of power and love and self-control.”
You do not need to be a natural leader.
You need to say yes and keep going.
And the relationship between Paul and Timothy is a picture of mentoring.
Paul invested in a younger man, trusted him with real work, and wrote to him with honesty and love.
Someone older who invests in you, or someone younger you invest in, may be one of God’s best gifts.
Who Lydia was.
Lydia was a businesswoman in the first century.
She came from the city of Thyatira, in what is now western Turkey, which was known for its dyed cloth.
She sold purple fabric, an expensive luxury, since real purple dye was made from sea snails and cost a great deal.
She was successful enough to own a home big enough to host guests, and she ran a household that included servants or family members.
She is described as “a worshiper of God,” which means she was not Jewish by birth, but she believed in the God of Israel and prayed to Him.
Why her story matters.
Lydia is the first person in Europe the Bible says became a follower of Jesus.
Her story is a small scene in the book of Acts, but it opened the door for the message to spread to a whole new continent.
A call to Macedonia.
Around AD 50, Paul was on his second missionary journey with Silas, Timothy and Luke.
They had tried to go into several places in Asia, but the Holy Spirit kept stopping them.
At Troas, on the coast, Paul had a vision during the night: a man from Macedonia stood and begged, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
“After he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.”
They sailed across the Aegean Sea and came to Philippi, a leading city of Macedonia and a Roman colony.
It was a big step: the Gospel was about to enter Europe.
Prayer by the river.
A Jewish synagogue needed ten Jewish men.
Philippi apparently did not have that many, so no synagogue existed.
On the Sabbath day, Paul and his friends went outside the city gate to the river, “where we supposed there was a place of prayer.”
They sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.
One of them was Lydia.
She was listening, and the Bible says, “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.”
That is an important line.
Paul gave the message, but it was God who opened her heart.
She was not talked into it by a clever speech.
She believed and was baptized, along with her whole household.
Then she did something typical of a generous person: “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.”
The Bible says, “And she prevailed upon us.” She insisted.
Her house.
While Paul stayed in Philippi, he got into trouble.
He freed a slave girl from a spirit, and her owners, who made money from her fortune-telling, dragged Paul and Silas before the authorities.
They were beaten and thrown into the inner prison with their feet in stocks.
At midnight they were praying and singing hymns when an earthquake shook the prison doors open.
The jailer, about to kill himself in fear, ended up believing and being baptized with his whole family.
When the officials released them the next morning, the Bible says, “They went out of the prison and visited Lydia.
And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.”
Lydia’s home had become the meeting place for the new church.
It is likely that early Christians in Philippi gathered there for worship and meals.
The church at Philippi.
A few years later, Paul wrote a letter to the church in Philippi, now the New Testament book of Philippians.
It is one of his warmest letters, full of joy even though he was in prison when he wrote it.
He tells them, “I thank my God in all my remembrance of you.”

He also thanks them for supporting him: “You Philippians yourselves know that in the beginning of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving, except you only.
Even in Thessalonica you sent me help for my needs once and again.”
The Bible does not say exactly who gave what, but a church that began in a successful businesswoman’s house, and was open-handed from the beginning, fits what we know about Lydia.
What does this mean for us today?.
Lydia’s story shows that faith often starts with a quiet hearing.
There was no miracle, no crowd, no dramatic moment.
A woman went to pray by a river, listened, and God opened her heart.
It also shows what a changed life looks like.
Lydia’s first response was to open her home.
She used what she had, her business, her house and her influence, for the work of God.
The first church in Europe began in a living room.
You do not need a big platform to matter in God’s plan.
Many people in the Bible are remembered because of one act of faith and welcome, and Lydia is one of them.
Who Priscilla and Aquila were.
Priscilla and her husband Aquila were a Jewish couple who lived in the first century, in Rome, Corinth and Ephesus.
Aquila was from Pontus, a region on the Black Sea in modern Turkey.
They were tentmakers, or leatherworkers, a trade that could be practiced anywhere in the empire.
Priscilla is sometimes called by the short form Prisca.
In the Bible, they always appear together.
Interestingly, Priscilla’s name is often listed first, which may suggest she was especially well known in the early church.
Why their story matters.
They were not apostles or famous preachers.
They were a working couple who opened their home, risked their lives and helped teach others.
Their story shows how much ordinary believers did for the early church.
Forced out of Rome.
In about AD 49, the Roman emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome.
The Roman historian Suetonius describes the order as being due to disturbances over someone called “Chrestus,” which may refer to arguments among Jews about Christ.
Priscilla and Aquila lost their home and their business and had to start over.
They moved to Corinth, a busy port city in Greece, known for trade and for its wild way of life.
They set up a tent-making business and began again.
Here the story of their lives crossed with Paul’s.
Paul arrived in Corinth on his second journey, alone and tired, after being run out of several cities.
He found Aquila and Priscilla, and since “he was of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers.”
Working with Paul.
Paul lived and worked with the couple.
Each week he went to the synagogue and tried to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy joined him, Paul began preaching full time.
Many in Corinth, including the synagogue leader Crispus and his whole household, believed and were baptized.
In a vision at night, the Lord told Paul, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you.”
Paul stayed eighteen months.
It is likely that Priscilla and Aquila were among the first believers there.
After more than a year, Paul decided to sail to Syria, and the couple went with him as far as Ephesus, a major city on the coast of Asia Minor.
Paul went on, but he left them in Ephesus.
They became the base for his next big mission.
Teaching Apollos.
An educated Jewish man from Alexandria named Apollos arrived in Ephesus.
He was a powerful speaker who knew the Scriptures well, and he taught about Jesus with enthusiasm.
But he only knew about the baptism of John.
He did not yet know the full story of Jesus’ death, resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit.
Priscilla and Aquila heard him in the synagogue.
They did not embarrass him in public.
Instead, “they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.”
It is a wonderful picture of correcting someone with kindness.
Apollos accepted the help, and soon afterward went to Greece with letters of recommendation from the believers.
There he “greatly helped those who through grace had believed” and powerfully refuted the Jews in public.
A couple of tentmakers had helped shape one of the church’s great teachers.
A church in their house.
Paul came back to Ephesus on his third journey and stayed over two years.
In his letter to the Corinthians, written from Ephesus, he writes: “Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord.”
There were no church buildings then.
Believers gathered in homes, and Priscilla and Aquila’s house was a center.
At some point, probably in Ephesus, they faced mortal danger for Paul.

When he later wrote to the church in Rome, he said: “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks.
Greet also the church in their house.”
The Bible does not say exactly what they did.
But they were so valued that churches among non-Jews thanked them.
By then they had moved back to Rome, probably after Claudius’ order was no longer enforced.
Years later, in Paul’s last letter, written from prison, he sent greetings to “Prisca and Aquila” again, so by then they were back in Ephesus.
What does this mean for us today?.
Priscilla and Aquila show that you do not need a title to make a big difference.
They worked a trade, opened their home and welcomed people.
They moved three times, lost one business and started again, and kept finding ways to serve.
Their kindness to Apollos is a model.
They saw something missing in a gifted man and, rather than criticize or ignore it, took him aside privately and taught him.
That is one of the best ways to help another believer grow.
And their home shows that a church is first of all a family of people, not a building.
A kitchen table and a shared meal can be the place where God’s people gather and are strengthened.
Many of the churches in the New Testament started exactly that way.
Who Adam and Eve were.
Adam and Eve are the first man and woman in the Bible.
The first two chapters of Genesis say God made them at the end of the creation week.
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.”
Adam’s name is the Hebrew word for “man,” and it is related to the word for “ground,” from which he was formed.
Eve’s name means “life,” or “living.”
They lived in a garden God had planted in Eden.
The Bible does not say exactly where Eden was, but it mentions four rivers flowing from it, including the Tigris and the Euphrates.
Why their story matters.
Almost everything in the Bible depends on this story.
It explains who we are, why the world is broken, and why we need a Savior.
The New Testament calls Jesus “the last Adam.”
Made and placed in a garden.
“Then the Lord God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.”
God planted a garden in Eden with every tree that was pleasing to the eye and good for food.
Adam’s job was “to work it and keep it.”
The first work in the Bible was a gift, not a punishment.
God gave one rule: Adam could eat from any tree in the garden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
“In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.”
Then God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone.”
He brought the animals to Adam to name, but none was a suitable partner.
So God put Adam into a deep sleep, took one of his ribs, or a part of his side, and made a woman.
Adam said, “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
“And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
It was a world of harmony: with God, with each other and with creation.
The serpent’s question.
Then comes the serpent, “more crafty than any other beast of the field.”
Later in the Bible, the serpent is identified with Satan.
He asked the woman, “Did God actually say, ‘You shall not eat of any tree in the garden’?” He twisted God’s words.
Eve answered that they could eat of all the trees but one, and God said they must not touch it or they would die.
The serpent said, “You will not surely die.
For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”
He suggested that God was holding something back, and that God could not be trusted.

“So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.”
The Bible does not say what kind of fruit it was.
The idea that it was an apple comes from later tradition.
Hiding and blame.
“Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked.
And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.”
That evening they heard the Lord God walking in the garden and hid among the trees.
The Lord called, “Where are you?”
God knew where they were.
The question gave Adam a chance to come out.
Adam said, “I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself.”
God asked, “Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”
Adam answered, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate.”
He blamed Eve and, indirectly, God.
Eve said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”
Neither said, “I did wrong.”
Sin brought fear, shame, blame and distance from God, and it has been with us ever since.
Consequences and a promise.
God spoke to the serpent first, cursing him.

Then He gave a promise that has been called the first gospel: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.”
Someone born of the woman would one day defeat the serpent, though it would cost him a wound.
The New Testament says this points to Jesus.
To the woman, God said that childbirth would be painful and her relationship with her husband would be strained.

To Adam, He said that the ground would be cursed, and work would be hard: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
Death had entered the world.
Yet even then there is kindness.
“And the Lord God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.”
Covering their shame required the death of an animal, the first picture of how God would cover our sin.
Out of the garden.
God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil.
Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever...”
So He sent them out of the garden.
At the east of Eden He placed cherubim, angelic guardians, and a flaming sword that turned in every direction to guard the way to the tree of life.
It was a judgment, but also a mercy: they would not live forever in a fallen state.
Outside Eden, Adam and Eve had children.
Cain was born first, then Abel.
Eve said, “I have gotten a man with the help of the Lord.”
After Abel’s death, Seth was born.
Adam lived 930 years and had other sons and daughters.
The Bible says only that “he died.”
The tree of life shows up again in the last chapters of the Bible, in the new Jerusalem, where God’s people will once again be able to eat of it.
What does this mean for us today?.
The story of Adam and Eve explains many things we know from experience.
We were made for a close relationship with God, and something has gone wrong.
We hide, blame and cover ourselves.
We know what we should do, and we do not.
The Bible says this goes back to the first choice to doubt God’s word and take life into our own hands.
But the story also gives hope.
God came looking for them in the garden: “Where are you?” He still does.
He gave them clothes, and He gave them a promise.
From the very beginning, the plan of rescue was in motion.
The apostle Paul says, “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.” Adam brought death. Jesus brings life.
What was lost in the first garden is restored by the Savior who prayed in a garden, died on a cross and rose from a tomb in a garden.
Who Cain and Abel were.
Cain and Abel were the first two sons of Adam and Eve, born after they were sent out of the Garden of Eden. Cain was the older.
He became a farmer who worked the ground.
Abel became a shepherd who tended flocks.
Both lived in a world outside the garden, knowing what had been lost.
Eve said when Cain was born, “I have gotten a man with the help of the Lord.”
She may have hoped he was the promised child who would crush the serpent.
The Bible tells their story in just sixteen verses, but it is one of the most important in Genesis.
Why their story matters.
This is the Bible’s first story of a family, of worship and of murder.
It shows how sin grows from an angry heart into a terrible act, and how God speaks to people before and after they do wrong.
Two offerings.
“In the course of time Cain brought to the Lord an offering of the fruit of the ground, and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions.
And the Lord had regard for Abel and his offering, but for Cain and his offering he had no regard.”
The Bible does not say exactly why.
The New Testament gives a clue: “By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain.”
It seems that Abel brought the first and best, with faith, while Cain’s offering came from a different heart.
Another New Testament passage says Cain “was of the evil one,” and that his deeds were evil, while his brother’s were righteous.
“So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.”
Anger and jealousy were growing inside him.
God’s warning.
God did not ignore Cain’s anger.
He spoke to him directly, and kindly.
“Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?
If you do well, will you not be accepted?
And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door.
Its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it.”
This is the first time sin is named in the Bible after the fall in Eden.
It is pictured like a wild animal waiting at the door.
God was telling Cain two things: he could do well and be accepted, and he had the power to master it.
God offered him a way out.
It is still the way God treats us: He warns us before we fall.
Cain heard the warning, and did nothing with it.
The first murder.
“Cain spoke to Abel his brother.
And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.”
The Bible says it in one short verse.
There is no long description.
The first death in human history is a murder, and the victim is a brother.
Then God asked, “Where is Abel your brother?”
Cain said, “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?”
That question has echoed through history.
God said, “What have you done?
The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground.
And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand.”
The ground would no longer give its strength to him.
He would be a fugitive and a wanderer.
The mark.
Cain said, “My punishment is greater than I can bear.
Behold, you have driven me today away from the ground, and from your face I shall be hidden.
I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me.”
Even here, God showed mercy. “Not so!
If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold.”
And the Lord put a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would attack him.
The Bible does not say what the mark was.
Cain went away from the presence of the Lord and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
He married and had a son, Enoch, and built a city.
His descendants included the first herders, the first musicians and the first metalworkers.
Civilization began, but it began far from God.
A new son.
Adam and Eve had another son, Seth.
Eve said, “God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him.”
From Seth’s family, a line of people began who “called upon the name of the Lord.”
The New Testament refers back to Abel.
Jesus called him righteous.
The letter to the Hebrews says that Abel, “though he died, still speaks” by his faith.
Hebrews also says that Jesus’ blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.”
Abel’s blood cried out for justice.
Jesus’ blood speaks forgiveness.
The first letter of John also uses Cain as a warning: “We should love one another.
We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother.
And why did he murder him?
Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.”
What does this mean for us today?.
The story of Cain shows how sin works.
First an offended feeling, then anger, then a plan, then a deed.
God’s warning came in the first stage.
When we notice jealousy or bitterness growing inside, that is the moment to bring it to God, before it gets bigger.
Cain’s question, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”, has an answer in the rest of the Bible: yes.
We are called to love and care for the people around us, and not to ignore their need.
But there is also hope here.
God spoke to Cain, protected him, and later gave Adam and Eve a new son.
And in Jesus, the blood that cries out is not for revenge but for mercy.
The story that begins with a murder points ahead to a rescue.
Who Noah was.
Noah was a descendant of Adam through the line of Seth, born after the world had grown corrupt.
His father, Lamech, named him “Noah,” which sounds like the Hebrew for “rest” or “comfort,” saying, “Out of the ground that the Lord has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work.”
The Bible says that by the time of Noah, the earth was filled with violence.
“The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” God was grieved.
“But Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord.”
Why his story matters.
Noah’s story is the Bible’s first great story of judgment and rescue.
It is also a story of faith that lasted a very long time, and of God’s promise never to destroy the earth by flood again.
A righteous man.
“Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God.”
The Bible does not say that he was perfect.
But he was faithful in a time when almost everyone else was not.
He had three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth.
God told Noah that He was going to destroy all flesh because of the violence.
“Make yourself an ark of gopher wood.
Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch.”
The ark was to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide and 30 cubits high, about 450 feet by 75 feet by 45 feet, three decks tall, with a door in the side and a window near the top.
It was a huge ship, about as long as one and a half football fields.
“Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.” It was a very big job.
The New Testament calls Noah “a herald of righteousness,” which suggests he warned others as he worked.
Building it took many years.
Imagine the neighbors’ comments about a giant boat on dry land.
Into the ark.
God said, “I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you.”
Noah was to bring two of every kind of animal, male and female, and more of the clean animals, as well as food for everyone.
Seven days before the flood began, they all entered. Noah was 600 years old.
“And the Lord shut him in.”
That small detail says something: the door was closed by God, not by Noah.
The ark was not only a boat but a place of safety.
Eight people were inside: Noah, his wife, their three sons and their wives. And the rain began.
The flood.
“On that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened.
And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights.”
The waters rose and lifted the ark above the earth.
“The waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered.”
For 150 days the waters held.
Every living thing on dry land died.
“But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark.”
God sent a wind over the earth and the waters began to recede.
In the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
The tops of the mountains became visible after about two and a half more months.
Noah opened the window and sent out a raven, which flew back and forth.
Then he sent out a dove, which returned because it found no place to land.
A week later he sent the dove again, and it came back in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in its beak.
The third time, the dove did not return.
Noah knew the land was drying.
A new start.
A year and ten days after the flood began, the earth was dry.
God said, “Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons’ wives with you.
Bring out with you every living thing... that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth.”
The first thing Noah did was build an altar to the Lord.
He took some of the clean animals and offered burnt offerings.
“And when the Lord smelled the pleasing aroma, the Lord said in his heart, ‘I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth.
Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done.’”
Even after the flood, human hearts were still sinful.
God did not rescue the world because people had become good.
He did it because of His mercy.
The rainbow.
God blessed Noah and his sons and told them to fill the earth.

Then He made a promise: “I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you... never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth.”
“I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant that is between me and you.”
The Hebrew word for rainbow is the same as the word for a warrior’s bow.
God hung up His weapon in the sky, pointing away from the earth.
The Bible then tells of one more sad scene.
Noah planted a vineyard, got drunk and lay naked in his tent.
His son Ham treated him disrespectfully, and the family was affected.
Noah lived 350 years after the flood and died at 950.
Even the best people are not perfect.
The story ends where it began: with the need for someone better.
What does this mean for us today?.
Noah trusted God when there was no rain, no sign of a flood and nobody else believed.
He built for many years based on what God had said.
The New Testament says, “By faith Noah, warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household.”
Faith often means acting on God’s word before we see the results.
The ark itself is a picture of salvation.
There was one door, one way in.
Those who went in were saved, and God Himself shut the door.
Jesus said, “I am the door.
If anyone enters by me, he will be saved.”
And the rainbow is a daily reminder.
Every time one appears in the sky after a storm, it tells us that God keeps His promises.
The storm does not have the last word.
Who Abraham was.
Abraham, first called Abram, is the father of the Jewish people and a great man of faith for Christians and Muslims also.
He lived about 2000 BC in Ur, a prosperous city in what is now southern Iraq, where people worshiped many gods.
His father Terah took the family north to Haran.
Abram was already married to Sarai, who could not have children.
Everything changed when God spoke to him.
It was the beginning of the story of the Bible’s main plot: God’s plan to bless the whole world.
Why his story matters.
Abraham’s story is the foundation of the Bible’s teaching about faith.
The apostle Paul says that Abraham was made right with God because he believed.
He is called “the friend of God.”
The call.
“Now the Lord said to Abram, ‘Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you.
And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.’”
Abram was 75 and childless.
He had no map and no idea where he was going.
“So Abram went, as the Lord had told him.”
He took Sarai, his nephew Lot, his servants and his flocks.
The promise included land, descendants and a blessing for all nations, and the Bible’s whole story is about how God made good on it.
Hebrews says, “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance.
And he went out, not knowing where he was going.”
Stars and a promise.
Abram arrived in Canaan and lived as a nomad in tents.
He and his nephew Lot had grown so rich that they needed to separate.
Abram generously let Lot choose first, and Lot chose the rich Jordan valley near Sodom.
Abram stayed in the hills.
Soon after, Lot was taken captive in a war between local kings.
Abram led 318 trained men and rescued him.
After the battle, a mysterious priest-king named Melchizedek blessed him.
Years went by and still there was no child. Abram complained to God.
God took him outside: “Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them...
So shall your offspring be.”
Then comes one of the most important verses in the Bible: “And he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness.”
Abram was not made right with God by his good works, but by trusting God’s promise.
The Bible gives that as the pattern of salvation, for Jews and non-Jews.
Waiting, laughing and interceding.
When Abram was 99, God appeared again and changed his name to Abraham, “father of a multitude.”
He gave circumcision as the sign of the covenant.
He also said Sarah would have a son within a year.
Abraham fell on his face and laughed, “Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?”
God told him to name the child Isaac, “he laughs.”
Soon after, the Lord visited Abraham with two angels and told him that He was about to destroy the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, where Lot lived.
Abraham stepped forward and argued: “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?...
Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?”
He kept asking: if there were fifty righteous people, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten? Each time, God agreed. Not even ten were found.
But God rescued Lot and his two daughters before the cities were destroyed.
Abraham’s boldness shows that God invites our prayers.
Isaac, and the hardest test.
When Abraham was 100 and Sarah 90, Isaac was born. The long wait was over.

Years later, “God tested Abraham and said to him, ‘Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you.’”
Abraham rose early the next morning, took Isaac, two servants, wood and fire and set out.
After three days, he saw the place.
He told the servants, “Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you.” Isaac carried the wood.
“Where is the lamb for a burnt offering?”
“God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.”
Abraham built the altar, bound Isaac and raised his knife.
The angel of the Lord called from heaven, “Abraham, Abraham!
Do not lay your hand on the boy.”
Abraham saw a ram caught in a thicket and offered it instead.
He called the place “The Lord will provide.”
Hebrews says Abraham “considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead.”
The story points ahead to God’s own Son, the Lamb whom God provided.
A wife for Isaac.
When Sarah died, Abraham was 137.
He bought the cave of Machpelah near Hebron for her burial.
Then he began to think about Isaac’s future.
He did not want Isaac to marry a Canaanite woman.
He sent his most trusted servant back to his relatives in Mesopotamia to find a wife.
At the well outside the town of Nahor, the servant prayed that the woman who offered water to him and his camels would be the one.
Before he finished praying, Rebekah came and did exactly that.
She was Abraham’s great-niece. She agreed to go.
When she first saw Isaac walking in the field, she covered herself with a veil.
“Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her.”
Death and legacy.
Abraham took another wife, Keturah, and had six more sons.
But he left everything to Isaac.
He died “in a good old age, an old man and full of years,” at 175.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him together in the cave of Machpelah with Sarah.
The promise to Abraham echoes through the whole Bible.
The nation of Israel came from him through Isaac and Jacob.
The Arab nations trace their origin through Ishmael.
And the New Testament teaches that all who believe in Jesus are Abraham’s spiritual children: “Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham...
And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you shall all the nations be blessed.’”
Abraham is also called “the friend of God.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Abraham’s story shows how faith works.
He did not know where he was going.
He did not understand everything God asked.
But he took God at His word and acted.
His faith was not perfect: he lied about Sarah and tried to help God with Hagar.
But he trusted, and God counted it as righteousness.
His story also shows that God keeps promises.
It took 25 years for Isaac to be born, and many centuries for the promise of blessing for all nations to come to full effect.
God works on a long timeline, and we can trust Him.
Finally, the ram on Mount Moriah shows that God provides.
At the moment of greatest need, a substitute was ready.
The apostle Paul says that God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all.”
“The Lord will provide” is true in the biggest sense.
Who Sarah was.
Sarah, first called Sarai, was the wife of Abraham, about 2000 BC.
She came from Ur, a great city in what is now southern Iraq, and moved with her husband’s family to Haran in the north.
The Bible says she was very beautiful.
It also says that she was Abraham’s half-sister, the daughter of his father but not of his mother, which was acceptable in that time, before the law of Moses.
Her hardest trial was that she could not have children.
In that world, this was a heavy burden for a woman, and Sarah carried it for decades.
Why her story matters.
Sarah is the mother of the people of Israel and is honored in the New Testament as a woman of faith.
Her story shows that God keeps His promises even when they seem impossible.
Leaving home.
When Sarah was about 65, God told Abraham to leave his country and his father’s house for a land God would show him.
He promised to make him a great nation and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abraham was 75.
They had no children, and they had no map.
They packed up their household, their servants and their animals, and left.
For Sarah this meant giving up family, familiar places and her own security.
A famine soon drove them to Egypt.
There Abraham, afraid that men would kill him to take his beautiful wife, asked her to say she was his sister.
Pharaoh took Sarah into his house, but God sent plagues on his household, and Pharaoh sent her back with Abraham.
It was one of Abraham’s worst moments, and God protected Sarah even when her husband failed.
Waiting and a wrong turn.
God had promised Abraham a son of his own.
Ten years passed in Canaan, and nothing changed. Sarah was about 75.
She told Abraham, “Behold now, the Lord has prevented me from bearing children.
Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her.”
That was a common custom at the time. Abraham agreed.
Hagar, an Egyptian servant, became pregnant.
At once there was tension.
Hagar began to look down on Sarah, and Sarah treated her so harshly that Hagar ran away into the desert.
There an angel found her and told her to go back.
Her son Ishmael was born when Abraham was 86.
The Bible does not hide this part of the story.
Sarah tried to help God’s promise happen in her own way, and it brought pain to her household that lasted for generations.
The laugh.
God spoke to Abraham again when he was 99 and changed their names: Abram became Abraham, “father of many,” and Sarai became Sarah, “princess.”
God said, “I will bless her, and moreover, I will give you a son by her.”
Soon after, three men visited Abraham by the oaks of Mamre.
Abraham hurried to welcome them and asked Sarah to bake bread.
One of them, who was the Lord, said, “I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.”
Sarah was listening at the tent door.
She laughed to herself, “After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?”
The Lord asked, “Why did Sarah laugh?… Is anything too hard for the Lord?”
Sarah was afraid and said, “I did not laugh.”
But He said, “No, but you did laugh.”
Isaac.
A year later, as the Lord had said, Sarah had a baby boy.
She was about 90, and Abraham was 100.
They named him Isaac, which means “he laughs.”
Sarah said, “God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me.
Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?
Yet I have borne him a son in his old age.”
Her laugh of doubt had become a laugh of joy.
When Isaac was weaned, Abraham held a great feast.
At the feast, Sarah saw Ishmael, now a teenager, mocking Isaac.
She told Abraham to send Hagar and Ishmael away.
Abraham was deeply troubled, but God said, “Do not be displeased because of the boy...
Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you, for through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”
God also promised to make a nation of Ishmael and cared for Hagar and her son in the wilderness.
Her death.
Sarah died at the age of 127 in Hebron.
Abraham “went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.”
He did not own any land in Canaan, so he went to the Hittites and asked to buy a burial site.
He chose the cave of Machpelah, in a field belonging to Ephron the Hittite.
Ephron offered it as a gift, but Abraham insisted on paying 400 shekels of silver in front of the town elders.
This was the first piece of the promised land owned by Abraham’s family.
Sarah was buried there, and later Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah would be buried there too.
Isaac, who lost his mother when he was in his thirties, was comforted three years later when he married Rebekah.
The Bible says, “Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.”
The New Testament remembers Sarah as a woman of faith: “By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Sarah’s story is honest.
She believed and she laughed in disbelief.
She trusted and she tried to take matters into her own hands.
God was not surprised by any of it, and He still kept His promise.
For anyone who has waited a long time for something, Sarah says: God’s timing is not ours, and it is never too late for Him.
“Is anything too hard for the Lord?” is the question the Bible puts to every one of us.
Her story also shows that when we try to speed up God’s plan, it can hurt other people.
Hagar and Ishmael paid a price for that.
Yet the Bible says God cared for them, too.
His mercy is wider than any one family.
Who Jacob was.
Jacob was the grandson of Abraham and the son of Isaac and Rebekah.
He lived about 1800 BC in Canaan.
He and his twin brother Esau were born after Rebekah had struggled to have children and Isaac had prayed for her.
Before they were born, God told Rebekah, “Two nations are in your womb... the older shall serve the younger.”
Esau came first, red and hairy.
Jacob came right after, holding on to Esau’s heel.
So he was named Jacob, which means “he grasps the heel,” and also “he cheats.”
That name described a good part of his early life.
Why his story matters.
Jacob’s story is about a flawed man whom God kept pursuing.
God changed his name to Israel, and from his twelve sons came the twelve tribes of the nation of Israel.
The birthright and the blessing.
Esau was a hunter and his father’s favorite.
Jacob was quiet and stayed in the tents, and was his mother’s favorite.
One day Esau came home from the field exhausted and hungry.
Jacob was cooking red lentil stew.
Esau said, “Let me eat some of that red stuff.”
Jacob said, “Sell me your birthright now.”
The birthright belonged to the firstborn and meant a double share of the inheritance and leadership of the family.
Esau said, “I am about to die; what good is a birthright to me?”
He swore an oath and sold it.
“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
Years later, when Isaac was old and blind, he told Esau to hunt wild game and prepare a meal, and then he would give him the blessing.
Rebekah overheard and told Jacob to pretend to be Esau.
She cooked a meal, put goatskins on Jacob’s hands and neck, and dressed him in Esau’s clothes.
Isaac was suspicious: “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” He blessed Jacob.
When Esau returned, he cried out with a loud and bitter cry.
Isaac said, “Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing.”
Esau planned to kill Jacob, so Rebekah sent him away to her brother Laban in Haran.
A ladder at Bethel.
Jacob left home with nothing but a staff.
On the first night, he lay down with a stone for a pillow.
“And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven.
And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it!”
The Lord stood above it and said, “I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac.
The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring...
Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land.”
Jacob woke up, afraid.
“Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it...
This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
He set up the stone as a pillar, poured oil on it and called the place Bethel, “house of God.”
He made a vow: if God would be with him and bring him back safely, “then the Lord shall be my God.”
God had chosen him not because he was good but because of His own promise.
Laban, Leah and Rachel.
In Haran, Jacob met Rachel, his cousin, at a well, and fell in love.
He agreed to work seven years for her father Laban in exchange for marrying her.
“So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.”
On the wedding night, Laban gave him Rachel’s older sister, Leah, instead, under the veil in the dark.
In the morning Jacob said, “What is this you have done to me?”
The deceiver had been deceived.
Laban said that in his country the older was married first.
He offered Rachel as well if Jacob worked another seven years.
Jacob’s household became a story of rivalry.
Leah had many sons, and Rachel was barren for a long time.
Their servants Bilhah and Zilpah also had sons.
Eventually Jacob had twelve sons and a daughter, Dinah.
Rachel finally gave birth to Joseph.
Jacob worked for Laban another six years for flocks of his own, and Laban kept changing his wages.
By then Jacob had grown wealthy, and Laban’s sons were jealous.
God told Jacob it was time to go home.
Wrestling with God.
Jacob was returning to Canaan with his family and flocks, but he was afraid of meeting Esau.
He heard that Esau was coming with 400 men.
Jacob sent gifts ahead of him: hundreds of goats, sheep, camels, cows and donkeys.
He prayed: “O God of my father Abraham...
I am not worthy of the least of all the deeds of steadfast love and all the faithfulness that you have shown to your servant...
Please deliver me from the hand of my brother.”
That night, he sent his family across the river Jabbok and stayed behind alone.
“And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day.”
When the man saw that he did not prevail, he touched Jacob’s hip socket and put it out of joint.
“Let me go, for the day has broken.”
Jacob said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” “What is your name?” “Jacob.”
“Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Jacob named the place Peniel, “the face of God.”
“I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered.” He limped away.
Meeting Esau.
Jacob saw Esau coming with his 400 men.
He divided his family, putting the servants first, then Leah and her children, and Rachel and Joseph last.
He went ahead of all of them and bowed seven times.
“But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.”
Jacob had expected revenge. He found forgiveness.
He said, “To see your face is like seeing the face of God, and you have received me favorably.”
Esau at first refused the gifts.
“I have enough, my brother.”
Jacob insisted, and Esau accepted them.
Esau had his own large family and had become wealthy.
Jacob’s struggle had been long, but at the end God had not only kept His word but also softened the heart of the brother he had wronged.
Loss and Egypt.
Back in Canaan, Jacob’s life was full of heartbreak.
His daughter Dinah was assaulted, and his sons took violent revenge.
Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin near Bethlehem, and Jacob set up a pillar on her grave.
His older sons sold Joseph into slavery, and for twenty-two years Jacob believed him dead.
When famine came, he sent his sons to Egypt for food, and Joseph was found alive.
“It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive.
I will go and see him before I die.”
Jacob traveled to Egypt at 130.
Pharaoh asked his age and Jacob said, “The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years.
Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life.”
Before he died at 147, Jacob blessed Joseph’s two sons and each of his own sons, and he told them to bury him in the cave of Machpelah with Abraham and Isaac.
The Bible says Joseph and his brothers carried him there.
The promises of God to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob would be carried on by the twelve tribes of Israel.
What does this mean for us today?.
Jacob’s life is a long story of struggle.
He lied, was lied to, ran, worked, was afraid and was hurt. Yet God stayed with him.
At Bethel He promised, “I am with you,” and He kept the promise through twenty years in a foreign land, a night of wrestling and many years of sorrow.
Jacob’s limp is a reminder.
He met God and was changed, but also marked.
The Bible does not say that a close encounter with God leaves us without scars.
It says it leaves us with a new name, a blessing and a new way of living.
And the story shows that God’s choice of Jacob was grace.
He did not wait for Jacob to be good.
He chose him, and then changed him.
If you ever feel that your past disqualifies you, remember the one whose name meant “cheater” and whom God renamed Israel.
Who Joseph was.
Joseph was the eleventh of Jacob’s twelve sons and the first son of Jacob’s beloved wife Rachel. He lived about 1900 BC.
His family were shepherds living in Canaan, in tents, with their flocks.
Jacob’s household was divided by favoritism and jealousy.
Jacob had four wives, including Leah, Rachel and their servants, and twelve sons from them.
Joseph’s life takes him from the bottom of a pit to the second-highest position in the greatest empire in the world.
It is one of the longest and best-told stories in Genesis.
Why his story matters.
Joseph’s story answers a question every person asks: where is God when bad things happen?
It shows how God can bring good out of betrayal, injustice and years of waiting.
The favorite son.
Joseph was seventeen.
He helped his brothers tend the flocks and brought his father bad reports about them.
Jacob loved him more than the others and made him a special robe, often called a “coat of many colors” or a long robe with sleeves, a sign of rank.
“And when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.”
Then Joseph told them two dreams.
In one, the brothers’ sheaves of grain bowed down to his.
In the other, the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed to him.
His brothers said, “Are you indeed to reign over us?”
His father rebuked him but kept the matter in mind.
Joseph probably did not realize how this would sound.
But these dreams were from God.
Sold by his brothers.
Jacob sent Joseph to check on his brothers, who were pasturing the flock near Dothan.
When they saw him coming in the distance, they said, “Here comes this dreamer.
Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits.”
The oldest, Reuben, persuaded them not to kill him, planning to rescue him later.
They stripped off his robe and threw him into an empty cistern.
While they ate, a caravan of traders came by on its way to Egypt.
Judah suggested they sell him rather than kill him.
They sold Joseph for twenty shekels of silver.
They dipped his robe in goat’s blood and brought it to Jacob.
“Is it your son’s robe or not?” “It is my son’s robe.
A fierce animal has devoured him.”
Jacob tore his clothes and mourned for many days.
“All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted.”
Slave, then prisoner.
In Egypt, Joseph was sold to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.
“The Lord was with Joseph, and he became a successful man.”
Potiphar put him in charge of the whole house.
Potiphar’s wife noticed him and wanted him to sleep with her. Joseph refused.
“How then could I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
She kept asking, day after day.
One day she grabbed his cloak.
He ran out, leaving it in her hand.
She accused him of attacking her, and Potiphar had him thrown into the king’s prison.
Even there, “the Lord was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love.”
The prison warden put him in charge.
Two of Pharaoh’s officials, the cupbearer and the baker, were imprisoned and each had a dream.
Joseph explained that the cupbearer would be restored in three days, and the baker would be executed.
Joseph asked the cupbearer, “Remember me, when it is well with you.”
Both things happened as Joseph said.
“Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.” Two more years passed.
Pharaoh’s dream.
Pharaoh had two troubling dreams.
In one, seven fat cows came up out of the Nile, followed by seven thin cows that ate them.
In the other, seven good ears of grain were swallowed by seven thin ears. No one could explain.
The cupbearer finally remembered Joseph.
Joseph was brought out, shaved and changed his clothes.
When Pharaoh said he heard Joseph could interpret dreams, he answered, “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.”
The dreams meant that Egypt would have seven years of great harvests, followed by seven years of terrible famine.
Joseph also suggested a plan: store up grain during the good years.
Pharaoh said, “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?”
He made Joseph, who was thirty, the second most powerful man in Egypt.
He gave him his signet ring, a gold chain, fine clothing and an Egyptian wife, Asenath.
They had two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
“For God has made me forget all my hardship...
God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
His brothers return.
The famine spread, and Jacob sent ten of his sons to Egypt to buy grain.
Joseph recognized them at once, but they bowed to him without knowing who he was, just as in his dreams.
He spoke harshly to them, accused them of being spies and put them in prison for three days.
He kept Simeon as a hostage and told the rest to bring their youngest brother, Benjamin.
Joseph was testing them to see if they had changed.
When they returned with Benjamin, he had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack and then accused him of theft.
He said that the one who had the cup would become his slave.
Judah, who had once suggested selling Joseph, stepped forward: “Let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers.
For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me?”
It was the evidence Joseph needed.
“God meant it for good”.
Joseph could not hold back any longer.
He sent everyone else out of the room and wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard it. “I am Joseph!
Is my father still alive?”
His brothers were too shocked to answer.
“Come near to me, please...
I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.
And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.”
Joseph invited his whole family to move to Egypt.
Jacob, now 130, saw his son again after twenty-two years.
The family settled in Goshen.
After Jacob died, the brothers were afraid Joseph would take revenge.
Joseph wept and said, “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today.”
He lived to 110 and, near the end, made the Israelites promise to carry his bones back to the promised land when God brought them out.
Centuries later, they did.
What does this mean for us today?.
Joseph spent thirteen years as a slave and prisoner for something he did not do.
The Bible repeats, “the Lord was with Joseph.”
It does not say God removed the trouble, but He was there in it, and He was working toward something Joseph could not yet see.
His forgiveness is also remarkable.
He had every reason for revenge and the power to carry it out.
Instead he said, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
He did not call what they had done good.
He said God was able to use it.
If you are in a pit or a prison right now, Joseph’s story is a reminder that the story is not over.
God is able to bring good out of even the worst things, and He keeps His promises.
In the end, Joseph’s bones went home.
Who Moses was.
Moses is the greatest prophet of the Old Testament and the man God used to bring Israel out of slavery in Egypt.
He lived about 1400 to 1250 BC, though scholars differ on the dates.
He was born a Hebrew, raised as an Egyptian prince and lived forty years as a shepherd in the desert before God called him.
The first five books of the Bible, the Torah, are traditionally ascribed to him.
The Bible says, “There has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face.”
Why his story matters.
Moses’ story is the story of the Exodus, the great rescue that Israel remembered for a thousand years and that the New Testament uses to explain what Jesus did.
It also includes the Ten Commandments, the Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea.
Saved from the river.
The Israelites had been in Egypt for generations and had grown into a large people.
A new Pharaoh feared them, made them slaves and finally ordered that every Hebrew baby boy be thrown into the Nile.
A woman from the tribe of Levi had a son and hid him for three months.
When she could hide him no longer, she made a basket of papyrus, coated it with tar, put the baby inside and set it among the reeds at the river’s edge.
His sister Miriam watched from a distance.
Pharaoh’s daughter came to bathe, saw the basket and opened it.
“Behold, the baby was crying.
She took pity on him and said, ‘This is one of the Hebrews’ children.’”
Miriam stepped out and offered to find a nurse, and brought the baby’s own mother.
The princess paid her to nurse him.
When he was older, he was brought to the palace and became her son.
She named him Moses, “because I drew him out of the water.”
He grew up with the best education in Egypt, but he knew he was a Hebrew.
Flight to the desert.
When Moses was grown, he went out to see his people and saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave.
