He looked around, saw no one, and killed the Egyptian, hiding the body in the sand.
The next day, he tried to stop two Hebrews from fighting, and one said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?
Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?”
Moses was afraid, and when Pharaoh heard, he tried to kill Moses. Moses fled.
He went to Midian, east of Egypt, and sat by a well.
He helped seven sisters, the daughters of the priest Jethro, water their flock against some shepherds who drove them away.
Jethro gave him his daughter Zipporah as his wife, and they had a son, Gershom, whose name means “a sojourner there.”
Moses spent forty years in the desert as a shepherd.
The prince of Egypt had become a nobody tending sheep.
It was the training he needed: he learned the wilderness he would one day lead a nation through.
The burning bush.
At the age of eighty, Moses was tending Jethro’s flock near Mount Horeb, also called Sinai, when he saw a bush on fire that was not burning up. He went to look.
God called from the bush, “Moses, Moses!” “Here I am.”
“Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.
I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face.
God said, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt...
So now, go, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.”
Moses made excuse after excuse. “Who am I?” “I will be with you.” “What is your name?” “I AM WHO I AM.”
“What if they do not believe me?”
God gave him signs: the staff that became a snake and a hand that turned leprous. “I am not eloquent.”
“Who has made man’s mouth?...
Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth.”
At last Moses said, “Send someone else.”
God was angry, but He gave him his brother Aaron as a spokesman.
The plagues and the Passover.
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh: “Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.”
Pharaoh said, “Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice?...
I do not know the Lord, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.”
He made the slaves’ work even harder.
Then came the plagues: the Nile turned to blood, frogs, gnats, flies, the death of livestock, boils, hail, locusts and three days of darkness.
Each time, Pharaoh promised and then changed his mind.
The tenth plague was the worst.
God told Israel that each family should take an unblemished lamb, kill it at twilight, put its blood on the doorposts and eat the meal in haste, ready to travel.
“The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are.
And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you.”
At midnight the firstborn of Egypt died, from Pharaoh’s son to the prisoner’s.
Pharaoh called Moses and said, “Up, go out from among my people.”
Israel has celebrated the Passover ever since.
The New Testament calls Jesus “our Passover lamb.”
The Red Sea and Sinai.
About 600,000 men, along with women and children, left Egypt, led by a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
Then Pharaoh changed his mind and chased them with chariots.
Israel was trapped between the army and the Red Sea.
The people cried out in fear.
Moses said, “Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the Lord.”
God told him to lift his staff over the sea.
“The Lord drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.”
Israel crossed on dry ground.
When the Egyptians followed, the waters returned.
Moses and Miriam led the people in a song.
Three months later, they reached Mount Sinai.
God spoke from the mountain in thunder, lightning, smoke and a loud trumpet.
He gave the Ten Commandments, beginning, “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.”
The commandments came after the rescue.
Moses was on the mountain forty days, and God gave him the instructions for the tabernacle and the law.
The golden calf and the wilderness.
While Moses was on the mountain, the people grew restless and asked Aaron, “Make us gods who shall go before us.”
Aaron collected their gold and made a calf.
Moses came down with the two tablets, saw the dancing and smashed them.
God was ready to destroy the people.
Moses prayed, “Alas, this people has sinned a great sin...
But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written.” God relented.
Moses asked, “Please show me your glory.”

God said no one can see His face and live, but He let His goodness pass by and said, “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.”
The people later refused to enter the Promised Land because of the fearful report of ten of the twelve spies.
As a result, they wandered forty years in the wilderness until that generation had passed.
Moses was patient with them but not perfect.
At Meribah, he struck a rock in anger instead of speaking to it as God had commanded, and God told him he would not enter the land.
Mount Nebo.
At the end of the forty years, Israel camped east of the Jordan.
Moses, now 120, gave a long farewell in the book of Deuteronomy.
He told them to remember what God had done, to love the Lord with all their heart, soul and might, and to teach these words to their children.
“I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse.
Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live.”
He gave a blessing to each tribe and appointed Joshua, “Be strong and courageous.”
God told him to climb Mount Nebo.
From the top, he could see the whole land that had been promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
“I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there.”
“So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord...
His eye was undimmed, and his vigor unabated.”
God buried him, and no one knows where.
Centuries later, Moses appeared with Elijah on a mountain beside Jesus at the Transfiguration, finally in the land.
What does this mean for us today?.
Moses’ life has three parts: forty years as a prince, forty years as a shepherd and forty years as a leader.
God did not waste any of them.
The hard years in the desert prepared him for what came next.
If you feel you are in a waiting season, it may be preparation.
Moses also shows that God uses people who feel unqualified.
He said, “Who am I?” and “I am not eloquent,” and God said, “I will be with you.”
What matters is not our strength but His presence.
Finally, the whole Exodus story points to Jesus.
A lamb’s blood saves from death.
A leader brings the people out of slavery.
The law given at a mountain is fulfilled in Him.
The Bible says, “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”
Who Aaron was.
Aaron was the older brother of Moses and Miriam.
He was a Levite, born in Egypt, three years before Moses.
While Moses was raised in Pharaoh’s palace and spent forty years in the desert, Aaron stayed with their people, who were slaves.
When Moses returned at eighty, Aaron was eighty-three.
Aaron became Moses’ spokesman, and then Israel’s first high priest.
His family, the priests, served at the tabernacle, and later at the Temple, for about 1,500 years.
Why his story matters.
Aaron’s life shows what it is to serve alongside a more famous brother, and how a good man can have a serious failure.
He also points forward to Jesus, the final High Priest.
Moses’ spokesman.
When God called Moses at the burning bush to lead Israel out of Egypt, Moses protested: “Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent...
I am slow of speech and of tongue.”
God said, “Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite?
I know that he can speak well.
And behold, he is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you he will be glad in his heart.”
Aaron met Moses at the mountain of God and they embraced.
Together they went to the elders of Israel, and Aaron told them everything God had said.
They went to Pharaoh together.
When Pharaoh demanded a miracle, Aaron threw down his staff and it became a serpent.
Pharaoh’s magicians did the same with their staffs, but Aaron’s serpent swallowed theirs.
For the plagues that followed, Aaron often stretched out the staff over the Nile and the land.
It was clearly a shared mission, though Moses was the leader.
The first high priest.
At Mount Sinai, God gave Moses detailed instructions for the tabernacle and the priesthood.
Aaron was to be high priest, and his sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, were to be priests.
They were consecrated with a seven-day ceremony of washing, anointing with oil and sacrifices.

Aaron’s clothing was beautiful and full of meaning: a blue robe with golden bells and pomegranates on the hem, a linen tunic, and a breastpiece with twelve precious stones, one for each tribe of Israel.
“Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place.”
On his turban was a golden plate engraved “Holy to the Lord.”
Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, he alone could enter the Most Holy Place with blood to make atonement for the people’s sins.
The golden calf.
Moses spent forty days on Mount Sinai.
The people got impatient and went to Aaron: “Up, make us gods who shall go before us.
As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.”
Aaron told them to bring their gold earrings.
He melted them and shaped a golden calf.
“These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!”
He built an altar and announced a feast to the Lord.
The next day they got up early and offered sacrifices and “rose up to play,” a polite way of saying they partied wildly.
God told Moses what was happening, and Moses came down, breaking the stone tablets in his anger.
He confronted Aaron: “What did this people do to you that you have brought such a great sin upon them?”
Aaron’s answer is almost funny, and sad: “They gave me the gold, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf!”
About 3,000 people died that day.
Moses prayed for the people, and in the end God did not destroy them.
Aaron himself was spared.
Fire from the Lord.
After the tabernacle was set up, Aaron and his sons began their work.
On the first day, fire came from the Lord and burned up the offering, and all the people shouted and fell on their faces.
Then two of Aaron’s sons, Nadab and Abihu, took their censers, put fire and incense in them and offered “unauthorized fire before the Lord, which he had not commanded them.”
Fire came out and consumed them.
Moses told Aaron what God had said: “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.”
The Bible adds, “And Aaron held his peace.”
He lost two sons in a day.
He and his family could not even mourn in the usual way since they were in the middle of their service.
The story is a hard one and shows that God is holy, and that approaching Him should not be treated lightly.
The staff that budded.
Later, a man named Korah and 250 others challenged Moses and Aaron: “You have gone too far!
For all in the congregation are holy.”
The ground opened and swallowed Korah and his men, and fire consumed the 250.
When the people grumbled again and blamed Moses and Aaron, a plague broke out.
Aaron ran into the middle of the crowd with his censer of incense and stood “between the dead and the living,” and the plague stopped, but 14,700 had died.
To settle the question of who was chosen, God told Moses to collect twelve staffs, one for each tribe, with Aaron’s name on the one for Levi.
They were placed in the tabernacle overnight.
In the morning, “behold, the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.”
It was placed before the ark as a reminder.
His death on Mount Hor.
Near the end of the forty years, Moses and Aaron were at Meribah, where the people complained again about the lack of water.
God told them to speak to the rock, but Moses struck it twice in anger.
Because they did not trust God enough to honor Him in front of the people, neither Moses nor Aaron would enter the promised land.
God told Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up Mount Hor.
There Moses removed Aaron’s priestly garments and put them on Eleazar.
“And Aaron died there on the top of the mountain.” He was 123.
The whole house of Israel mourned for thirty days.
Aaron’s blessing is still used today: “The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.”
The letter to the Hebrews says that Jesus is a better and permanent High Priest, who “always lives to make intercession” for us.
What does this mean for us today?.
Aaron is a reminder that God uses people with real weaknesses.
He stood by Moses faithfully for years and also gave in to the crowd at the foot of Sinai.
Good leaders can fail, and the Bible does not hide it.
Yet God still gave him the priesthood.
His story also shows how serious and how wonderful it is to approach God.
The priests needed washing, special clothing and a sacrifice every time.
All of that points ahead to Jesus, who made one perfect sacrifice.
The letter to the Hebrews tells us, “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace.”
And Aaron’s blessing is a good prayer for anyone: that the Lord bless you and keep you, and give you peace.
Who Miriam was.
Miriam was the older sister of Moses and Aaron.
She was born in Egypt, in the time when the Israelites were slaves and the king had ordered every newborn Hebrew boy to be thrown into the Nile.
She is the first woman in the Bible called a prophet.
She was probably about ten or twelve years old when her baby brother was born.
Her whole family lived under the threat of death, and she was part of a plan that saved Moses’ life.
Why her story matters.
Miriam shows up at three key moments: when Moses was a baby, when Israel crossed the sea, and when she made a serious mistake.
Her story is about courage, praise, and being forgiven.
The girl by the river.
Moses’ mother hid him for three months.
When she could hide him no longer, she made a small waterproof basket of papyrus, coated it with tar, put the baby inside and set it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile.
The Bible says his sister “stood at a distance to know what would be done to him.”
Tradition has said that this sister was Miriam, though the Bible does not name her here.
Pharaoh’s daughter came to bathe, saw the basket and had pity on the crying baby.
“This is one of the Hebrews’ children,” she said.
Then Moses’ sister stepped forward and asked, “Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” The princess said, “Go.”
The girl brought her own mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said, “Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.”
By being brave and quick, Miriam kept her brother with his own family and raised in the palace, in the very household of the king who wanted him dead.
The song at the sea.
Years later, Moses led Israel out of Egypt.
Pharaoh’s army chased them to the shore of the Red Sea.
God opened the sea, the Israelites crossed on dry land, and the water closed over the Egyptian chariots.
Moses and the people sang a long song of praise to the Lord.
Then the Bible says: “Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.
And Miriam sang to them: ‘Sing to the Lord, for He has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider He has thrown into the sea.’”
Miriam would have been about 85 or 90 years old at the time.
The Bible’s first picture of worship after the rescue shows a woman leading the people in joyful singing and dancing.
The prophet Micah later listed her along with Moses and Aaron as one of the three leaders God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt.
A mistake.
Some time later, Miriam and Aaron began to talk against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married.
Then they said, “Has the Lord indeed spoken only through Moses?
Has He not spoken through us also?”
The Bible adds a remarkable comment: Moses was “very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.”
The Lord heard them.
He called all three to the tent of meeting and came down in a pillar of cloud.
He explained that Moses was different: God spoke to him “mouth to mouth,” clearly, not in riddles.
“Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?”
When the cloud lifted, Miriam’s skin was covered with a white disease, “like snow.”
Aaron begged Moses, “Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly.”
And Moses did something kind: he prayed, “O God, please heal her.”
God said she must be shut outside the camp for seven days, like a person with a skin disease.
And the whole people of Israel waited and did not move on until she was brought back.
Her death.
Near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, the Israelites came to a place called Kadesh in the desert of Zin.
The Bible says, in one short verse, “Miriam died there and was buried there.”
There is no long speech and no long account of her last words, only a quiet record that she was gone.
The very next verse says there was no water for the people, and they grumbled again.
Moses, grieving and tired, struck a rock in anger instead of speaking to it as God had told him.
That moment cost Moses the chance of entering the promised land.
Many have wondered if the loss of his sister, who had been beside him from the very beginning, was part of what he was carrying.
What does this mean for us today?.
Miriam’s life is long, and it has high points and low points.
She was brave as a young girl, joyful as a worship leader, and wrong when she let jealousy talk.
The Bible does not hide her failure, and it also does not forget her as a leader.
The best part of her story is what happened after she was wrong.
Moses prayed for her, God healed her, and the whole nation waited for her to come back.
God’s people do not leave someone behind who has failed and is sorry.
It also reminds us that worship does not need a crowd or a stage.
Miriam’s tambourine and her song were part of the Bible’s record of what God did.
Praise is a good answer to what God has done for us.
Who Joshua was.
Joshua, the son of Nun, was born a slave in Egypt, from the tribe of Ephraim.
His original name was Hoshea, “salvation.”
Moses changed it to Joshua, “the Lord saves.”
In Greek, the same name is Jesus.
He was Moses’ assistant for about forty years, and then he led Israel into the promised land around 1400 BC.
He was a soldier, a leader and, above all, a man who trusted God to do what He said He would do.
Why his story matters.
Joshua’s story is about taking God at His word, finishing what someone else started, and the battles that come before a promise is fully received.
It also gives some of the Bible’s best-known calls to courage.
Moses’ assistant.
Joshua first appears just after the Israelites left Egypt.
A fierce desert tribe, the Amalekites, attacked them.
Moses told Joshua to choose men and fight.
While Joshua fought in the valley, Moses stood on a hilltop with the staff of God in his hands.
When Moses’ arms were up, Israel prevailed; when they dropped, Amalek did.
Aaron and Hur held up Moses’ arms until sunset, and “Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.”
Joshua was also Moses’ close helper.
When Moses went up Mount Sinai, Joshua went partway with him.

When Moses met with God in the tent outside the camp, Joshua stayed in the tent: “When Moses turned again into the camp, his assistant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent.”
He also went as one of the twelve spies and, along with Caleb, brought back a faithful report.
For that, God said they would be the only two of their generation to enter the promised land.
“Be strong and courageous”.
Moses died on Mount Nebo, in sight of the land.
Joshua, perhaps about eighty, was now the leader of two million people and an unfinished task.
God spoke to him: “Moses my servant is dead.
Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them.”
Three times in one chapter, God told him to be strong and courageous.
“No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life.
Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.
I will not leave you or forsake you.”
He also told him how: “This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it.
For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.”
Courage comes from knowing what God has said.
“Have I not commanded you?
Be strong and courageous.
Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go.”
Crossing the Jordan.
It was the time of the spring harvest, and the Jordan River was at flood stage.
Joshua told the priests to carry the ark of the covenant to the water’s edge.
“As soon as the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the Lord... rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off.”
As soon as the priests’ feet touched the water, the river stopped and piled up far upstream near a town called Adam.
The priests stood in the middle of the dry riverbed while the entire nation crossed.
Joshua had twelve men, one from each tribe, take a large stone from the riverbed and set them up at Gilgal, as a memorial.
“When your children ask in time to come, ‘What do those stones mean to you?’ then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off.”
After that, the manna stopped.
Israel ate the produce of the land for the first time.
Jericho and a setback.
Near Jericho, Joshua met a man with a drawn sword.
“Are you for us, or for our adversaries?”
“No; but I am the commander of the army of the Lord.” Joshua fell on his face.
“Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy.”
God gave Joshua a strange plan: march around the city once a day for six days, seven times on the seventh, with priests blowing trumpets.
At the shout, the walls fell flat, and Israel took the city.
Rahab and her family were spared.
God had commanded that everything in Jericho be devoted to Him.
A man named Achan secretly kept a beautiful robe, silver and gold.
When Israel attacked the little town of Ai, they were beaten, and thirty-six men died.
Joshua tore his clothes and fell before the ark.
God told him that someone had sinned.
By lot, Achan was identified.
He confessed, and he and his family were judged in the valley of Achor.
After that, Israel took Ai.
The long day.
The people of Gibeon had tricked Joshua into a treaty, pretending to come from a far country.
When five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon, Joshua marched all night from Gilgal to rescue them.
The Lord threw the enemy into a panic and sent great hailstones from heaven.
More died from hail than from swords.
Then Joshua spoke to the Lord in front of the people: “Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon.”
“And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies...
There has been no day like it before or since, when the Lord heeded the voice of a man, for the Lord fought for Israel.”
The Bible does not explain how it happened.
The point is that God answered a prayer of faith in a big way.
Joshua went on to conquer the south and the north over several years.
“As for me and my house”.
After many years of war, the land was divided among the tribes.
Joshua gave Caleb the hill country of Hebron, and took for himself a city in the hill country of Ephraim, Timnath-serah.
Near the end of his life, he called all Israel to Shechem and reminded them of their history, from Abraham to the conquest.
Then came a challenge: “Now therefore fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness.
Put away the gods that your fathers served...
And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day whom you will serve...
But as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.”
The people answered, “Far be it from us that we should forsake the Lord.”
Joshua warned them, “You are not able to serve the Lord.”
They insisted, so he made a covenant with them and set up a large stone under an oak as a witness.
Joshua died at 110.
The Bible calls him “the servant of the Lord.”
He was buried at Timnath-serah.
The bones of Joseph, which Israel had carried out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem.
“Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Joshua’s courage was not self-confidence.
It was trust in God’s promise.
God said, “I will be with you,” and that was enough.
Whatever Jordan River is in front of you, this is the promise that matters.
Joshua’s story also shows that obedience is not always logical.
Marching around a city, walking into a flooded river and asking the sun to stop all seem odd.
But God does not always use the method we would pick. He asks us to trust.
And his famous line is a good one to keep: “Choose this day whom you will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.”
A good life and a good family are built by a decision made again and again.
The name Joshua is the same as Jesus.
The first Joshua led Israel into the promised land, and Jesus leads His people into God’s rest.
Who Caleb was.
Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, was a man of the tribe of Judah who lived about 1400 BC.
He grew up as a slave in Egypt, saw the plagues, crossed the Red Sea, and stood at the foot of Mount Sinai when God gave the Law.
By the time of this story he was about 40 years old.
He was one of the twelve men Moses chose to explore the land of Canaan, the land God had promised to Abraham’s family.
Why his story matters.
Caleb’s story is about a person who trusted God when almost everyone else did not.
It also shows what it means to follow God “wholeheartedly,” a phrase the Bible uses about Caleb more than once.
Twelve spies.
Israel had been camped for a long time in the wilderness, and now they stood on the border of the promised land.
Moses sent twelve men, one from each tribe, to see what the land and the people were like. Caleb represented Judah.
Joshua represented Ephraim.
For forty days they traveled through the land.
They came to Hebron, where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were buried, and to the valley of Eshcol.
There they cut a single cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole between them, along with pomegranates and figs.
When they returned, they showed the fruit to everyone: “It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit.”
A different report.
Then ten of the spies added: “But the people who live there are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large.
We also saw descendants of Anak there.”
The Anakites were famous for their size.
The ten said, “We seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and we looked the same to them.”
The people cried all night.
Some said they should choose a new leader and go back to Egypt.
Caleb tried to calm them: “We should go up and take possession of the land, for we are well able to overcome it.”
Caleb and Joshua tore their clothes and said, “The land is exceedingly good.
If the Lord delights in us, He will bring us into this land.
Only do not rebel against the Lord.
Do not fear the people of the land. The Lord is with us.”
The crowd threatened to stone them.
Forty years.
God was angry that after all He had done, they still would not trust Him.
He said that no one from that generation over twenty years old, except Caleb and Joshua, would see the land.
They would wander in the wilderness one year for every day the spies had explored: forty years.
The ten spies who had spread fear died of a plague.
About Caleb, God said, “My servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed Me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it.”
Caleb then spent forty years in the desert, watching all his friends die one by one.
He could have given up or become bitter.
The Bible does not say he did.
Over those years he kept trusting the promise.
“Give me this mountain”.
After Moses died, Joshua led Israel into the land. The conquest took years.
Eventually, as the land was being divided among the tribes, Caleb came to Joshua at Gilgal.
He said: “I was forty years old when Moses sent me to spy out the land.
And now, behold, I am eighty-five years old.
I am still as strong today as the day Moses sent me.
As my strength was then, so my strength is now, for war and for going and coming.”
Then he made his request: “So now give me this hill country of which the Lord spoke on that day.
For you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities.
It may be that the Lord will be with me, and I shall drive them out as the Lord said.”
In other words, at 85 he asked for the hardest place of all, the very mountain full of the giants that had frightened Israel.
Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron.
Caleb drove out the three Anakite clans, and the land had rest from war.
A family of faith.
Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captured the city of Kiriath Sepher.
His nephew Othniel did it and married her.
Othniel later became the first of Israel’s judges and rescued Israel from an invader.
When Achsah married, she asked her father for a field, and then for something more: “Give me a blessing.
Since you have given me land in the Negeb, give me also springs of water.”
Caleb gave her upper and lower springs.
Water was life in a dry land, and she was wise to ask.
Caleb’s home was marked by trust in God and boldness in asking.
Hebron, Caleb’s mountain, kept its place in the story.
Centuries later it became the first capital of King David.
What does this mean for us today?.
Caleb teaches us that a majority can be wrong.
Ten of the twelve spies saw the same land and the same giants as Caleb.
The difference was not what they saw.
It was whom they were looking at.
Caleb looked at the Lord first.
His story also shows that faith lasts.
It is one thing to be brave on a good day.
Caleb held on to a promise for 45 years and still asked for a mountain at age 85.
Following God can be a long road, and the Bible says it is worth it.
If you are older, Caleb’s story says it is never too late to take a mountain.
And if you are young, it says that who you follow now will shape the rest of your life.
Who Rahab was.
Rahab lived in Jericho, a walled city in the Jordan valley, about 1400 BC.
Her house was built into the city wall.
The Bible calls her a prostitute.
That means she was part of a pagan city and lived a life God’s law did not approve of.
She was an outsider to Israel in every way: wrong nation, wrong religion, wrong reputation.
Yet she appears in the Bible as a woman of great faith, and she is named in the family line of Jesus.
Why her story matters.
Rahab’s story shows that God’s mercy reaches people no one else would choose.
It also shows what faith looks like when it has to act.
Two spies at her door.
Israel had finally arrived at the east bank of the Jordan River after forty years in the wilderness.
Moses had died, and Joshua was now the leader.
Joshua secretly sent two spies across the river to look at the land, especially Jericho, the first big city in their way.
The two men went to Rahab’s house.
Maybe it was a place where strangers would not be noticed.
But someone saw them, and the king of Jericho was told.
He sent a message to Rahab: “Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land.”
This was dangerous.
If she was caught hiding enemies, she could be killed.
If she gave them up, they would die.
Hiding the spies.
Rahab had already taken the two men up to the roof and hidden them under stalks of flax that she had laid out there.
To the king’s messengers, she said, “True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from.
And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out.
I do not know where the men went.
Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them.”
The messengers left, and the city gate was shut behind them.
The Bible’s later comments on Rahab’s lie are not about the lie itself.
They praise what she did: she protected God’s servants at great risk to herself.
A confession of faith.
Before the men went to sleep, Rahab went up to the roof and said: “I know that the Lord has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us.
All the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.
For we have heard how the Lord dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt...
And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the Lord your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.”
Notice what she says: they had heard the stories from forty years before, and the people of Jericho were terrified, but only Rahab drew the right conclusion.
She said that the Lord is God.
Then she asked for a favor: “Please swear to me by the Lord that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father’s house.”
The spies agreed: “Our life for yours!”
They told her to tie a scarlet cord in her window and keep her whole family inside her house.
Then she let the men down by a rope through the window, since her house was on the wall.
When the walls fell.
A few weeks later Israel crossed the Jordan.
God told Joshua to march the army around Jericho once a day for six days, with priests carrying the ark and blowing trumpets.
On the seventh day they marched around seven times.
Then the priests blew the trumpets, the people shouted, and the walls of the city fell flat.
Before the attack, Joshua told the two spies, “Go into the prostitute’s house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her.”
They brought out Rahab, her father, mother, brothers and all her family.
The Bible says she “has lived in Israel to this day.”
Rahab in the family of Jesus.
The story does not end at Jericho.
Matthew’s Gospel opens with Jesus’ family tree.
In it, we read: “Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab.”
Rahab married an Israelite named Salmon, and their son was Boaz, the kind man who later married Ruth.
Boaz’s grandson was Jesse, and Jesse’s son was King David.
And from David came Jesus.
So the woman from Jericho became part of the line of the Messiah.
Matthew, who mentions only four women in his genealogy besides Mary, names Rahab among them.
The New Testament also praises her twice.
The letter to the Hebrews says, “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.”
James says she was shown to be right with God by what she did.
What does this mean for us today?.
Rahab is proof that no one is too far from God.
Her past, her city and her reputation were all against her, yet she is remembered for her faith, not her failures.
The Bible says what matters is not where you came from, but what you do with what you have heard about God.
Her faith was practical.
She did not just believe in her heart; she risked her life and her home.
And the scarlet cord on her window has long reminded people of how God saves: those inside the marked house were spared.
If you have ever felt you are too far gone to belong, Rahab is the answer.
God put a woman from the wrong side of the wall into the family tree of His own Son.
Who Deborah was.
Deborah lived about 1200 BC, in the time of the judges.
This was a period when Israel kept turning away from God, being attacked by neighbors, crying out for help, and being rescued by a leader God raised up.
Deborah was one of those leaders, and the only woman among the judges.
The Bible calls her a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth.
She held court under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, and Israelites came to her to settle their disputes.
Why her story matters.
Deborah’s story is about faith, leadership and teamwork.
It shows that God uses people of any background, and that the real victory belongs to the Lord.
Twenty years of oppression.
Israel had done evil again, and God let them fall into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, who ruled from the city of Hazor in the north.
His army commander was Sisera, and he had 900 chariots fitted with iron.
For the Israelite farmers, who fought on foot with simple weapons, that was a terrifying force, especially on flat ground.
“And he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.”
Finally the people cried out to the Lord for help.
The roads were unsafe, and villagers stopped traveling.
God’s answer came through a woman sitting under a tree.
The call to Barak.
Deborah sent for a man named Barak, from the tribe of Naphtali.
She said to him: “Has not the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you, ‘Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and Zebulun.
And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin’s army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand’?”
Barak answered, “If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go.”
It was either caution or a wish for Deborah’s support.
Deborah said: “I will surely go with you.
Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the Lord will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.”
She went with him, and the army gathered.
The battle at the Kishon.
Sisera heard that Barak was at Mount Tabor, and he brought all 900 chariots and his army to the Kishon River in the valley below.
Deborah said to Barak, “Up!
For this is the day in which the Lord has given Sisera into your hand.
Does not the Lord go out before you?”
Barak led the 10,000 men down the mountain.
“And the Lord routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword.”
Deborah’s victory song later says that heavy rain flooded the Kishon, “the torrent Kishon swept them away,” which would have turned the plain to mud and trapped chariots.
The great strength of Sisera’s army became a trap.
Sisera jumped down from his chariot and fled on foot.
The whole army was killed.
Jael and the tent peg.
Sisera ran to the tent of a woman named Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite.
Heber’s family was at peace with King Jabin, so Sisera thought he would be safe.
Jael welcomed him: “Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid.”
She covered him with a rug, gave him milk when he asked for water, and promised to say no one was there.
Exhausted, Sisera fell asleep.
Jael took a tent peg and a hammer, went quietly to him and drove the peg through his head into the ground.
When Barak arrived looking for Sisera, Jael went out to meet him: “Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking.”
He was lying dead with the tent peg in his temple.
Just as Deborah had said, the honor of killing Sisera went to a woman.
Soon after, the Israelites destroyed King Jabin as well.
The song of Deborah.
Deborah and Barak then sang a long song that is one of the oldest poems in the Bible.
It begins, “That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the Lord!”
It praises the tribes who came to fight and mentions those who stayed home.
It describes how the stars and the river fought against Sisera. And it praises Jael.
Deborah also describes herself in the song: “Until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel.”
The song ends with a prayer: “So may all your enemies perish, O Lord!
But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.”
The Bible then says, “And the land had rest for forty years.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Deborah shows that God does not look for the person that culture expects.
She had no army, no throne, no title beyond the judge’s seat under a palm tree.
But she listened to God, spoke clearly and led with courage.
Her faith gave Barak courage, too.
Her story also shows teamwork.
Deborah, Barak, Jael and 10,000 ordinary soldiers each had a part. Nobody did it alone.
The Bible’s praise goes to “those who offered themselves willingly.”
And note who gets the credit: the Lord.
The song says, “To the Lord I will sing; I will make melody to the Lord, the God of Israel.”
When we are faced with a force that looks too big, the question is not whether we have the iron chariots.
It is whether God is going out before us.
Who Gideon was.
Gideon was a judge of Israel, about 1150 BC.
He came from the tribe of Manasseh and lived in the village of Ophrah.

For seven years Israel had been under the harsh control of the Midianites, a nomadic people from the desert who came every harvest like swarms of locusts with their camels, destroying crops and livestock.
The Israelites hid in mountain caves and dens.
God chose a young man who was hiding his own grain from the raiders.
Why his story matters.
Gideon’s story is about God using someone who feels small, afraid and unqualified.
It shows how God wins victories in a way that makes sure He gets the credit.
Threshing wheat in a winepress.
Gideon was threshing wheat inside a winepress, a pit in the ground, to hide it from the Midianites.
Normal threshing was done on an open hilltop where the wind could blow away the chaff.
Gideon was clearly afraid.
The angel of the Lord sat down under an oak and said, “The Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor.”
Gideon’s answer was blunt: “Please, my lord, if the Lord is with us, why then has all this happened to us?
And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us?”
The Lord told him, “Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?”
Gideon objected: “Please, Lord, how can I save Israel?
Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.”
God said, “But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.”
Tearing down the idol.
Before Gideon could lead, he had to deal with the idols at home.
God told him to take his father’s bull and pull down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.
Gideon took ten servants and did it at night, because he feared his family and the townspeople.
In the morning the town was furious and demanded Gideon be killed.
His father, Joash, surprised everyone: “Will you contend for Baal?
If he is a god, let him contend for himself.”
Gideon was given a new name, Jerubbaal, “let Baal contend against him.”
The Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon, and he blew a trumpet, calling the Israelites to gather. Tens of thousands came.
But Gideon still had doubts.
The fleece.
Gideon asked God for proof.
“If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor.
If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand.”
In the morning he wrung out a bowl of water from the fleece, and the ground was dry.
Then he asked for it the other way: dry fleece and dew on the ground. God did that too.
The Bible does not criticize Gideon for asking.
God was patient with his fear.
It is worth noticing, though, that God had already clearly said what He would do.
The fleece was not so much about finding God’s will as about building Gideon’s trust.
Too many soldiers.
Gideon had 32,000 men.
The Midianites had 135,000.
But God said, “The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’”
He told Gideon to announce, “Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return.”
Twenty-two thousand went home. Ten thousand remained.
“The people are still too many.”
God told him to take them down to the water.
Those who knelt and drank directly with their mouths went on one side.
Those who scooped water in their hands and lapped it like a dog went on another side. Only 300 lapped.
“With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand.”
Gideon was now outnumbered by about 450 to 1.
That night, God told him that if he was still afraid, he could sneak down to the Midianite camp.
He heard a man telling his friend a dream of a loaf of barley bread that tumbled into the camp and knocked down a tent.
His friend said, “This is no other than the sword of Gideon...
God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp.”
Gideon worshiped, and returned to the camp with confidence.
Trumpets and jars.
Gideon gave every man a trumpet and an empty clay jar with a torch inside.
“Look at me, and do likewise.”
About midnight, just after the guards changed, the 300 men surrounded the Midianite camp.
On Gideon’s signal they blew their trumpets, smashed the jars and held up their torches, shouting, “A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!”
“Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran.
They cried out and fled.”
In the confusion the Midianites turned their swords on each other.
The huge army fled across the Jordan, and Israelite forces from several tribes chased them.
Gideon pursued and captured the two Midianite kings, Zebah and Zalmunna.
The Midianites “lifted up their heads no more.”
The victory was so well known that centuries later the prophet Isaiah called it “the day of Midian.”
After the victory.
The Israelites came to Gideon: “Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian.”
He said, “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you.” It was a good answer.
Then he asked for something: the gold earrings from the plunder.
It came to about 1,700 shekels of gold.
He made an ephod, a priestly garment, and put it in his hometown.
“And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house.”
Gideon had 70 sons from many wives, and one concubine’s son, Abimelech, later murdered his brothers and tried to make himself king.
The land had peace for forty years during Gideon’s lifetime.
When he died, the people again turned to Baal.
Still, the book of Hebrews lists Gideon among those who “through faith conquered kingdoms... were made strong out of weakness.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Gideon wasn’t a natural hero.
He was scared and asked for proof twice.
But God called him a mighty man of valor before he had done anything.
God sees what He is going to do in us before we do.
The 300 men show us that God likes to work in a way that gets Him the glory.
If Israel had won with 32,000, they would have taken credit.
God used a small, odd force and made it clear whose victory it was.
Gideon’s story ends with a warning.
He could resist being a king but still got caught by a golden ephod. Success can be a danger.
A good start does not finish the race, and every generation has to choose to follow God.
Who Samson was.
Samson was one of the judges of Israel, about 1100 BC.
He came from the tribe of Dan and the village of Zorah.
For forty years, Israel had been under the control of the Philistines, a strong people on the coast with iron weapons.
The Philistines were the main danger in Samson’s time, and also in the time of Saul and David.
Samson is known for his enormous physical strength.
But his story is also one of the saddest in the Bible: a man with great gifts who kept making bad choices.
Why his story matters.
Samson’s story is about a person set apart by God from before birth, and how he nearly threw it away.
It shows God’s patience, and that He can use even a flawed person to do His work.
A promised baby.
Manoah and his wife had no children.
The angel of the Lord appeared to the woman and said she would have a son.
“Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son.
No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines.”
A Nazirite was someone who made a special vow to God.
He could not drink wine, touch a dead body or cut his hair.
Normally it was a temporary vow, but Samson’s was for life.
Manoah prayed that the man of God would come back to teach them how to raise the child.
The angel came again and repeated the instructions.
When Manoah offered a sacrifice, the angel went up in the flame, and the couple fell on their faces.
The boy was born and named Samson.
“The boy grew, and the Lord blessed him.
And the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him.”
A lion, a riddle and a bad choice.
Samson went down to the Philistine town of Timnah and saw a young woman he wanted to marry.
His parents objected: “Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?”
He insisted: “Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes.”
The Bible adds that this was “from the Lord,” who was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines.
On the way, a young lion attacked him, and “the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and though he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat.”
Later he passed the carcass and found bees and honey in it.
He scooped out some honey and ate it, breaking his Nazirite vow, since he had touched a dead animal.
At the wedding feast he gave thirty Philistine men a riddle: “Out of the eater came something to eat.
Out of the strong came something sweet.”
His bride was pressured by her people and pried the answer out of him by crying for seven days. The men answered.
Furious, Samson went to Ashkelon, killed thirty Philistines and gave their clothes to the men.
His wife was then given to another man.
A jawbone.
Samson took revenge by catching 300 foxes, tying torches to their tails and setting them loose in the Philistines’ grain fields, vineyards and olive groves.
The Philistines retaliated by burning his wife and her father.
Samson attacked them “hip and thigh with a great slaughter.”
The Philistines then came to Lehi in Judah, demanding Samson.
Three thousand men of Judah went to get him, and Samson let them tie him with two new ropes.
When he came to Lehi, “the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire.”
He grabbed the jawbone of a donkey and killed a thousand men.
Exhausted, he cried out to God, “You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst?”
God split a hollow place in the ground and water came out.
The Bible says that “he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.”
Delilah.
Samson fell in love with a woman named Delilah, who lived in the valley of Sorek.
The Philistine rulers came to her and each offered 1,100 pieces of silver if she would find out the secret of his great strength.
Three times she asked, and three times he gave a false answer: bind me with seven fresh bowstrings, with new ropes, or weave my hair into a loom.
Each time she called, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” and each time he broke free.
Yet he did not leave her.
Day after day she nagged him, “until his soul was vexed to death.”
At last he told her everything: “A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb.
If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me.”
Delilah lulled him to sleep on her lap and had a man shave off his seven locks.
“And his strength left him.”
She called, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!”
He woke and thought, “I will go out as at other times and shake myself free.”
“But he did not know that the Lord had left him.”
Blind and bound.
The Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes and took him down to Gaza.
They bound him with bronze shackles and made him grind grain in the prison, work normally done by slaves and animals.
The man who had once carried off the gates of their city was now blind and chained.
“But the hair of his head began to grow again after it was shaved.”
The Bible does not say much, but the sign is clear: God had not given up on him.
The Philistine rulers held a great feast in the temple of their god Dagon, to celebrate.
“Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hands.”
They brought Samson out to entertain them.
About 3,000 people were on the roof, and the temple was full of men and women.
His last prayer.
Samson asked the young servant leading him by the hand to let him feel the pillars supporting the building so that he could lean against them.

Then he prayed, for the first time in the story, a prayer of real dependence: “O Lord God, please remember me, please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes.”
He took hold of the two middle pillars and braced himself, his right hand on one and his left on the other.
“Let me die with the Philistines.”
He pushed with all his might, and the house fell on the rulers and all the people inside.
“So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.”
His brothers and family came down and buried him in the tomb of his father Manoah.
Though Samson was flawed, the book of Hebrews lists him among the people of faith.
He did what God had called him to do: he “began to save Israel.”
Completing it was left to Samuel and David.
What does this mean for us today?.
Samson was gifted and foolish.
He kept going back to the people and places that harmed him.
The Bible shows that talent and God’s calling do not make a person wise.
Character, daily obedience and humility matter a great deal.
Small compromises, like the honey from the lion, led to bigger ones.
But the story also shows God’s mercy.
At the very end, Samson prayed, and God answered.
It was never too late for him to turn back, and it is never too late for us.
His strength, we are told, came from the Spirit of the Lord, not from his hair.
The hair was a sign of his vow.
When he stopped honoring the vow, he lost the sign, and without knowing it, he lost the relationship.
The warning is to keep our hearts close to God.
Who Ruth was.
Ruth was a young woman from Moab, a country east of the Dead Sea.
The Moabites were Israel’s neighbors and often their enemies, and they worshiped a god named Chemosh.
Ruth lived about 1100 BC, in the time of the judges, a time of trouble in Israel.
Her story starts with an Israelite family from Bethlehem, which means “house of bread.”
There was a famine in Bethlehem, so a man named Elimelech took his wife Naomi and two sons, Mahlon and Chilion, to live in Moab.
Ruth’s story begins with tragedy.
Why her story matters.
The book of Ruth is a short love story and also a story of loyalty, kindness and God’s care in ordinary life.
Ruth, an outsider, became the great-grandmother of King David and an ancestor of Jesus.
Three widows.
In Moab, Elimelech died.
Naomi’s two sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth.
After about ten years, both sons died too.
Naomi was left with two daughters-in-law and no one else.
She was far from home with no income, no children and no husband.
When she heard that God had provided food in Bethlehem, she decided to go back.
She urged her daughters-in-law to return to their own families.
“The Lord grant that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband!”
Orpah kissed her and went back.
But Ruth would not leave.
Her answer is one of the most famous in the Bible: “Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you.
For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge.
Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.
Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried.
May the Lord do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you.”
Naomi saw that Ruth was determined, and said no more.
Gleaning in the field.
They arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
The whole town was stirred.
“Is this Naomi?” the women asked.
She said, “Do not call me Naomi (pleasant); call me Mara (bitter), for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.”
God’s law told farmers to leave the edges of their fields and any fallen grain for the poor, the foreigner and the widow.
Ruth went out to glean, which meant walking behind the harvesters picking up leftover stalks.
It was hard, humbling work.
“As it happened, she came to the part of the field belonging to Boaz,” a relative of Naomi’s late husband.
The Bible says “as it happened,” but the story makes clear that God was leading her.
Boaz, a wealthy and respected man, arrived from town and greeted his workers, “The Lord be with you!” “The Lord bless you.”
He noticed Ruth and asked who she was.
Boaz’s kindness.
The foreman told Boaz she was the Moabite who came back with Naomi and had been working hard since morning.
Boaz went to her: “Now, listen, my daughter, do not go to glean in another field or leave this one, but keep close to my young women.
Let your eyes be on the field that they are reaping, and go after them.
Have I not charged the young men not to touch you?
And when you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn.”
Ruth bowed to the ground and asked, “Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?”

Boaz answered that he had heard what she had done for her mother-in-law: “The Lord repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge!”
At mealtime he invited her to eat with them, gave her roasted grain until she was full and had some left over, and secretly told his workers to pull out stalks for her to find.
She came home with about an ephah of barley, nearly a bushel, and Naomi said, “Blessed be the man who took notice of you!”
It turned out Boaz was a close relative, one of the family’s “redeemers.”
At the threshing floor.
A “kinsman-redeemer” was a close relative who could buy back a family’s land and marry a widow to carry on the family name.
Naomi told Ruth to wash, put on perfume and her best clothes, and go to the threshing floor at night where Boaz was sleeping after the harvest feast.
She was to lie down at his feet and ask him to be her redeemer.
In the night, Boaz woke up and found a woman at his feet. “Who are you?”
“I am Ruth, your servant.
Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer.”
Boaz was kind and respectful.
“May you be blessed by the Lord, my daughter.
You have made this last kindness greater than the first in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich.
And now, my daughter, do not fear.
I will do for you all that you ask, for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman.”
But there was a complication: another relative was closer than he was.
Boaz sent her home before dawn with six measures of barley, so no one would gossip.
The wedding.
Boaz went up to the town gate, where business was done, and sat down with ten elders.
When the closer relative came by, Boaz told him that Naomi was selling her late husband’s land, and gave him first chance. “I will redeem it.”
Then Boaz added that he would also have to marry Ruth the Moabite, to raise up an heir for her dead husband.
The man said, “I cannot redeem it, lest I impair my own inheritance.”
He took off his sandal to seal the deal.
Boaz announced to the elders, “You are witnesses this day that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech...
Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife.”
The elders and the people said, “May the Lord make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel.”
Boaz and Ruth married, and they had a son.
The women said to Naomi: “Blessed be the Lord, who has not left you this day without a redeemer...
He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him.”
Naomi took the baby and held him on her lap.
A king’s grandmother.
The neighbor women named the baby Obed.
He became the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.
The book ends with the family line from Perez to David.
That list shows that Ruth, a Moabite foreigner, became the great-grandmother of Israel’s greatest king.
The story continues to the New Testament.
In Matthew’s Gospel, the family tree of Jesus includes “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth.”
Only five women are mentioned in that genealogy, and Ruth is one of them.
The family of the Messiah included a widow from a foreign land, a woman who chose loyalty and faith.
What does this mean for us today?.
Ruth’s story shows how God works in ordinary events.
There are no miracles in the book, no angels or fire from heaven.
There are famine, grief, a field, a man’s kindness and a decision to be loyal.
Yet in all of it, God was bringing about something big.
Ruth’s love was costly and practical.
She left her home to care for an older woman who could give her nothing.
Real love often looks like that: staying when it would be easier to go.
And Boaz is a picture of Jesus.
He saw a poor foreigner, welcomed her, provided for her and paid the price to make her part of his family.
The Bible says that Jesus is our Redeemer, who took notice of us when we had nothing and brought us into His family.
Who Hannah was.
Hannah lived in the hill country of Ephraim around 1100 BC, in the time of the judges, a period of Israel’s history when, as the Bible puts it, “everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
Her husband Elkanah loved her deeply.
But Hannah had a great sorrow: she could not have children.
In that culture, a woman with no children often felt shame and was looked down on.
Elkanah also had another wife, Peninnah, who had many children and who made a habit of taunting Hannah.
Why her story matters.
Hannah’s prayer in Shiloh is one of the best-known prayers in the Bible.
Her story is about bringing real pain to God, and about what happens when we give back to Him what He gives us.
Years of sorrow.
Every year the family traveled to Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, to worship and offer a sacrifice.
Elkanah gave Peninnah’s children their portions of the meat.
To Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, though “the Lord had closed her womb.”
Peninnah used these trips to hurt Hannah.
“Year by year, as often as she went up to the house of the Lord, she used to provoke her.
Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat.”
Elkanah tried to comfort her: “Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart sad?
Am I not more to you than ten sons?”
He meant well, but he did not understand.
Her husband’s love did not take away her longing for a child.
A prayer with tears.
After one of the meals, Hannah got up and went to pray.
The priest Eli was sitting by the doorpost of the tabernacle.
Hannah was “deeply distressed and prayed to the Lord and wept bitterly.”

She made a vow: “O Lord of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me, and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head.”
She prayed so long, and her lips moved but no sound came out, that Eli thought she was drunk.
He scolded her: “How long will you go on being drunk?
Put your wine away from you.”
Hannah answered, “No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit.
I have been pouring out my soul before the Lord.”
Eli realized his mistake and said, “Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to him.”
The Bible says she went on her way and ate.
“And her face was no longer sad.”
She had not yet received an answer, but she had given her burden to God.
A son named Samuel.
The next year, Hannah had a son.
She named him Samuel, a name that sounds like the Hebrew for “heard by God.”
“Because I have asked for him from the Lord.”
When the family went to Shiloh the next year, Hannah stayed home.
She told her husband, “After the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear in the presence of the Lord and dwell there forever.”
In that time, children were often nursed for about three years.
When the day came, Hannah brought Samuel to Shiloh with a three-year-old bull, a measure of flour and a skin of wine.
She found Eli and said: “Oh, my lord!
As you live, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here in your presence, praying to the Lord.
For this child I prayed, and the Lord has granted me my petition that I made to him.
Therefore I have lent him to the Lord.
As long as he lives, he is lent to the Lord.”
She left the little boy with Eli, to grow up serving at the tabernacle.
Hannah’s song.
Hannah then prayed again, this time not with tears but with praise.
“My heart exults in the Lord; my horn is exalted in the Lord.
My mouth derides my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation.
There is none holy like the Lord: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God.”
Her song says that God turns things upside down.
“The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength.
Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger.
The barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn.
The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts.
He raises up the poor from the dust.”
The song ends by looking forward to a king, “His anointed.”
Centuries later, Mary’s song after learning she would bear Jesus echoes Hannah’s words in many places.
What happened next.
Hannah did not forget her son.
Every year she made him a small robe and brought it to him at Shiloh when the family went up for the sacrifice.
Eli blessed Elkanah and Hannah, asking the Lord to give them children to replace the one they had given.
“And the Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters.”
Meanwhile, Samuel grew up in the tabernacle.
The Bible says, “The boy Samuel grew in the presence of the Lord,” and that he “continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the Lord and also with man.”
He became one of the greatest prophets in Israel’s history, the one who anointed both Saul and David as king.
What does this mean for us today?.
Hannah brought her honest sorrow to God.
She did not pretend to be fine.
The Bible shows that God welcomes tears and long prayers, even when other people misunderstand them.
She also kept her promise.
The child she had waited years for, she gave back to the Lord.
It must have been hard to leave her little boy at Shiloh, but her trust paid off beyond what she could imagine.
Her son changed a nation.
Whatever you are waiting for or asking God for, Hannah shows a way to pray: pour out your heart, trust, and leave the answer with Him.
Not every prayer is answered the way hers was, but the Bible says God hears each one.
Who Samuel was.
Samuel was the last of Israel’s judges and one of its greatest prophets, living about 1100 to 1020 BC.
He was born in answer to his mother Hannah’s prayer, and she gave him to serve at the tabernacle in Shiloh when he was a small child.
He grew up with the old priest Eli, in a time when the nation was in trouble.
Samuel is the link between two eras: the rough, unstable time of the judges, and the time of the kings.
He anointed Israel’s first two kings, Saul and David.
Why his story matters.
Samuel’s life is about listening to God and speaking His word, even when it is hard.
It is also about what happens when a nation asks for a king instead of trusting God.
The voice in the night.
In those days, “the word of the Lord was rare; there was no frequent vision.”
Eli was old, almost blind.
His two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests, but they were corrupt: they stole from the offerings and mistreated the people.
One night, Samuel was lying down in the tabernacle near the ark of God when he heard a voice: “Samuel!”
He ran to Eli, “Here I am, for you called me.”
“I did not call; lie down again.”
It happened a second time, then a third.
Then Eli understood that the Lord was calling the boy.
He told Samuel, “Go, lie down, and if he calls you, you shall say, ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.’”
Samuel did.
The Lord told him a hard message: He was about to judge Eli’s family, because Eli’s sons were wicked and Eli had not stopped them.
In the morning Samuel was afraid to tell Eli. Eli made him say it all. “It is the Lord.
Let him do what seems good to him.”
From then on, the Bible says, “the Lord was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.”
All Israel knew that Samuel was a prophet.
The ark is lost.
Some years later, Israel went to war with the Philistines and lost about 4,000 men.
The elders decided to bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh into the camp, as though it were a good luck charm.
They shouted so loudly the ground shook.
But the Philistines won an even bigger victory, killing 30,000 Israelite soldiers, killing Eli’s two sons and capturing the ark itself.
A messenger ran to Shiloh with the news.
Eli, 98 years old and blind, was sitting by the gate.
When he heard the ark had been taken, he fell backward off his seat, broke his neck and died.
His daughter-in-law, in labor, named her newborn son Ichabod, meaning “the glory has departed from Israel.”
But the Philistines found the ark was no trophy.
Wherever they put it, they suffered plagues, and after seven months they sent it back to Israel.
Ebenezer.
For twenty years Israel was oppressed.

Then Samuel told the people: “If you are returning to the Lord with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the Lord and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.” They did.
Samuel gathered everyone at Mizpah and prayed for them.
When the Philistines came up to attack, the Lord thundered with a great voice against them, and they were thrown into confusion.
Israel chased them and won.
Afterward Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen.
He named it Ebenezer, which means “stone of help,” and said: “Till now the Lord has helped us.”
Samuel became a judge who traveled every year to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, and then returned home to Ramah to settle disputes and build an altar.
“Give us a king”.
As Samuel grew old, he made his sons judges, but they took bribes and did not follow his example.
The elders came to Samuel and said, “Appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations.” Samuel was upset.
But the Lord said to him, “Obey the voice of the people... for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.”
Samuel warned them what a king would do: take their sons for the army, their daughters to work in the palace, their best fields and a tenth of everything they had. They said, “No!
But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations.”
God led Samuel to a tall young man named Saul.
Samuel poured oil on his head and kissed him: “Has not the Lord anointed you to be prince over his people Israel?”
He presented Saul before all Israel at Mizpah, and the people shouted, “Long live the king!”
Saul rejected, David anointed.
Saul began well, but he did not stay faithful.
Twice he disobeyed God’s instructions.
The second time, he spared the best of the Amalekites’ livestock, when God had told him to destroy everything.
When Samuel confronted him, Saul said he saved the animals to sacrifice to the Lord.
Samuel answered: “Has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying the voice of the Lord?
Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.”
Then he told Saul that the Lord had rejected him as king.
Samuel mourned for Saul.
God said, “How long will you grieve over Saul?
Fill your horn with oil and go.
I will send you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons.”
Samuel looked at Jesse’s oldest, tall and impressive Eliab, and thought, “Surely the Lord’s anointed is before him.”
God said, “Do not look on his appearance...
For the Lord sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.”
Seven sons passed by, and none was chosen.
“Are all your sons here?”
“There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep.”
David was brought in, and God said, “Arise, anoint him, for this is he.”
Samuel anointed him in front of his brothers, and the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon David.
What does this mean for us today?.
Samuel’s answer to God as a boy is a good prayer for anyone: “Speak, for your servant is listening.”
He spent his whole life saying it.
He spoke hard words to Eli, to Israel and to Saul, and none of what he said fell to the ground.
The story also shows that God cares about the heart.
People saw tall Saul and tall Eliab.
God saw David, a shepherd nobody had thought to invite.
When we judge by appearance, we often miss what God is doing.
Finally, “Till now the Lord has helped us” is a good stone to set up in our own lives.
Looking back and remembering how God has helped is one way to trust Him for what comes next.
Who Saul was.
Saul was the first king of Israel, around 1050 BC.
He came from the tribe of Benjamin, the smallest of the twelve tribes.
His father was Kish, a wealthy man.
The Bible describes Saul as a handsome young man and the tallest man in Israel, “from his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people.”
Israel had never had a king.
For centuries, the tribes had been led by judges.
Now the people were being attacked by the Philistines and others, and they wanted a king “like all the nations.”
God told the prophet Samuel to give them one.
Why his story matters.
Saul’s story is one of the saddest in the Bible.
He started well and ended in ruin.
It shows how a person with every advantage can lose it all through pride, disobedience and jealousy.
Looking for donkeys.
Saul was sent by his father to look for some lost donkeys.
After days of searching, his servant suggested they ask the prophet in the nearby town for help. That prophet was Samuel.
The day before, God had told Samuel, “Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel.”
When Samuel saw Saul he knew.
“Behold the man of whom I spoke to you!
He it is who shall restrain my people.”
Saul answered with surprising humility: “Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel?
And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin?”
Samuel gave him a place of honor at the feast and the next morning poured oil on his head and kissed him.
When Samuel later announced him as king before all Israel, they could not find him.
“He has hidden himself among the baggage.”
They ran and brought him out, and he stood head and shoulders above everyone. “Long live the king!”
A good beginning.
Soon after, Nahash, king of the Ammonites, surrounded the town of Jabesh-gilead and said he would make peace only if he could put out every man’s right eye.
The people of the city sent for help.
When Saul heard, the Spirit of God came upon him powerfully.
He cut up a pair of oxen and sent the pieces through all Israel, saying that anyone who did not follow him would be treated the same way. Over 300,000 men came.
Saul divided them into three groups and attacked at dawn, and the Ammonites were routed.
The people wanted to kill those who had earlier doubted Saul as king.
Saul said, “Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the Lord has worked salvation in Israel.”
At this point, Saul gave God the credit and showed mercy. It was a good start.
Where it went wrong.
Saul’s troubles began with impatience.
Facing the Philistine army, Samuel had told him to wait seven days at Gilgal.
When Samuel did not come on time and the soldiers began to scatter, Saul offered the burnt offering himself, which was the priest’s job.
Samuel arrived right after.
“You have done foolishly.
You have not kept the command of the Lord your God.”
Saul’s dynasty would not last.
The second failure was worse.
God told Saul to completely destroy the Amalekites, an enemy who had attacked Israel when they left Egypt.
Saul spared their king Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle.
Samuel confronted him, and Saul said the animals were for sacrifice.
Samuel’s answer: “To obey is better than sacrifice.”
When Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed his robe and it tore.
“The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day.”
Saul admitted, “I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people.”
He cared more about his image than about being right with God.
Jealousy and the spear.
The Spirit of the Lord left Saul, and “a harmful spirit from the Lord tormented him.”
His servants recommended a musician, and a young shepherd named David came to play the harp. It calmed him.
Then David killed Goliath and became a hero.
As the army returned, women danced and sang: “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
“And Saul eyed David from that day on.”
The next day, while David played for him, Saul threw his spear, trying to pin David to the wall. David escaped twice.
Saul sent David on dangerous missions, hoping the Philistines would kill him.
He even tried to have his own son Jonathan, David’s best friend, put to death for helping David.
For years Saul hunted David through the wilderness with 3,000 soldiers.
Twice David had the chance to kill him, once in a cave at En Gedi and once while Saul slept in his camp, and each time David spared him: “I will not put out my hand against the Lord’s anointed.”
Saul wept and said, “You are more righteous than I.” But it did not last.
The last night.
By the end, Saul was desperate.
The Philistine army gathered at Shunem.
“When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.”
He had thrown out mediums and necromancers from the land, which was right, but now God was not answering him by dreams or prophets.
In the night, in disguise, he went to a medium in Endor and asked her to bring up Samuel, who had died.
The Bible says Samuel appeared with a hard message: “Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me.”
The next day, on Mount Gilboa, the Philistines overran Israel.
Saul’s three sons, including Jonathan, were killed.
Saul was wounded by archers.
Rather than be captured and abused, he fell on his own sword.
The Philistines hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan.
Brave men from Jabesh-gilead, the town Saul had rescued at the start of his reign, crossed the Jordan at night, took the bodies down and buried them.
When David heard, he sang a lament: “How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle!
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely!
In life and in death they were not divided.”
He mourned the king who had tried to kill him.
What does this mean for us today?.
Saul had height, looks, a throne and a good start.
What he lacked was a heart that would obey God when it cost him something.
He wanted to look good more than to be good.
His story shows that how you begin matters less than how you finish.
Jealousy poisoned him.
Instead of being thankful for David’s success, he saw it as a threat, and it ruined his mind and his home.
The Bible warns that envy “makes the bones rot.”
