Celebrating others’ victories is a spiritual discipline.
Samuel’s words are a useful test for our own lives: “To obey is better than sacrifice.”
God does not want our religious show.
He wants our trust and obedience.
And Saul’s story is also a reminder that God keeps His promises: He had a plan for Israel, and He raised up David to carry it on.
Who David was.
David, son of Jesse from Bethlehem, was Israel’s greatest king, ruling about 1010 to 970 BC.
He started as the youngest of eight brothers, a shepherd boy no one thought important.
He became a musician, a warrior, a poet, a fugitive and finally a king.
The Bible calls him “a man after God’s own heart.”
He also wrote many of the Psalms, the songs and prayers that people have used for 3,000 years.
The Gospel writers call Jesus “the Son of David.”
Why his story matters.
David’s story is long and full.
It has victories like his defeat of Goliath and the greatest sin of his life, and shows what a person can do when he is honest with God.
It is also the story of a promise God made to David that ends in Jesus.
The shepherd who was anointed.
God had rejected King Saul, and He sent the prophet Samuel to Jesse’s house in Bethlehem to anoint a new king.
Samuel looked at Jesse’s oldest son, tall and impressive, and thought, “Surely the Lord’s anointed is before him.”
God said, “Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature...
For the Lord sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.”
Seven sons passed by.
“Are all your sons here?” Samuel asked.
“There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep.” David was brought in.
“Now he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome.”
The Lord said, “Arise, anoint him, for this is he.”
Samuel poured oil on his head, “and the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon David from that day forward.”
For now, David went back to the sheep.
He had been told he would be king, but he would not take the throne for about fifteen years.
Goliath and Jonathan.
David first came to the palace to play the harp for King Saul, whose mind was troubled.
Then came the famous day in the Valley of Elah, when David, a teenager with a sling and five stones, defeated the Philistine giant Goliath.
“You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts.”
After the battle, David met Saul’s son Jonathan.
“The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.”
Jonathan gave him his robe, armor, sword, bow and belt.
It was a gift of friendship and also a recognition that David was going to take the throne that would have been Jonathan’s.
Jonathan did not resent it.
They made a covenant to be loyal to each other and each other’s families.
Years on the run.
David was successful in everything Saul sent him to do, and the women sang, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
Saul became jealous, threw a spear at him twice and then hunted him through the wilderness.
David lived in caves, gathered about 400 men who were in distress or in debt, and wrote many psalms during these years.
Twice David had a chance to kill Saul.
In a cave at En Gedi, Saul came in to relieve himself while David and his men were hiding at the back.
David only cut off a corner of his robe, and even that bothered his conscience.
“I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is the Lord’s anointed.”
He called after Saul from a distance and showed him the piece of cloth.
Saul wept: “You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil.”
David refused to take the throne by violence.
He waited for God to give it.
King in Jerusalem.
When Saul and Jonathan died in battle, David mourned them with a song.
He became king over the tribe of Judah in Hebron at age thirty and reigned there seven and a half years.
Then the other tribes came to him, and he became king over all Israel.
He captured the fortress of Jebus, which became Jerusalem, “the city of David.”
He brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem with shouting and trumpets.
“David danced before the Lord with all his might.”
Then he told the prophet Nathan he wanted to build a house for God.
God answered through Nathan: no, but David’s son would build it.
And more: “Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me.
Your throne shall be established forever.”
It is a promise that points to Jesus, the greatest Son of David.
The great sin.
In the spring, when kings went out to battle, David stayed in Jerusalem.
One evening from his roof he saw a woman bathing.
She was Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, one of his soldiers.
David sent for her and slept with her. She became pregnant.
David tried to cover it up by calling Uriah home from the war.
When that failed, he sent a letter to Joab, his commander, to put Uriah in the front line of the fiercest fighting and then withdraw. Uriah was killed. David married Bathsheba.
“But the thing that David had done displeased the Lord.”
The prophet Nathan told David a story about a rich man who took a poor man’s only lamb.
David was furious: “The man who has done this deserves to die!”
Nathan said, “You are the man!”
David answered, “I have sinned against the Lord.”
Nathan said that the Lord had forgiven him, but there would be consequences.
The child died, and violence and trouble followed in his family.
David’s prayer of repentance is Psalm 51: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love...
Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”
Absalom and the end.
David’s family continued to suffer.
His son Absalom, handsome and charming, gradually won the loyalty of the people and led a rebellion.
David had to flee Jerusalem barefoot and weeping.
He told his generals to deal gently with Absalom, but Absalom was caught by his hair in an oak tree and was killed by Joab.
When David heard, he cried out, “O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!
Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!”
David returned to Jerusalem.
In his last years, he gathered materials for the Temple, which Solomon would build.
He charged Solomon: “Be strong, and show yourself a man, and keep the charge of the Lord your God, walking in his ways.”
David died at about seventy and was buried in the city of David.
His last words in the Bible include: “The Spirit of the Lord speaks by me; his word is on my tongue.”
What does this mean for us today?.
David was a great man and a great sinner.
The Bible shows both honestly.
He is called “a man after God’s own heart,” not because he never failed but because when he did, he came back to God. Psalm 51 is the proof.
We can come to God with our worst failures and find mercy.
His life also shows how to deal with injustice.
When Saul was hunting him, David refused to take matters into his own hands.
He trusted God to do what He had promised, in His time.
And the Psalms are David’s gift to everyone.
He sang in the cave, in the palace, in joy and in fear.
“The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
They are a model for how to pray honestly, and they remind us that the shepherd boy’s greatest descendant, Jesus, is our King forever.
Who Solomon was.
Solomon was the son of King David and Bathsheba.
He ruled Israel for forty years, from about 970 to 931 BC, at the height of its wealth and power.
His name comes from the Hebrew word for “peace.”
The prophet Nathan also gave him the name Jedidiah, “beloved of the Lord.”
Solomon became king when he was young, probably still in his late teens or early twenties.
His older brother Adonijah had tried to take the throne while David was dying, but David had Solomon crowned instead.
David’s last advice to Solomon was to be strong and to walk in God’s ways.
Why his story matters.
Solomon is known for his wisdom and his wealth, and for building the Temple in Jerusalem.
His story also shows how a man who began so well could end badly.
“Give me an understanding mind”.
Early in his reign, Solomon went to the city of Gibeon to offer a thousand burnt offerings.
That night, God appeared to him in a dream: “Ask what I shall give you.”
Solomon answered with humility: “You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father...
And now, O Lord my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child.
I do not know how to go out or come in...
Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?”
God was pleased.

“Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for understanding to discern what is right, behold, I now do according to your word.
Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you.
I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor.”
The two mothers.
Soon after, two women came before the king with one baby.
They lived in the same house and each had given birth within three days.
One woman’s baby died in the night.
She said the other woman had taken her live baby and left her the dead one.
The other woman said the living baby was hers.
Solomon called for a sword.
“Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other.”
The first woman said, “Please, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death!”
The other said, “He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him.”
Solomon said, “Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother.”
“And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.”
The Temple.
David had wanted to build a house for God, but God said David was a man of war and his son would build it.
In the fourth year of his reign, Solomon began. It took seven years.
The Temple was built of huge stones cut at the quarry so that no hammer or iron tool was heard at the site.
The walls were lined with cedar from Lebanon and the inside was covered with gold.
The most holy place, where the ark of the covenant would be kept, was a perfect cube covered with gold.
At the dedication, the priests brought the ark into the Temple, and a cloud filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister.
Solomon stood before the people and prayed: “But will God indeed dwell on the earth?
Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!”
He asked God to hear the prayers of His people, and of foreigners too, whenever they prayed toward the Temple.
Fire fell from heaven on the altar, and all the people bowed down.
Fame and wealth.
Solomon’s fame spread.
He spoke 3,000 proverbs and wrote 1,005 songs.
He taught about plants and animals.
“And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.”
The queen of Sheba, from far to the south, perhaps in what is now Yemen or Ethiopia, traveled with a great caravan to test him with hard questions.
After seeing his wisdom, his palace, his food, his servants and the burnt offerings he offered at the Temple, “there was no more breath in her.”
She said, “The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom, but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it.
And behold, the half was not told me.” She praised the Lord.
Solomon received about 25 tons of gold a year and made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones.
A heart turned away.
Solomon’s great weakness was that he did not obey God’s command about kings.
The law said a king should not “multiply wives for himself” or gold.
Solomon had 700 wives and 300 concubines, many of them from foreign nations to seal political alliances.
The Bible says, “His wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the Lord his God.”
He built shrines on the hills for the gods of his foreign wives, including Molech and Chemosh.
God was angry and told him: “Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant...
I will surely tear the kingdom from you.”
For David’s sake, it would not happen in his day, but in his son’s.
Solomon died after forty years.
His son Rehoboam answered the people harshly when they asked for lighter taxes, and the kingdom split in two, just as God had said.
The wisest man in the world had failed to guard his own heart.
His book Ecclesiastes, which tradition says he wrote near the end, ends: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Solomon’s story begins with a very good prayer: “Give me an understanding mind.” God honored it.
Wisdom is still the best thing to ask for, and the Bible says that if anyone lacks wisdom, he should ask God, “who gives generously to all without reproach.”
But wisdom in the head is not the same as obedience in the heart.
Solomon knew the right thing and still drifted, one small compromise at a time.
His story warns that blessing and success can be more dangerous than hardship, because they make us feel we do not need God.
Jesus later said, “Behold, something greater than Solomon is here.”
Solomon built a temple, but Jesus is the true Temple.
Solomon was wise, but Christ is “the wisdom of God.”
Who Esther was.
Esther was a young Jewish woman who became queen of Persia around 480 BC.
Her Hebrew name was Hadassah.
Her parents had died, and she was raised by her older cousin Mordecai in the city of Susa, one of the capitals of the Persian empire.
Her family was part of the Jewish people who had been taken from Judah into exile in Babylon generations earlier.
When Persia conquered Babylon, many Jews stayed in the empire.
The Persian Empire was the biggest the world had seen, stretching from India to Ethiopia.
Its king, Xerxes, called Ahasuerus in the Bible, ruled it from a palace of great luxury.
Why her story matters.
The book of Esther never names God, yet His care is on every page.
It is the story of a young woman who found herself in the right place at the right time, and was brave enough to act.
The queen who said no.
In the third year of his reign, King Xerxes gave a feast for all the officials and princes of his empire.
It lasted 180 days, and ended with a week-long banquet for everyone in Susa.
On the seventh day, drunk with wine, the king ordered his seven eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti, wearing her royal crown, to show off her beauty to the guests.
Vashti refused to come. The king was furious.
His advisers told him that if the queen’s refusal became known, all women in the empire would despise their husbands.
They recommended that Vashti be removed as queen, and the king agreed.
Later, when his anger cooled, the king thought of what he had done.
His servants suggested a solution: gather beautiful young women from the whole empire, and he could choose a new queen.
A new queen.
Esther was among the many young women taken to the palace.
Mordecai had told her not to reveal her people or her family.
A year of beauty treatments followed for each woman before she was taken to meet the king.
A man named Hegai was in charge of the women.
“The young woman pleased him and won his favor.”
He gave her the best place in the harem.

When Esther’s turn came, “the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.”
He gave a great banquet in her honor.
Mordecai sat at the king’s gate every day to keep an eye on her.
One day, he overheard two palace guards plotting to assassinate the king and reported it through Esther.
The plot was uncovered and the men were hanged.
It was written in the king’s record book, and then forgotten.
A death decree.
A few years later, the king promoted a man named Haman above all other officials.
Everyone bowed to him, except Mordecai.
Furious, Haman decided to destroy not only Mordecai but all of Mordecai’s people.
He told the king they were a people with different laws who could not be trusted, and offered a great sum of money.
The king gave him his signet ring and permission to do as he wished.
A decree was sent out to every province: on a certain day, kill all the Jews, young and old, and take their goods.
When Mordecai heard, he put on sackcloth and ashes and wailed in the city.
Esther sent clothes, but he would not wear them.
He told her to go to the king and plead for her people.
Esther replied that no one could approach the king without being called, on penalty of death, and she had not been called for thirty days.
Mordecai answered: “If you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish.
And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
“If I perish, I perish”.
Esther’s answer was courageous: “Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and neither eat nor drink for three days, night or day.
I and my young women will also fast as you do.
Then I will go to the king, though it is not according to the law, and if I perish, I perish.”
On the third day she dressed in her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace.
The king saw her and held out his golden scepter.
“What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request?
It shall be given you, up to half of my kingdom.”
She asked only that the king and Haman come to a banquet she had prepared.
At the banquet, the king asked again.
Esther said only, “Let the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said.”
She waited for the right moment.
The truth revealed.
That night the king could not sleep, and the royal records were read to him.
The reading brought up Mordecai’s unrewarded service.
The next day the king had Haman himself lead Mordecai through the city on the king’s horse to honor him.
Haman, humiliated, then went to the second banquet.
There, the king asked Esther again.
She answered: “If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request.
For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated.”
“Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?” “A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!”
Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.
The king could not cancel his own decree, but he allowed Mordecai to write a new one that permitted Jews to defend themselves.
They did, and they were victorious.
Esther, the orphan, had saved her people.
Purim.
Mordecai wrote down all that happened and sent letters throughout the empire telling the Jews to celebrate every year on the 14th and 15th of the month of Adar.

“As the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor.”
The festival was called Purim, from the “pur,” or lot, that Haman had cast.
Jewish communities still celebrate it every year.
The book of Esther is read aloud, and when Haman’s name is mentioned, people make noise to drown it out.
They give gifts to friends and to the poor.
Mordecai became second only to King Xerxes, and the Bible says he “sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Esther’s story asks a question that fits every life: “Who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
God places people where they are for a reason.
Esther had a position she had never planned on, and a moment came when it mattered.
It also shows that courage is not the absence of fear. Esther was afraid.
She fasted and prayed with her friends first, then walked into the court anyway.
And though God is never named, the book shows how He works behind the scenes.
The sleepless king, the forgotten record and the timing of the banquets all turned out right.
When God seems quiet, the Bible says He is still at work.
Who Hezekiah was.
Hezekiah was king of Judah, the southern kingdom, from about 715 to 686 BC. He became king at 25.
His father, Ahaz, was one of Judah’s worst kings: he worshiped foreign gods, shut the doors of the Temple, and even sacrificed his own son in a fire.
Hezekiah grew up in a palace where that was normal.
The Bible says that Hezekiah “trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him or among those who were before him.”
Why his story matters.
Hezekiah’s story has three big scenes: a spiritual revival, a deadly enemy at the gates, and a death sentence that was turned back.
It shows what a leader can do when he turns to God, and also how one proud moment can cost a lot.
Reopening the Temple.
In the first year of his reign, in the first month, Hezekiah opened the doors of the Temple and repaired them.
He gathered the priests and Levites and said, “Listen to me, Levites!
Consecrate yourselves, and consecrate the house of the Lord.
Our fathers have been unfaithful and have done what was evil.”
It took sixteen days to carry the filth out of the Temple and to purify it.
Then the king led a great service of worship.
He invited the whole nation, including the northern tribes, to come to Jerusalem for the Passover, which had not been kept properly for years.
Messengers went all over the land.
Some people laughed at them, but many came.
The Bible says, “There was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon the son of David there had been nothing like this.”
Hezekiah also broke the bronze snake that Moses had made in the wilderness.
Over the centuries, people had started burning incense to it as an idol.
He called it Nehushtan, which means “a piece of bronze.”
The Assyrian army.
Assyria was the superpower of the time and had already destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel.
Hezekiah refused to keep paying tribute to Assyria.
In 701 BC, Sennacherib invaded and captured 46 walled cities of Judah.
Assyrian records, which still survive, brag that he shut Hezekiah up “like a bird in a cage” in Jerusalem.
Hezekiah prepared.
He blocked the springs outside the city, and he had workers dig a tunnel about 1,750 feet long through solid rock to bring water from the Gihon spring inside the walls.
The tunnel can still be walked through in Jerusalem today.
He also repaired the wall and gathered the people.
“Be strong and courageous.
Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria...
With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God, to help us and to fight our battles.”
Sennacherib’s spokesman stood outside the wall and shouted in Hebrew so everyone on the wall could hear: Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you.
No god has ever saved his people from Assyria. Why would yours?
A letter spread before the Lord.
Sennacherib sent a letter of threat.
Hezekiah read it, went into the Temple and spread it out before the Lord.
He prayed: “O Lord, the God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth...
Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear; open your eyes, O Lord, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib...
So now, O Lord our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O Lord, are God alone.”
The prophet Isaiah sent word that the Lord had heard.
Sennacherib would not enter the city, not even shoot an arrow into it.
That night the angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp.
When the people of Jerusalem woke up, the dead were everywhere.
Sennacherib left and went home to Nineveh.
Years later, in 681 BC, his own sons killed him while he was worshiping in a temple, just as Isaiah had said.
Fifteen more years.
Around that time Hezekiah got sick and was near death.
Isaiah came to him with a message: “Set your house in order, for you shall die; you shall not recover.”

Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed, weeping bitterly: “Remember now, O Lord, how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight.”
Before Isaiah had left the courtyard, God sent him back: “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you.
On the third day you shall go up to the house of the Lord.
And I will add fifteen years to your life.”
A poultice of figs was put on the boil.
As a sign, God made the shadow on the stairway go back ten steps.
Hezekiah had no son yet.
His son Manasseh was born during those added years, and he was twelve when he became king.
The Bible says Manasseh turned out to be as bad as Ahaz or worse.
God’s gift of life did not guarantee what came after.
The visitors from Babylon.
After Hezekiah’s recovery, messengers came from Babylon, a rising power then still small, with letters and a gift. Hezekiah was pleased.
He showed them everything: the silver, the gold, the spices, the armory and every treasure in his storehouses.
“There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.”
Isaiah asked, “What did these men say?
Where did they come from?
What have they seen in your house?”

Then he gave a message from God: “Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left.”
Some of Hezekiah’s own descendants would become servants in the palace of the king of Babylon.
Hezekiah’s answer was, “The word of the Lord that you have spoken is good.
For there will be peace and security in my days.”
It was a sad moment for a great king: he was relieved that the disaster would not come in his own lifetime.
About a hundred years later it came true.
What does this mean for us today?.
Hezekiah’s best moment was a simple one: he took a threatening letter into the Temple and spread it out before God.
When something seems too big, that is a pattern we can follow.
Bring it to the Lord, and say it as it is.
His story also shows that prayer changes things.
Hezekiah was told that he would die and he prayed.
The Bible says God heard.
But it also warns us about success.
After the victory and the healing, Hezekiah got proud and showed off his treasures.
How we handle blessing matters as much as how we handle trouble.
Staying humble and thinking about the generations after us is part of a faithful life.
Who Josiah was.
Josiah was king of Judah, the southern kingdom, from about 640 to 609 BC.
He became king at only eight years old.
His father, King Amon, was killed by his own officials after ruling just two years, and the people put the boy on the throne.
His grandfather was Manasseh, who ruled 55 years and was one of the most wicked kings Judah ever had.
Manasseh built altars to foreign gods in the Temple itself and even sacrificed his own son.
So Josiah grew up in a kingdom full of idols, with a royal family that had turned away from the Lord.
Why his story matters.
Josiah’s story is about a young person who chose to follow God even though everything around him pulled the other way.
It is also about what happens when God’s Word is rediscovered after being lost and ignored.
A boy who sought God.
The Bible says that in the eighth year of his reign, when he was still a boy of about sixteen, Josiah began to seek the God of his ancestor David.
Four years later, at twenty, he began to clean up the land.
He had the high places, the Asherah poles and the carved and cast idols torn down.
He ordered the altars of the Baals to be smashed in his presence and the incense altars above them cut down.
He ground the idols to dust and scattered it over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.
It took courage.
These altars had stood for generations.
The priests and officials who profited from them were still in power.
A young king still in his early twenties took on the whole system.
The lost book.
When Josiah was 26, he ordered the Temple repaired.
It had been neglected and damaged under the idol-worshiping kings.
Workers were paid and carpenters and builders were hired.
While they were working, Hilkiah the high priest found the Book of the Law of the Lord.
It was probably the book of Deuteronomy, or at least a large part of the Law of Moses.
Somehow it had been lost in the Temple of all places.
A secretary named Shaphan read it aloud to the king.
As Josiah heard the words, especially the warnings of what would happen if Israel turned away from God, he tore his clothes in grief.
“Great is the wrath of the Lord that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book.”
He realized how far the whole nation had drifted from what God had said.
The prophetess Huldah.
Josiah sent his officials to ask the Lord what they should do.
They went to a prophetess named Huldah, who lived in Jerusalem.
Her answer had two parts.
First, God would indeed bring disaster on Jerusalem, as the book warned, because the people had abandoned Him.
Second, because Josiah’s heart was tender, because he humbled himself and wept before God, he would be gathered to his grave in peace and not see the disaster.
It is worth noting that the king, the high priest and the secretary chose to ask a woman prophet for God’s word, and the Bible treats her answer with full respect.
Josiah did not simply sit back and accept that disaster would come later.
He kept leading the nation back to God as hard as he could.
The covenant and the cleanup.
Josiah called all the elders, priests, prophets and people, from the least to the greatest, up to the Temple.
He read the entire Book of the Covenant aloud to them.
Then he stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the Lord: to follow Him and keep His commands with all his heart and soul.
All the people joined in.
Then came the great cleanup.
He removed everything built for Baal and Asherah from the Temple, burned it and scattered the ashes.
He shut down the pagan priests, tore down the places of male prostitution connected to worship, and destroyed the place in the valley where children were sacrificed to the god Molech.
He went north into the old territory of Israel, to the altar at Bethel that Jeroboam had set up 300 years earlier, and broke it down.
That was exactly what a prophet had foretold, even naming Josiah, before Josiah was born.
The greatest Passover.
Josiah commanded the people to celebrate the Passover, the yearly meal remembering the rescue from Egypt, which had long been neglected.
The Bible says no Passover like it had been held since the days of the prophet Samuel.
Josiah himself gave thousands of lambs and goats and cattle for the people to use.

The Bible gives Josiah very high praise: “Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the Lord with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might, according to all the Law of Moses.”
But in 609 BC, the Egyptian king Pharaoh Necho marched north to help Assyria against the rising power of Babylon.
Josiah went out to stop him at Megiddo.
He was hit by archers and died of his wounds in Jerusalem.
All of Judah mourned, and the prophet Jeremiah wrote a lament for him.
About twenty years later, Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, just as Huldah had said.
What does this mean for us today?.
Josiah shows that no one is too young to follow God, and that a family’s history does not have to decide your future.
His grandfather was a terrible king, and Josiah was one of the best.
His story also shows what the Bible does in a life.
When he heard God’s Word, he did not just admire it.
He changed what he was doing.
The book had been in the Temple the whole time, and nobody noticed.
We may have a Bible on a shelf or phone and still need to open it and listen.
And Josiah’s sorrow at God’s warning was not wasted.
God saw his humble heart.
The Bible says that God notices when people take His words seriously.
Who Elijah was.
Elijah was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel, about 870 to 850 BC.
He came from Tishbe in Gilead, east of the Jordan, a rugged area.
The Bible tells us nothing about his family.
He appears suddenly in the story, wearing a rough garment and a leather belt, and goes to the king.
King Ahab, with his wife Jezebel, had led Israel into the worship of Baal.
Elijah’s name means “My God is the Lord.”
His whole life was an answer to the question of who is God.
Why his story matters.
Elijah is one of the most dramatic people in the Bible.
His story has fire from heaven, a miracle at a widow’s house, a ride in a whirlwind, and a time when he sat down under a tree and asked to die.
It shows God’s power and God’s tenderness.
No rain, and the ravens.
Elijah walked into the court of King Ahab and said, “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.”
It was a direct challenge to Baal, who was supposed to be the god of rain and storms.
God told him to hide by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan.
“You shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
Every morning and evening, ravens brought him bread and meat.
After a while the brook dried up because of the drought.
God sent him to the town of Zarephath, in the territory of Sidon, which was Jezebel’s own homeland.
There a widow was gathering sticks to cook a last meal for herself and her son.
Elijah asked her for some bread.
“The jar of flour shall not be spent, and the jug of oil shall not be empty, until the day that the Lord sends rain upon the earth.”
She trusted him, and for many days the jar and jug did not run out.
A boy raised.
Some time later, the widow’s son became sick and died.
She said to Elijah, “What have you against me, O man of God?
You have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to cause the death of my son!”
Elijah took the boy from her arms, carried him up to the upper room and laid him on his own bed.
He cried out to the Lord, “O Lord my God, let this child’s life return to him.”
He stretched himself over the child three times.
“And the Lord listened to the voice of Elijah.
And the life of the child returned to him, and he revived.”
Elijah gave him back to his mother.
She said, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is truth.”
It is the first account in the Bible of someone being brought back from the dead.
Showdown on Carmel.
In the third year, God told Elijah to go to Ahab, and He would send rain.
Elijah told Ahab to gather all Israel and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.
“How long will you go limping between two different opinions?
If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” The people said nothing.
Each side would prepare a bull on an altar.
The god who answered by fire would be God.
The prophets of Baal called from morning until noon, danced around the altar and cut themselves with swords.
Elijah teased them: “Cry aloud, for he is a god.
Either he is musing, or he is relieving himself, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened.” Nothing happened.

At the time of the evening sacrifice, Elijah repaired the Lord’s altar with twelve stones, dug a trench around it and had them pour four large jars of water over the offering three times, until the trench was full.
He prayed a brief prayer: “O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that you are God in Israel...
Answer me, O Lord, answer me, that this people may know that you, O Lord, are God.”
Fire fell and burned up the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust and the water.
All the people fell on their faces: “The Lord, he is God!”
Elijah then prayed seven times for rain, and the servant finally saw a cloud as small as a man’s hand.
Then the sky grew black with heavy rain.
Under the broom tree.
Ahab told Jezebel everything.
She sent a message: “So may the gods do to me and more also, if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow.”
Elijah, who had just stood against 450 prophets, was afraid.
“Then he arose and ran for his life.”
He left his servant in Beersheba, went a day’s journey into the wilderness and sat down under a broom tree.
“It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.” He lay down and slept.
An angel touched him: “Arise and eat.”
He found a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water.
He ate, drank and slept again.
The angel came a second time.
“Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you.” God did not scold him.
He fed him and let him rest.
Then, strengthened, Elijah walked forty days to Mount Horeb, the mountain where God gave Moses the law.
The gentle whisper.
At Horeb, Elijah went into a cave.
God asked, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”
Elijah answered, “I have been very jealous for the Lord, the God of hosts.
For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away.”
God told him to stand on the mountain.
“And behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the Lord, but the Lord was not in the wind.
And after the wind an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake.
And after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire.
And after the fire the sound of a low whisper.”
Elijah covered his face with his cloak and stood at the mouth of the cave.
Again, God asked what he was doing.
Elijah gave the same answer.
God gave him new work, to anoint two kings and a successor, Elisha.
And He added something Elijah did not know: “Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal.” Elijah was not alone.
The whirlwind.
Elijah’s last years included a confrontation with Ahab over the murder of Naboth and a message of judgment on the house of Ahab.
Then, one day, he and Elisha walked from Gilgal to Bethel, to Jericho and to the Jordan.
Elijah struck the water with his cloak, and it divided so they could cross on dry ground.
He asked Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.”
“Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me.”
“And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them.
And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.”
Elisha cried, “My father, my father!
The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” He saw him no more.
Only one other person in the Bible, Enoch, is said to have been taken to heaven without dying.
The last verses of the Old Testament promise that God would send Elijah before the great day of the Lord.
Jesus said that John the Baptist was the Elijah who was to come.
And at the Transfiguration, Elijah appeared with Moses, talking with Jesus.
What does this mean for us today?.
Elijah was bold and he was human.
On Carmel he stood alone against hundreds, and a few days later he was running in fear.
The Bible does not hide that.
Spiritual high points are often followed by exhaustion.
He was not ashamed to tell God exactly how he felt.
God’s response is very kind.
He gave Elijah sleep, food, water and a quiet place.
Sometimes what we need most is rest and a meal.
After that, He spoke gently, and reminded Elijah that he was not alone.
The whisper at Horeb is also a good lesson.
God can use fire and storms, but He often speaks quietly.
In a noisy world, we may need to be still to hear Him.
Elijah’s story says that God is powerful enough to send fire and gentle enough to be found in a whisper.
Who Elisha was.
Elisha was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel, about 850 to 800 BC.
He was the son of a farmer named Shaphat from the village of Abel Meholah.
His mentor was the great prophet Elijah, and Elisha eventually took his place.
Israel was ruled by kings who worshiped Baal, and God’s prophets were often in danger.
Elisha’s ministry is known for many miracles, and for the way he cared for ordinary people, widows, foreigners and soldiers.
Why his story matters.
Elisha’s story shows God’s power and His care at a personal scale.
It also shows that God’s kindness goes beyond Israel’s borders.
The cloak.
One day Elijah found Elisha plowing a field with twelve pairs of oxen.
That means the family was fairly wealthy, and Elisha was working with the twelfth pair.
Elijah walked up and threw his cloak over him, the sign of passing on a prophet’s calling.
Elisha asked to say goodbye to his parents and Elijah let him.
Then Elisha did something drastic.
He took the pair of oxen, killed them, used the plow as firewood to cook the meat and gave it to the people to eat.
He had destroyed his old way of life and was not planning to go back.
He got up, followed Elijah, and served him.
The double portion.
Years later, Elijah’s time was ending.
Three times Elijah told Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha said, “As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.”
At the Jordan River, Elijah struck the water with his cloak and it divided so they crossed on dry ground.
Elijah asked, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.”
Elisha said, “Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me.”
As they walked and talked, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah went up in a whirlwind into heaven.
Elisha cried out, “My father, my father!
The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”
He picked up Elijah’s cloak, struck the Jordan and said, “Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?”
The water divided again, and the prophets watching said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.”
A widow and a woman from Shunem.
A widow of one of the prophets came to Elisha in desperation.
Her husband had died with debts, and a creditor was about to take her two sons as slaves.
“What shall I do for you?
Tell me, what have you in the house?”
“Your servant has nothing in the house except a jar of oil.”
Elisha told her to borrow empty jars from her neighbors, as many as she could, close the door and pour.
The oil kept flowing until every jar was full.
She sold the oil, paid her debt and lived on the rest.
In the village of Shunem, a wealthy woman noticed Elisha passing by and built a small upstairs room for him, with a bed, table, chair and lamp.
Wanting to repay her, Elisha promised her a son, though her husband was old.
A year later, she had a boy.
Some years later, the child got a terrible headache in the field and died in his mother’s lap.
She laid him on Elisha’s bed and rode to find the prophet.
Elisha stretched himself over the child, mouth to mouth, and the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
Naaman.
Naaman was the commander of the army of Syria, a great man but with a skin disease often translated “leprosy.”
His wife’s servant girl was a captive Israelite.
She said, “If only my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria!
He would cure him of his leprosy.”
The Syrian king sent Naaman with a huge gift of silver, gold and clothing.
Elisha did not even come out.
He sent a messenger: “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored.” Naaman was furious. He had expected a show.
Rivers in his own country were cleaner.
But his servants said, “If the prophet had commanded you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?
How much more, when he says to you, ‘Wash, and be clean’?”
Naaman went down, dipped seven times, and “his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child.”
He told Elisha, “Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel.”
Elisha refused any payment.
Elisha’s servant Gehazi, however, ran after Naaman and lied to get some of the gifts.
When he came back, Elisha knew.
Naaman’s leprosy came on Gehazi instead.
More than those with us.
The king of Syria kept losing battles because Elisha told the king of Israel where the Syrians were hiding.
The Syrian king sent horses and chariots and a great army to Dothan, where Elisha was staying, and surrounded the city at night.
Elisha’s servant got up early, saw the army and cried, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?”
Elisha answered, “Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”
Then he prayed, “O Lord, please open his eyes that he may see.”
The Lord opened the servant’s eyes, “and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.”
Elisha then prayed that the Syrian army be struck blind. He led them to Samaria.
When their eyes were opened they were in the middle of the Israelite capital.
The king of Israel wanted to kill them.
Elisha said, “Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and go to their master.”
A great feast was prepared, and the Syrians went home.
“And the Syrians did not come again on raids into the land of Israel.”
His last miracle.
Elisha was old and fell ill.
King Joash of Israel came to him, weeping: “My father, my father!
The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” the same words Elisha had said when Elijah was taken.
Elisha told the king to shoot an arrow out the window and then to strike the ground with the arrows.
Joash struck only three times.
Elisha was angry: five or six times would have meant complete victory over Syria. He had stopped short.
Elisha died and was buried.
Not long afterward, a funeral party was burying a man when they saw a band of raiders coming.
They threw the body into Elisha’s tomb and ran.
“And as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet.”
Even after death, God’s power was still at work.
What does this mean for us today?.
Elisha showed God’s power, but he also showed God’s kindness.
He helped a widow with her jar of oil, a family with a lost child, and a foreign general with an illness.
The same God who parts rivers takes interest in small needs.
The story of Dothan is for anyone who feels outnumbered.
We often see only the army around us.
Elisha prayed for his servant to see what was real.
The Bible says that God’s angels are “ministering spirits sent out to serve.”
Naaman’s story also reminds us that God’s way is often simpler than we expect.
Naaman wanted a grand ceremony. God asked him to wash.
Trusting what God says, even when it seems too plain, is often the first step to healing.
Who Isaiah was.
Isaiah, the son of Amoz, was a prophet in Jerusalem from about 740 to 680 BC.
He served under four kings of Judah: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.
He lived in a dangerous time.
The mighty Assyrian empire was swallowing the countries around Judah, and the northern kingdom of Israel was destroyed in 722 BC.
Isaiah often spoke directly to kings, and he seems to have been well connected in the capital.
His name means “the Lord saves.”
The book of Isaiah has 66 chapters and is one of the most quoted books in the New Testament.
Why his story matters.
Isaiah gave some of the most famous promises in the Bible, including the promise of a child who would be called “God with us” and a servant who would suffer for others.
Jesus Himself read from Isaiah when He began His public ministry.
The year King Uzziah died.
In 740 BC, King Uzziah died.
He had been a good king for 52 years, and the country felt shaken.
In that year, Isaiah went into the Temple and saw a vision.
“I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple.”
Above him stood seraphim, angelic beings with six wings, calling out to each other: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!”
The doorposts shook and the house filled with smoke.
Isaiah’s reaction was not excitement but fear: “Woe is me!
For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts!”
“Here I am. Send me.”.
One of the seraphim flew to Isaiah with a burning coal taken from the altar.
He touched Isaiah’s mouth with it and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.”
God had met Isaiah’s confession with cleansing.
Then Isaiah heard the Lord say, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”
And he answered, “Here I am! Send me.”
God’s commission was hard.
He told Isaiah that the people would hear and not understand.
Isaiah asked how long, and God said until the cities were ruined.
But He also promised that a holy seed, a remnant, would remain, like the stump of a tree after it is cut down.
A sign for the house of David.
About 734 BC, King Ahaz of Judah was terrified.
Two kings from the north, Syria and Israel, were marching against him.
Isaiah met Ahaz at the end of the water channel and told him to stay calm and trust God.
He even invited Ahaz to ask for a sign.
Ahaz refused, putting on a religious face.
In fact he had already decided to ask Assyria for help.
Isaiah said, “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign.
Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.”
The name means “God with us.”
Matthew’s Gospel applies this to the birth of Jesus.

Isaiah also wrote, “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.”
The suffering servant.
In chapter 53, Isaiah describes a servant who is “despised and rejected by men; a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.”
“Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted.
But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.”
It goes on, “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.”
Written about 700 years before Jesus, it reads like a description of the crucifixion.
When the Ethiopian official in Acts was reading this passage in his chariot, Philip started with this very text and told him the good news about Jesus.
Comfort and the future.
Later chapters speak to people who will be in exile, long after Isaiah’s own lifetime.
They begin: “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.”
Isaiah says that grass withers and flowers fade, “but the word of our God will stand forever.”
He promises that “those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.”
He also looks ahead to a new creation where “the wolf shall dwell with the lamb” and “they shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain.”

When Jesus stood up in the synagogue in Nazareth, He read from Isaiah 61, “The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor,” and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
The Bible does not record Isaiah’s death.
Jewish tradition says he was killed under the evil King Manasseh, but the Bible does not say.
What does this mean for us today?.
Isaiah’s story begins with seeing how holy God is, and then seeing how sinful he himself was.
Many people in the Bible have the same experience: the closer they get to God, the more they see their need.
But God’s answer was not to throw Isaiah out.
It was to cleanse him and send him.
When God asks, “Whom shall I send?”, He is asking each of us in some way.
Isaiah’s answer is a good one: “Here I am.”
Finally, Isaiah’s promises are for everyone. A child will be born. A servant will suffer. A new world is coming.
Whatever the headlines look like, the Bible says that the word of our God will stand forever.
Who Jeremiah was.
Jeremiah was a prophet in Judah for over forty years, from about 627 BC until after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC.
He was the son of Hilkiah, a priest from the village of Anathoth, just a few miles north of Jerusalem.
He served under the last five kings of Judah.
They were years of terrible danger: the mighty Assyrian empire was collapsing, Babylon was rising, and Judah was caught between great powers.
He is often called “the weeping prophet.”
His message was hard, his life was lonely, and he was rejected by almost everyone, yet he kept speaking God’s word.
Why his story matters.
Jeremiah’s story shows what it costs to tell the truth when no one wants to hear it, and how God keeps people going.
It also contains some of the Bible’s greatest promises of hope.
“I am only a youth”.
God told Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
Jeremiah, probably in his teens or early twenties, answered, “Ah, Lord God!
Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth.”
God’s reply was direct: “Do not say, ‘I am only a youth’; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak.
Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you.”
God touched his mouth and said, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.”
The job was to “pluck up and break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
In other words, hard truth first, hope after.
God also warned him that the people would fight against him, “but they shall not prevail against you.”
The Temple sermon.
The people of Judah felt safe.
They had the Temple of the Lord in Jerusalem and thought God would never let it be destroyed.
Jeremiah stood at the Temple gate and told them, “Do not trust in these deceptive words: ‘This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord.’”

He told them that if they truly changed their ways, if they stopped oppressing foreigners, orphans and widows, stopped shedding innocent blood and stopped following other gods, God would let them stay.
But they were stealing, murdering, swearing falsely and then coming to the Temple saying, “We are delivered!”
Jeremiah asked, “Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?”
Jesus later quoted this very phrase when He cleared the Temple.
The priests and prophets seized Jeremiah and said he must die.
The officials stopped them.
The burned scroll.
Jeremiah could not go to the Temple, so he dictated all of God’s words to his friend and secretary Baruch, who wrote them on a scroll.
Baruch read the scroll aloud at the Temple on a day of fasting.
The officials took it to King Jehoiakim.
It was winter, and the king sat by a fire in his winter house.
As each section was read, he cut it off with a knife and threw it into the fire, until the whole scroll was burned.
He ordered Jeremiah and Baruch arrested, but “the Lord hid them.”
God told Jeremiah to take another scroll and write the same words again, adding many more.
The king could burn the paper.
He could not burn the word of God.
Rescued from the well.
By the time Babylon besieged Jerusalem, in 588 BC, Jeremiah told the people that resisting would only lead to death, and that surrender was the way to live.
The officials said he was weakening the soldiers’ morale and had him thrown into a cistern, an empty well with mud in the bottom. He sank into the mud.
A court official named Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian, went to the king, King Zedekiah, and said what they had done was evil.
The king allowed him to take thirty men and rescue Jeremiah. Ebed-melech was careful.
He took old rags and worn clothes, let them down on ropes so that the ropes would not cut into Jeremiah’s arms, and pulled him up.
Later God sent Jeremiah a word of promise to Ebed-melech: because he trusted God, he would be spared when the city fell.
A letter to the exiles.
Some of the people of Judah had already been taken to Babylon.
Prophets there were telling them the exile would be over in two years.
Jeremiah wrote them a letter that said the opposite: “Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce.
Take wives and have sons and daughters...
Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the Lord on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare.”
The exile would last seventy years.
Then comes one of the most loved verses in the Bible: “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.
Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you.
You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart.”
That promise was given to people in exile, not in comfort.
A field and a new covenant.
With the Babylonian army outside the city and Jeremiah locked in the palace guard’s courtyard, God told him to buy a field in his hometown of Anathoth from his cousin. It was a strange order.
The land was in enemy hands.
Jeremiah weighed out seventeen shekels of silver, signed the deed in front of witnesses and put it in a clay jar to last many days.
It was a sign: “Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.”
Jeremiah also gave a promise that points forward to Jesus: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel...
I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts.
And I will be their God, and they shall be my people...
For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.”
At the Last Supper, Jesus said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”
The fall of Jerusalem.
In 586 BC, after a long siege, Babylon broke through the walls, burned the Temple, the palace and the houses, and took most of the people to Babylon.
The Babylonian commander released Jeremiah and let him choose where to go.
He chose to stay with the poor who were left in the land.
A few months later, the governor appointed by Babylon was murdered, and the remaining leaders, afraid of revenge, decided to flee to Egypt.
Jeremiah warned them that God said to stay.
They did not listen, and they took him and Baruch with them to Egypt.
The Bible does not record how Jeremiah died.
Jewish tradition says he died there in Egypt.

A book of mourning called Lamentations, traditionally credited to him, grieves the fall of the city, and in the middle of it comes this line: “The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Jeremiah was not popular and was not successful in any way people measure.
He was ignored, mocked, beaten and jailed.
Yet his words have lasted 2,600 years, and the things he said would come true did.
Faithfulness matters more than being listened to.
He also shows that you can be honest with God.
In chapters often called his “confessions,”
Jeremiah complained and argued and said how much he hurt.
God did not tell him to be quiet.
He told him to keep going.
And the hope in his book is for people who are in a hard season.
The promise of a future and a hope was given to exiles, who felt far from home.
God says that even then He has a plan, and He will be found by anyone who seeks Him with all their heart.
Who Daniel was.
Daniel was a young Jewish nobleman from Jerusalem who was taken as a captive to Babylon in 605 BC, when he was probably around sixteen.
He lived in Babylon for about seventy years and served under several kings, first Babylonian and later Persian.
His name means “God is my judge.”
He was trained for three years in the language and writings of the Babylonians and was given a new name, Belteshazzar.
But he stayed loyal to the God of Israel, and God gave him a special ability to understand visions and dreams.
Why his story matters.
Daniel’s life shows that you can serve in a foreign culture, even a powerful and hostile one, and still stay true to God.
His book includes some of the most famous stories in the Bible and some of its most mysterious visions of the future.
A test of loyalty.
Daniel and three friends, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, were chosen for the king’s service.
They were to be fed from the king’s own table.
“But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king’s food, or with the wine that he drank.”
He asked the chief of the court officials for permission.
The official was afraid he would be punished if they looked worse than the others.
Daniel suggested a ten-day test: give them only vegetables and water, then compare.
After ten days they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who ate the king’s food.
The guard let them keep eating that way.
God gave them knowledge and skill.
In every matter of wisdom the king asked, he found them ten times better than all his magicians and enchanters.
The king’s dream.
Nebuchadnezzar had a troubling dream and demanded his wise men tell him what it was and what it meant.
They said it was impossible.
He ordered them all to be killed, including Daniel and his friends.
Daniel asked for time, and the four friends prayed.
That night, God revealed the dream to Daniel in a vision.
Daniel went to the king and made clear that the wisdom was from God, not himself.
The dream was a huge statue with a head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, feet partly iron and partly clay.
A stone, cut without human hands, struck the feet, and the whole statue crumbled to dust.
The stone became a great mountain that filled the earth.
Daniel explained that the statue stood for a series of kingdoms, and the stone for a kingdom God would set up that would never be destroyed.
Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face: “Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings.”
He made Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon.
Writing on the wall.
Many years later, in 539 BC, King Belshazzar held a huge feast for a thousand nobles.
He ordered that the gold and silver cups taken from God’s Temple in Jerusalem be brought, and they drank from them, praising their idols.
Suddenly the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster wall.
The king’s face turned pale, and his knees knocked together.
No one could read it.
The queen mother remembered Daniel.
Now an old man, he was brought in.
He refused the king’s offer of rewards and told him, “You have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven.”
The words were Mene, Mene, Tekel, Parsin.
Daniel explained: God had numbered the days of his kingdom and brought it to an end; the king had been weighed and found wanting; his kingdom would be divided and given to the Medes and Persians.
“That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed.”
Babylon fell to the Persian army.
The lions’ den.
Under the new Persian rule, Daniel did so well that King Darius planned to put him over the whole kingdom.
The other officials were jealous.
They looked for something to accuse him of and found nothing.
They concluded, “We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it in connection with the law of his God.”
They persuaded the king to sign a law that for thirty days anyone who prayed to any god or man other than the king would be thrown into the lions’ den.
Daniel heard that it was signed.
“He went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem.
He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.”
The officials found him praying.
The king was upset, since he liked Daniel, but could not change the law.
He told Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!”
A stone was put over the mouth of the den.
The king spent the night fasting and could not sleep.
Shut mouths.
At first light, the king hurried to the den.
In a troubled voice he called, “Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?”
Daniel answered, “O king, live forever!
My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm.”
The king was overjoyed and had Daniel lifted out.
No kind of harm was found on him “because he had trusted in his God.”
The men who had accused him were thrown into the den with their families, and the lions overpowered them before they hit the floor.
Darius then sent a message to the whole empire: “For he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and his dominion shall be to the end.
He delivers and rescues; he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth.”
Visions of the future.
Daniel lived to be very old, serving in Persia until at least 536 BC.
He read the book of Jeremiah and realized the seventy years of exile were almost over.
He prayed a long prayer of confession for himself and the whole nation: “To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame.”
Even as he prayed, the angel Gabriel arrived with an answer.

Daniel’s book also records visions of great beasts representing empires, and one of the most famous passages in the Bible: “I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days...
And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away.”
Jesus often called Himself the “Son of Man,” and when He was on trial, He said that they would see “the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”
At the end, God told Daniel, “Go your way till the end.
And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotment at the end of the days.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Daniel lived in a culture that did not share his faith, and he did not hide it.
But he was also respectful, hard-working and honest.
Even his enemies could find nothing wrong with him except his devotion to God. That is a good goal.
His prayer life was steady.
He prayed three times a day, with the window open, before the lions’ den and after.
His courage came from habit.
When the pressure came, he did not have to decide whether to pray. He was already praying.
And Daniel’s book gives hope for the long view.
Kingdoms of gold, silver, bronze and iron rise and fall.
Kings are proud and then humbled.
But God’s kingdom has no end.
When the news looks bad, Daniel reminds us who holds history.
Who Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were.
Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were three young Jewish men from Judah.
Their Hebrew names were Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah.
About 605 BC, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacked Jerusalem and took some of the best young men of the royal family and nobility back to Babylon.
The three were probably teenagers.
They were taken with a friend named Daniel.
The Babylonians gave them new names that honored Babylonian gods.
The Bible uses the Babylonian names in the story of the furnace: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.
Why their story matters.
Their story is about being faithful to God in a foreign land where the powers that be demand something else.
They did not have a temple, a king or an army.
They had only their decision about whom they would obey.
Training in Babylon.
Babylon was the largest city in the world, with huge walls, a famous hanging garden and a great tower temple.
The king wanted the best young men trained in the language and literature of the Babylonians for three years before entering his service.
They were to be fed the king’s own food and wine.
Daniel and his three friends decided not to defile themselves with the king’s food, which probably included foods the law of Moses forbade, and was likely dedicated to Babylon’s gods.
They asked the chief official to let them test a diet of vegetables and water for ten days.
At the end of ten days they looked healthier than all the others.
So the guard took away the royal food, and they ate vegetables from then on.
The Bible says God gave the four young men knowledge and skill in learning.
When the king examined them, he found them ten times better than all his magicians and enchanters.
The golden statue.
Some years later, Nebuchadnezzar built a gold statue on the plain of Dura.
It was 60 cubits high and 6 cubits wide, about 90 feet by 9 feet.
He called all the officials of the empire to a dedication ceremony.
A herald announced that when the horn, flute, zither and other instruments sounded, everyone had to fall down and worship the statue.
Anyone who refused would be thrown into a blazing furnace at once.
The music played, and the whole crowd bowed.
Everyone except three men.
Some Babylonian officials who envied them went to the king.
“There are certain Jews whom you have set over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.
These men pay no attention to you, O king.
They do not serve your gods or worship the golden image.”
Nebuchadnezzar flew into a rage and had them brought in.
“Even if He does not”.
The king offered them another chance.
“If you are ready when you hear the music, fall down and worship.
But if you do not, you will be thrown into the furnace.
And who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?”
Their answer is one of the bravest in the Bible: “O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter.
If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and He will deliver us out of your hand, O king.
But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up.”
They did not know whether God would save them.
They said He could, and that they would obey even if He did not.
That is real faith: not a guarantee of an easy outcome, but trust in God no matter what.
The fiery furnace.
Nebuchadnezzar was furious.
He ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual.
The strongest soldiers tied up the three men, still wearing their robes, trousers and turbans, and threw them in.
The fire was so hot that it killed the soldiers who carried them.
The king stood up in alarm and asked his advisors, “Did we not cast three men bound into the fire?” “True, O king.”
“But I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are not hurt.
And the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.”
The king went near the furnace door and called out, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!”
They walked out, and the officials gathered around.
The fire had not harmed their bodies.
Not a hair was singed, their clothes were not burned, and there was no smell of smoke on them.
The Bible does not say exactly who the fourth man was, but tradition has said it was the Son of God, Jesus, before He was born as a man.
The king’s response.

Nebuchadnezzar said, “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent His angel and delivered His servants, who trusted in Him, and set aside the king’s command, and yielded up their bodies rather than serve and worship any god except their own God.”
He announced that anyone who spoke against their God would be punished.
“For there is no other god who is able to rescue in this way.”
The king then gave the three men higher positions in Babylon.
It is the only time in the book of Daniel that we see Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, but their faith left a mark on a pagan king who ruled the world’s greatest empire.
Their story may have been well known, because the New Testament book of Hebrews recalls people of faith who “quenched the power of fire.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Most of us will never face a literal furnace, but we face pressure to bow: to what our workplace expects, what our friends are doing, or what the culture says is normal.
These three men show that you can live in a world that doesn’t share your faith and still be loyal to God.
Their words, “but if not,” matter.
They trusted God whether or not He rescued them.
Faith that depends on a particular outcome is not faith in God.
It is faith in the outcome.
And they were not alone.
The king saw a fourth person in the fire with them.

The Bible promises that God is with His people in hard places: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned.”
Who Jonah was.
Jonah was a prophet from Gath-hepher, a village in Galilee, about 780 BC.
The Bible mentions him in the book of 2 Kings, where he told King Jeroboam II of Israel that his kingdom would recover its borders.
That was good news for Israel, so Jonah was a popular prophet.
Then God gave him a very different assignment: to go to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, and speak to the people there.
Assyria was Israel’s enemy, known for violent conquest and cruelty.
About sixty years later, Assyria destroyed Israel.
Why his story matters.
The book of Jonah is a short story with a big lesson.
It is the story of a prophet who ran from God’s call, and of the surprising mercy of God.
Jesus Himself pointed to Jonah as a sign.
Running the wrong way.
“Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.”
But Jonah “rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.”
Tarshish was probably in southern Spain, about as far in the opposite direction as he could go.
He went down to the port of Joppa, found a ship, paid the fare and went below deck to sleep.
We learn later why he ran.
It was not because he was afraid of the Ninevites.
It was because he was afraid God would forgive them.
Jonah did not want Assyria to be forgiven.
He wanted them to be punished.
The storm.
“But the Lord hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up.” The sailors were afraid.
Each cried out to his own god and threw the cargo overboard to lighten the ship.
Meanwhile Jonah was fast asleep in the hold.
The captain woke him: “How can you be sleeping?
Arise, call out to your god!”
The sailors cast lots to find out whose fault it was, and the lot fell on Jonah.
They asked him who he was.
“I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”
The sailors were terrified.
“What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?”
“Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you.”
The sailors tried hard to row back to land, but could not.
They prayed to the Lord and threw Jonah in.
The sea stopped raging at once.
The men “feared the Lord exceedingly and offered a sacrifice to the Lord.”
Even the pagan sailors showed more respect for God than Jonah had.
Inside the great fish.
“And the Lord appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah.
And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.”
The Bible says “great fish” and does not say what kind.
From inside, Jonah prayed: “I called out to the Lord, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice...
The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head.”
He ended his prayer with, “Salvation belongs to the Lord!”
Then “the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.”
Jesus later used this story.

When some religious leaders demanded a sign, He said, “For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.”
Jonah’s rescue pointed ahead to Jesus’ resurrection.
Nineveh repents.
God told Jonah a second time: “Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it the message that I tell you.” This time he went.
Nineveh was so large that it took three days to walk across.
On the first day Jonah began to preach: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!”
The result was far beyond what he expected.
“And the people of Nineveh believed God.
They called for a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least.”
When the news reached the king, he got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth and sat in ashes.
He announced that no person or animal should eat or drink, that everyone must call out to God and turn from violence. “Who knows?
God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish.”
“When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.”
An angry prophet.
“But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.”
He prayed: “O Lord, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country?
That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster.
Therefore now, O Lord, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
God asked, “Do you do well to be angry?”
Jonah went out of the city and made a shelter to see what would happen.
God made a plant grow up over him to give shade, and Jonah was very glad.
The next morning God sent a worm that killed the plant, and a hot east wind blew.
Jonah was faint and angry again, wanting to die.
God said, “You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow...
And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?”
The book ends on that question.
It never says what Jonah answered.
What does this mean for us today?.
Jonah’s story is mostly about a prophet who did not want God to be merciful to his enemies.
It confronts us: who are the people we would rather see punished than forgiven?
God’s love is bigger than our dislike, and He asks us to care for the people He cares about.
It also shows us that we cannot run from God.
Jonah went down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sea, and down into the fish.
But even at the lowest point, God heard his prayer.
Wherever we are, the Bible says, God is near.
And the story points to Jesus.
Jonah was three days in the fish, and Jesus three days in the tomb.
Jonah preached and a pagan city repented.
Jesus said, “The people of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment... for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.”
Who Job was.
Job lived in a land called Uz, and the Bible does not say exactly when.
His way of life, with large herds and the father acting as priest for his family, looks like the time of Abraham or soon after.
The Bible says he was “blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.”
He was the richest man in the East.
He had 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 donkeys and many servants.
He also had seven sons and three daughters.
Every time his children held feasts, Job offered sacrifices for each one, just in case they had sinned.
Why his story matters.
The book of Job is about suffering, and the question every person asks: why does a good person suffer?
The book does not give a simple answer.
It shows what faith looks like when answers are not available.
