Everything lost in a day.
The book opens in heaven.
God points to Job as an example of a faithful man, and Satan, the accuser, says that Job only serves God because of his blessings.
“Stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face.”
God allowed Satan to test him, but not to touch Job himself.
On one day, messengers came one after another.
Raiders had stolen the oxen and donkeys and killed the servants.
Fire from heaven burned up the sheep and shepherds.
Another band took the camels.
And finally a great wind from the desert struck the house where Job’s ten children were eating and killed them all.
Job tore his robe, shaved his head, fell to the ground and worshiped.
“Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return.
The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.”
The Bible says, “In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.”
Sores and silence.
Satan said, “Skin for skin!
All that a man has he will give for his life.
But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face.”
God allowed it again, but told Satan to spare Job’s life.
Job was struck with painful sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head.
He sat in the ashes and scraped himself with a piece of broken pottery.
His wife, who had also lost her children, said, “Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die.”
Job replied, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak.
Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?”
Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, heard of his trouble and came to comfort him.
When they saw him, they could hardly recognize him.
They wept, tore their robes and sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights.
No one said a word, “for they saw that his suffering was very great.”
That silence was the best thing they did for him.
The friends’ answers.
Then Job spoke, and his words were full of pain.
He wished he had never been born.
His friends tried to explain.
Their argument was simple: God is just; God punishes sin; you are suffering; so you must have sinned.
Eliphaz said, “Who that was innocent ever perished?”
They urged Job to repent.
Job said they were wrong.
He knew he was not perfect, but this suffering did not fit any sin of his.
“Miserable comforters are you all.”
Through all his complaining, he kept holding on to God.
In one of the great lines of the book, he said, “For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.
And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God.”
He wanted to bring his case before God Himself.
A younger man named Elihu then spoke, defending God’s justice.
The book gives long speeches before God finally answers.
God answers from the whirlwind.
Then “the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind.”
God did not explain why Job had suffered.
Instead He asked questions: “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?
Tell me, if you have understanding.
Who determined its measurements? ...
Have you commanded the morning since your days began? ...
Do you give the horse his might?”
For four chapters, God described the stars, the sea, the storm, the lion, the eagle and the great creatures Behemoth and Leviathan.
The point was not to scold Job but to show him the scale of God’s wisdom and care.
Job realized how little he knew.
“I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes.”
What changed Job was not an explanation but an encounter.
He had asked for a hearing, and now he had met God.
Restored.
God then turned to Eliphaz and said, “My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.”
God told them to bring sacrifices, and Job would pray for them.
It was a remarkable moment: Job, who had been blamed and accused, prayed for his friends.
After he prayed for them, “the Lord restored the fortunes of Job, and gave Job twice as much as he had before.”
His family and friends came to eat with him and comfort him.
He ended with 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen and 1,000 donkeys.
He had seven more sons and three daughters.
He named his daughters Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and the Bible says that nowhere in all the land were there women so beautiful.
He lived another 140 years and saw four generations of his family.
The New Testament remembers him: “You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Job’s story tells us that suffering is not always a punishment.
His friends were sure of their answers, and they were wrong.
When we are tempted to explain someone else’s pain, the best thing may be what they did on the first day: sit with them, and say nothing.
It also gives us permission to be honest with God.
Job complained, argued and asked.
God did not reject him for it.
In the end, God said Job had spoken rightly of Him, and the friends with the neat answers had not.
Finally, the book teaches that we do not need to know why in order to trust Him.
Job never got an answer to his “why”.
What he got was God Himself.
And the Bible says the story ends well, because “the Lord is compassionate and merciful.”
Who Pharaoh was.
“Pharaoh” was the title of the king of Egypt, not a personal name.
The Bible tells the story of two different pharaohs in the book of Exodus: the one who began to oppress the Israelites, and a later pharaoh who faced Moses.
The Bible does not give their names, and scholars have long debated which kings they were.
Some think the Exodus happened in the 1400s BC, and others in the 1200s BC.
Egyptians believed their pharaoh was a god in human form, the son of the sun god Ra.
That is why a confrontation with Pharaoh was also a confrontation with Egypt’s gods.
Why his story matters.
The story of Pharaoh and Moses is the story of the rescue that Israel remembered for the rest of its history.
Every year the Jewish people still celebrate Passover to remember it.
It is the story of what the Lord does for people who cannot save themselves.
A king who forgot.
Centuries before, Joseph had saved Egypt from famine, and his family, the Israelites, settled in the land of Goshen.
They grew into a great nation.
A new pharaoh arose who did not remember Joseph.
He saw the Israelites as a danger: if war came, they might join Egypt’s enemies.
So he put them to forced labor, building the store cities of Pithom and Raamses with mud bricks.
They were forced to work “with harsh labor.”
Even so they kept multiplying.
Pharaoh then told two Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill every Hebrew baby boy at birth.
They feared God and refused, telling Pharaoh that Hebrew women gave birth too quickly.
When that failed, Pharaoh ordered every newborn boy thrown into the Nile.
One baby was hidden for three months, then placed in a basket on the river.
Pharaoh’s own daughter found him, and he grew up in the palace. His name was Moses.
“Let my people go”.
Moses fled Egypt as a young man after killing an Egyptian, and lived forty years as a shepherd in Midian.
Then God spoke to him from a burning bush.
The old pharaoh had died, and God sent Moses back with his brother Aaron.
They went to Pharaoh and said, “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Let My people go, that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.”
Pharaoh answered, “Who is the Lord, that I should obey His voice?
I do not know the Lord, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.”
That day he made the work worse, ordering the slaves to make the same number of bricks while gathering their own straw.
The Israelite foremen blamed Moses.
Moses went back to God, troubled.
But God said, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh.”
God was about to show Egypt and Israel who He was.
The ten plagues.
Over the next months, ten plagues struck Egypt.
The Nile turned to blood.
Frogs, gnats and flies swarmed the land. The livestock died.
Boils broke out on people and animals.
Hail destroyed the crops.
Locusts ate whatever was left.
Then three days of thick darkness covered Egypt, while the Israelites in Goshen had light.
Many of these plagues hit things Egypt worshiped: the Nile, frogs, cattle, and the sun.
The Bible says God was bringing “judgment on all the gods of Egypt.”
After several plagues Pharaoh said he would let Israel go, then changed his mind when the plague stopped.
The Bible says that Pharaoh hardened his own heart, and later that God hardened it too.
Pharaoh was given chance after chance and kept choosing to refuse.
At one point his own officials told him, “Do you not yet understand that Egypt is destroyed?”
The Passover night.
God told Moses that one more plague would come.
At midnight every firstborn son in Egypt would die, from Pharaoh’s own son to the child of the lowest prisoner.
God gave Israel a way to be spared.
Each family was to kill a young lamb with no defect, put some of its blood on the doorposts, and eat the meal in a hurry, ready to leave.
“When I see the blood, I will pass over you.”
That night a loud cry rose across Egypt, because there was not a house without someone dead.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron in the night and said, “Rise up, go out from among my people, you and the Israelites. Go, serve the Lord.”
This is why Jesus is called “the Lamb of God.”
The Bible teaches that His blood covers people the way the lamb’s blood covered those homes.
Jesus ate a Passover meal with His disciples on the night before He died.
The sea.
Israel left, about 600,000 men on foot plus women and children, and a large mixed crowd with them.
But Pharaoh soon regretted it.
“What have we done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?”
He took 600 of his best chariots and the whole Egyptian army.
They caught the Israelites camped by the sea.
The people panicked: the sea in front, the army behind.
Moses said, “Do not be afraid.
Stand firm and see the salvation of the Lord.”
God told Moses to lift his staff.
A strong east wind blew all night and the sea split.
Israel walked through on dry ground with walls of water on both sides.
Pharaoh’s army followed.
When the Israelites were safely across, Moses stretched out his hand again, and the water came back and covered the chariots, the horsemen and the whole army. Not one survived.
The Bible does not say whether Pharaoh himself drowned; it says the entire army did.
The people saw the Egyptians dead on the shore.
Then Moses and Miriam led Israel in a song: “The Lord is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.”
What does this mean for us today?.
Pharaoh is a picture of a human heart that says, “Who is the Lord, that I should obey Him?”
Every plague was a new chance to say yes.
Each time he refused, it became harder to turn.
The Bible warns us not to harden our hearts when we hear God.
The apostle Paul writes that God raised up Pharaoh so that His power would be shown and His name proclaimed in all the earth.
Even a mighty ruler could not stop God’s plan.
The story is also good news.
The Israelites did nothing to earn their rescue.
They were slaves with no army, and God saved them, the way the Bible says He saves us.
No power on earth is too strong for Him.
Who Goliath was.
Goliath was a Philistine warrior from the city of Gath.
The Philistines were Israel’s main enemy for hundreds of years.
They lived on the coastal plain, had advanced iron weapons, and often attacked Israel’s farmland.
The Hebrew text of the Bible says Goliath was six cubits and a span tall, which is about 9 feet 9 inches.
Some very old copies of the Bible say four cubits and a span, about 6 feet 9 inches.
Either way, he was far bigger than anyone around him.
Why his story matters.
Goliath’s story is one of the most famous in the Bible.
It is not mainly about a boy beating a giant.
It is about who Israel trusted when everyone was afraid.
It also shows how God works through people nobody expected.
The army that was afraid.
Around 1020 BC the Philistines gathered their army at Socoh in Judah.
King Saul and the Israelite army camped on the opposite hill.
Between them lay the Valley of Elah, a wide valley with a stream running through it.
Goliath came out of the Philistine camp every morning and every evening for forty days.
He wore a bronze helmet and a coat of scale armor that weighed about 125 pounds.
He had bronze armor on his legs, a javelin slung on his back, and a spear with a shaft like a weaver’s beam, tipped with an iron head weighing about 15 pounds.
A shield bearer walked ahead of him.
His challenge was simple.
Send one man to fight me.
If he wins, we will be your slaves.
If I win, you will be ours.
When Saul and the Israelites heard it, they were “dismayed and terrified.”
Saul was the king, and he stood a head taller than anyone else in Israel, yet he stayed in his tent.
Nobody moved for forty days.
A shepherd boy arrives.
David was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem.
He was probably a teenager.
He went back and forth between Saul’s court, where he played the harp, and the family sheep.
His three oldest brothers were in Saul’s army, so one day Jesse sent David to the camp with grain, ten loaves and ten cheeses.
David arrived as Goliath came out for his challenge.
He heard it, and he saw the soldiers run back.
He asked a question nobody else had asked: “Who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should defy the armies of the living God?”
His oldest brother, Eliab, got angry and accused him of showing off. David kept asking.
Someone told Saul, and David was brought in.
He told the king he had killed both a lion and a bear while watching his father’s sheep.
“The Lord who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.”
Saul, with no better option, said, “Go, and the Lord be with you.”
Five smooth stones.
Saul tried to dress David in his own bronze helmet, coat of armor and sword.
David walked around a bit and said he couldn’t wear it, because he had not tested it. He took it all off.
Instead he took his shepherd’s staff, picked five smooth stones from the stream and put them in his bag, and took his sling.
A sling was a real weapon.
Skilled slingers could hit a target with great speed and accuracy.
Goliath saw him coming and was insulted.
“Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?”
He cursed David by his gods and said he would feed his body to the birds.
David answered, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the Lord of hosts.
This day the Lord will deliver you into my hand.
And all this assembly will know that the Lord saves not with sword and spear.
For the battle is the Lord’s.”
The stone and the sword.
David did not hang back.
He ran toward the battle line, took a stone from his bag, slung it, and hit Goliath in the forehead.
The giant fell on his face.
David had no sword, so he ran up, took Goliath’s own sword out of its sheath, and used it to cut off his head.
When the Philistines saw their champion dead, they ran.
The men of Israel and Judah shouted, chased them all the way to Gath and Ekron, and then returned to take the Philistine camp.
David took the head to Jerusalem, and put the armor in his own tent.
Later, when he was running from Saul and needed a weapon, a priest at Nob gave him the one thing he had stored there: the sword of Goliath.
He said, “There is none like it. Give it to me.”
After the giant.
The women of Israel came out singing and dancing: “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
The song made Saul jealous, and from that day he watched David with suspicion.
It started a long chain of events: David had to run for years, but he eventually became Israel’s greatest king.
The Philistines did not disappear.
Later the Bible tells of other warriors from Gath who were also of great size, and David’s men fought and defeated them.
Gath itself, Goliath’s home city, would one day shelter David when he was a fugitive.
What does this mean for us today?.
Almost everyone has a “Goliath”: a problem that looks too big, a fear that has been shouting at you for forty days.
This story does not say the problem was small.
It says David did not measure the giant against himself.
He measured him against God.
It also shows that God does not need what the world calls impressive.
Israel had a tall king and a trained army, and nobody would go.
God used a young shepherd with a sling because he trusted the Lord.
The story points ahead to Jesus, who came from David’s town of Bethlehem and defeated sin and death, the biggest enemies of all.
Courage in the Bible is not feeling brave.
It is trusting that the battle belongs to the Lord.
Who Jezebel was.
Jezebel was a princess from Sidon, a rich port city on the coast of what is now Lebanon.
Her father, Ethbaal, was king of the Phoenicians.
The Phoenicians were sailors and traders, and their main god was Baal, a storm and fertility god, along with a goddess named Asherah.
Around 874 BC Jezebel was married to Ahab, who became king of Israel, the northern kingdom.
The marriage was a political deal between two kingdoms.
The Bible says Ahab did more evil than any king before him.
One reason was that he married Jezebel, and she brought her religion with her.
Why her story matters.
Israel was supposed to worship only the Lord, the God who rescued them from Egypt.
Jezebel is the best-known example in the Bible of what happens when a powerful person tries to replace the worship of God.
She did not just believe in another god.
She used the power of the crown to push everyone else toward it.
A queen with a mission.
Ahab built a temple for Baal in the capital, Samaria, and set up an Asherah pole.
Jezebel fed hundreds of Baal’s prophets at her own table: 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah.
At the same time she went after the prophets of the Lord.
The Bible says she was “killing off” the Lord’s prophets.
A man named Obadiah, who ran Ahab’s palace, secretly hid 100 of them in two caves and fed them bread and water.
That one detail tells us how dangerous it was to follow the Lord in Israel in those years.
A drought had also been sent on the land, because Israel had turned from God.
So the people of Israel were being pushed hard to choose a side, and the queen was the one pushing.
The showdown on Mount Carmel.
The prophet Elijah told Ahab to gather all Israel and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.
Each side would prepare a sacrifice.
The god who answered with fire would be the true God.
The prophets of Baal shouted and danced from morning until evening. Nothing happened.
Elijah joked that maybe their god was busy or asleep.
Then Elijah soaked his own altar with water, prayed a short prayer, and fire fell from heaven and burned up the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the water.
The people fell on their faces and said, “The Lord, He is God!”
The prophets of Baal were taken down to the valley and killed, and soon after, rain finally came.
When Ahab told Jezebel everything, she did not repent.
She sent Elijah a message: by this time tomorrow he would be dead like those prophets.
Elijah, who had just stood alone against 450 prophets, ran for his life into the desert.
Jezebel’s anger was that frightening.
Naboth’s vineyard.
Next to Ahab’s palace in Jezreel was a vineyard that belonged to a man named Naboth.
Ahab wanted it for a vegetable garden and offered to buy it or trade for a better one. Naboth said no.
The land was his family inheritance, and under God’s law an Israelite family was not supposed to sell its land away.
Ahab went home sulking and would not eat.
Jezebel took charge.
She wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his royal seal.
She told the city leaders to hold a public fast, seat Naboth in a place of honor, and bring two worthless men to swear that he had cursed God and the king. They did.
Naboth was taken outside the city and stoned to death.
Jezebel told Ahab to go and take the vineyard.
God sent Elijah to meet Ahab there.
Elijah told him that dogs would lick up his blood and that dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.
It was God’s answer to a murder that used the law itself as a weapon.
What happened after.
About three years later Ahab was killed in a battle at Ramoth Gilead.
A stray arrow found a gap in his armor.
His son Ahaziah became king and died after a fall.
Another son, Joram, followed him.
Jezebel stayed in the palace as the queen mother, and her influence continued.
Her daughter Athaliah married into the royal family of Judah, the southern kingdom.
After her husband and son died, Athaliah tried to destroy the whole royal family of David and ruled Judah herself for six years.
One baby, Joash, was hidden in the Temple and saved.
So Jezebel’s harm reached beyond her own kingdom.
The end of Jezebel.
God sent a prophet to anoint an army commander named Jehu as king and to end the house of Ahab.
Jehu killed King Joram and rode to Jezreel.
Jezebel heard he was coming.
She put on eye makeup, arranged her hair and looked down from a window.
She called out, “Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?”
She was comparing Jehu to an earlier man who had killed a king and lasted only seven days.
Even then, she was trying to stare down her enemy.
Jehu shouted up, “Who is on my side?”
Two or three palace officials looked out.
“Throw her down!” he said. They did.
She was trampled by horses.
Later, when Jehu sent men to bury her, they found only her skull, her feet and the palms of her hands, because dogs had eaten the rest.
Jehu remembered what Elijah had said, and it had come true word for word.
What does this mean for us today?.
Jezebel’s story is a warning about power.
She had wealth, a palace and an army, and she used them to silence the truth and take what belonged to someone else.
In the end none of it saved her, and God’s word came true exactly as spoken.
The Bible mentions her once more, in the book of Revelation.
Jesus warns the church in Thyatira about a woman there He calls “Jezebel,” who was leading people into false worship.
The name had become a symbol for anyone who pulls God’s people away from Him.
The story also gives courage.
Elijah looked alone, Naboth looked powerless, and Obadiah hid 100 prophets in a cave. God saw each of them.
Standing for what is right can cost something, but the Bible is clear that God notices, and He has the last word.
Who Haman was.
Haman is the villain in the book of Esther.
The Bible calls him “the Agagite,” which means he was probably a descendant of Agag, the king of the Amalekites.
The Amalekites were an ancient enemy of Israel, and centuries earlier King Saul had been told to destroy them and had spared Agag.
Now, about 474 BC, Haman’s family line was alive again in Persia.
King Xerxes, called Ahasuerus in the Bible, ruled the vast Persian Empire from India to Africa.
He promoted Haman above all the other officials.
Everyone at the palace gate had to bow when Haman passed.
Why his story matters.
Haman’s plan was to destroy every Jewish man, woman and child in the empire in a single day.
The book of Esther never mentions God by name, yet the story shows God’s hand in every turn.
Jews still celebrate the rescue each year at the festival of Purim.
The man who would not bow.
Everyone at the king’s gate bowed to Haman.
One man would not: Mordecai, a Jew whose family had been carried off from Jerusalem to Babylon generations earlier.
Day after day the other officials asked why he disobeyed.
Mordecai said he was a Jew.
He would not give honor that belonged to God alone.
When Haman heard, he was furious.
Killing one man was not enough for him.
He found out who Mordecai’s people were and decided to destroy them all.
He would do it legally, using the empire’s own government.
Haman cast the “pur,” which means lots, to choose a day.
The lot chose the 13th day of the twelfth month, nearly a year away.
Then he went to the king and said there was a certain people scattered through the empire whose laws were different and who did not obey the king’s laws.
He offered 10,000 talents of silver to the royal treasury, an enormous amount, if the king would order them destroyed.
Xerxes took his signet ring off and handed it to Haman.
“Keep the money, and do with the people as you please.”
Mordecai and Esther.
Letters were sent in every language to every province: on the 13th day of the twelfth month, kill all the Jews, young and old, and take their property.
Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, and the city of Susa was in confusion.
Mordecai put on sackcloth and ashes and went into the city weeping.
Esther, his cousin whom he had raised, had been made queen without telling anyone she was Jewish.
Mordecai sent word that she must go to the king and plead for her people.
Esther answered that anyone who went to the king without being called could be put to death unless he held out his golden scepter.
She had not been called in thirty days.
Mordecai’s reply is one of the best-known lines in the Bible: “Who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
Esther told him to gather the Jews in Susa and fast for her for three days.
“Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish.”
The banquet and the gallows.
On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court.
The king saw her and held out the golden scepter.
She did not make her request.
She invited the king and Haman to a banquet.
At the banquet she invited them to a second one the next day.
Haman left happy, until he passed Mordecai at the gate and Mordecai still would not stand or tremble.
At home Haman bragged about his riches, his sons, and his honors, then said none of it mattered while he saw Mordecai the Jew sitting at the gate.
His wife and friends told him to build a gallows 50 cubits high, about 75 feet, and ask the king in the morning to hang Mordecai on it.
Haman liked the idea and built it that night.
That same night the king could not sleep.
He asked for the royal records to be read to him, and the reader came to the day when Mordecai had uncovered a plot to assassinate the king.
Nobody had ever rewarded him.
The turn.
In the morning Haman walked in to ask the king for permission to hang Mordecai.
Before he could speak, the king asked him, “What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?”
Haman thought, “Who would the king delight to honor more than me?”
He described a grand parade: the king’s robe, the king’s horse, a royal crown, and a noble leading him through the city square shouting his praise.
“Go quickly,” the king said, “and do just as you have said for Mordecai the Jew.”
Haman had to dress Mordecai, put him on the king’s horse, and lead him through the city shouting, “This is what is done for the man the king delights to honor!”
Then Mordecai went back to the gate, and Haman hurried home with his head covered in shame.
His wife and advisors told him, “If Mordecai is of Jewish descent, you will not overcome him, but will surely fall before him.”
Before they finished speaking, the king’s men arrived to take him to Esther’s second banquet.
Haman’s end.
At the second banquet the king asked Esther again what she wanted.
She said, “If I have found favor with you, O king, let my life be given me, and my people.
For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed and to be annihilated.”
The king asked who dared to do this. Esther pointed. “A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!”
The king stormed out into the garden.
Haman, terrified, stayed to beg Esther for his life, and fell on the couch where she was reclining.
The king came back and saw him.
“Will he even assault the queen in my presence?”
Servants covered Haman’s face.
One of them said, “The gallows that Haman made for Mordecai stands at Haman’s house, 75 feet high.”
The king said, “Hang him on that.”
Haman was hanged on his own gallows.
Persian law could not be canceled.
So the king let Mordecai write a second decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves on that day.
On the 13th they defended themselves and won.
Mordecai became the second most important man in the empire, and the people celebrated.
What does this mean for us today?.
Haman’s hatred started with a small thing: one man would not bow.
Pride and anger, left alone, grew into a plan to destroy a whole people.
The Bible shows how dangerous unchecked pride can be, and how it often destroys the person who carries it.
The story also shows that God works behind the scenes.
His name is never mentioned in Esther, yet the right person was in the right place: a sleepless king, a forgotten act of loyalty, and a queen who was willing to risk her life.
When it seems that God is silent, He may be arranging things we cannot yet see.
And Esther’s courage still speaks to us.
“For such a time as this” is a question every believer may face: you have been put where you are for a reason, and God may ask you to step forward.
Who Herod the Great was.
Herod was king of Judea from 37 BC until his death in 4 BC.
He was not a full Israelite by descent.
His family came from Idumea, the land of Edom, south of Judea, and had been forced to adopt Judaism a century earlier.
Rome made him king because he was loyal to Rome.
The Roman Senate named him “King of the Jews” in 40 BC, and he then spent three years fighting to take Jerusalem.
He was one of the greatest builders of the ancient world.
He also became one of its most feared rulers.
Why his story matters.
Herod appears in the Bible at the moment Jesus was born.
He is the first king to hear that a new king of the Jews has been born, and the first to try to kill Him.
His story shows what happens when a ruler is more afraid of losing power than of God.
The great builder.
Herod built a whole new harbor city on the coast, called Caesarea, named for the emperor.
He built the fortress-palaces of Herodium and Masada, and added to many cities.
His biggest project was the Temple in Jerusalem.
Around 20 BC he began to rebuild it on a much larger scale, with huge white stones, gold decoration and massive courts.
It was still being worked on in Jesus’ day.
John’s Gospel records someone saying it had been under construction “forty-six years.”
He did it to win favor with the Jewish people, who never fully trusted him, and with Rome.
Many of his buildings could be seen for miles, and some walls still stand today, including part of the foundation around the Temple Mount.
A king afraid of losing his throne.
Herod was famously suspicious.
He had his wife Mariamne, from the old Jewish royal family, executed.
He also had her brother and her grandfather killed.
Later he had two of his sons by Mariamne strangled.
Just five days before he died, he ordered the execution of his oldest son, Antipater, for plotting against him.
The Jewish historian Josephus, who wrote about Herod, describes a man full of fear, rage and illness in his last years.
So when wise men arrived in Jerusalem and asked, “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews?”, Herod’s reaction is not a surprise.
Matthew says he was “troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.”
Everyone knew what Herod did when he felt threatened.
The wise men.
The wise men, or magi, came from the East, probably Persia or Babylon, following a star.
They went straight to Jerusalem, the capital, because that is where a king would be born.
Herod gathered the chief priests and teachers of the law and asked where the Messiah was to be born.
They answered from the prophet Micah: Bethlehem in Judea.
Herod secretly called the magi, learned exactly when the star had appeared, and sent them to Bethlehem.
“Go and search carefully for the child.
As soon as you find him, report to me, so that I too may go and worship him.”
He did not want to worship.
He wanted to find the child.
The priests knew the Scripture and were only five or six miles away, yet none of them went to see Jesus. The magi did.
They found the child with Mary, bowed down and gave gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh.
A warning came in a dream, and they went home another way.
Bethlehem.
God warned Joseph in a dream that Herod was going to search for the child to kill Him.
Joseph got up in the night and took Mary and Jesus to Egypt.
Herod saw that the wise men had tricked him and was furious.
He sent soldiers to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and the surrounding area who were two years old and under.
Based on what the wise men had told him about the star, he chose the age to be safe.
The Bible does not give a number.
Bethlehem was a small town, so historians think the number was small, but every child was a terrible loss.
Matthew says this fulfilled a prophecy of Jeremiah about Rachel weeping for her children.
Herod’s cruelty fits what history tells us about him.
It also shows that the birth of Jesus was a real threat to the powers of the world from the very beginning.
How Herod died.
Herod died around 4 BC.
Josephus describes his final illness as painful and terrible, and says he lived his last days in fear that no one would mourn him.
Before he died he ordered important men to be locked up, so there would be mourning at his death.
The order was not carried out.
After his death an angel told Joseph in a dream that it was safe to return.
Herod’s kingdom was divided among three sons.
Archelaus took Judea and was so cruel that Joseph was afraid to settle there, so he took Jesus to Nazareth in Galilee instead.
Herod Antipas, another son, ruled Galilee and later killed John the Baptist.
Herod’s family kept showing up in the Gospels and in the book of Acts, still opposing Jesus and His followers.
What does this mean for us today?.
Herod had a palace, an army and a great temple, and he died in fear.
A baby in a poor family’s house in Bethlehem outlasted him.
Herod’s throne is gone, and Jesus is still worshiped around the world.
The story is also a warning.
The priests knew the Scriptures and ignored the news.
Herod heard the same news and tried to destroy it.
The wise men, who were outsiders, simply followed and worshiped.
How a person reacts to Jesus shows what is really in the heart.
Finally, the story is comfort for anyone who has suffered because of a powerful person’s selfishness.
God was present in Bethlehem’s sorrow, and the Bible shows that Jesus came into a world with real evil in it, to defeat it.
Who Pilate was.
Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from about AD 26 to 36 or 37.
His official title was prefect.
He was appointed by the emperor Tiberius and lived mostly in the coastal city of Caesarea, traveling to Jerusalem for big festivals such as Passover to keep order.
In 1961, archaeologists found a stone at Caesarea with his name and title on it.
Roman writers like Tacitus also mention him.
Jewish writers of the time describe him as harsh.

Philo and Josephus tell of him bringing Roman military standards with the emperor’s image into Jerusalem, which nearly caused a riot, and using Temple money to build an aqueduct, which led to protests that his soldiers put down by force.
Luke mentions a time when Pilate killed some Galileans while they were offering sacrifices.
Why his story matters.
Pilate is the man who sentenced Jesus to death.
His name is in the Apostles’ Creed, which the church has said for centuries: “suffered under Pontius Pilate.”
That line fixes the death of Jesus in real history, at a real time, under a real governor.
Jesus brought to Pilate.
After Jesus was arrested in the garden of Gethsemane, the Jewish council tried Him during the night and decided He deserved death for claiming to be the Son of God.
Under Roman rule they did not have the authority to carry out a death sentence, so at dawn they brought Jesus to Pilate.
They stayed outside the palace so that they would not become ritually unclean before the Passover meal.
Because they could not charge Him with a religious crime in a Roman court, they changed the charges.
They said Jesus was stirring up the people, telling them not to pay taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be a king.
Pilate, who cared mostly about order and about Caesar, asked Jesus: “Are you the King of the Jews?”
The question of truth.
Pilate took Jesus inside.
Jesus answered that His kingdom was not of this world.
If it were, His followers would be fighting.
“You say that I am a king.
For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world, to testify to the truth.
Everyone who is of the truth listens to My voice.”
Pilate said, “What is truth?” and went back out without waiting for an answer.
He told the crowd, “I find no guilt in Him.”
The charge was not true, and Pilate knew it.
Luke adds that when Pilate learned Jesus was from Galilee, he sent Him to Herod Antipas, who ruled there and happened to be in Jerusalem.
Herod and his soldiers mocked Jesus and sent Him back.
The crowd and Barabbas.
It was Pilate’s custom to release one prisoner at Passover.
He offered the crowd a choice between Jesus and a known criminal, Barabbas, who had taken part in a riot and murder.
Pilate understood that the chief priests had handed Jesus over “out of envy.”
He expected the crowd to ask for Jesus.
Meanwhile his wife sent him a message: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of Him today in a dream.”
But the chief priests persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas.
“What shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” Pilate asked. “Let Him be crucified!” Pilate asked, “Why? What evil has He done?”
They shouted all the louder.
Pilate had Jesus whipped.
Roman soldiers put a purple robe on Him and a crown of thorns, and mocked Him as king.
Pilate brought Him out and said, “Behold the man!”
Still the crowd shouted for crucifixion.
Washing his hands.
The leaders then said, “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar.” That was a real threat.
A report to Rome that Pilate had let a man claiming to be king go free could end his career, or his life.
Pilate sat on his judgment seat, the stone pavement, and said, “Behold your King!”
They shouted, “Away with Him! Crucify Him!”
“We have no king but Caesar,” the chief priests said.
Pilate took water and washed his hands before the crowd.
“I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves.”
But the water did not make it so. He still gave the order.
He knew Jesus was innocent and put Him to death anyway.
Pilate also had a sign written and fixed to the cross: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,” in Hebrew, Latin and Greek.
When the priests asked him to change it, he said, “What I have written, I have written.”
After the cross.
That evening a wealthy member of the council named Joseph of Arimathea, a secret follower of Jesus, asked Pilate for the body.
Pilate was surprised Jesus had died so quickly.
He checked with the centurion and then gave permission.
The next day the chief priests asked Pilate to seal the tomb and post guards, since Jesus had said He would rise on the third day.
Pilate said, “You have a guard of soldiers.
Go, make it as secure as you can.”
They sealed the stone and set the guard.
On the third morning, the tomb was empty.
The Bible says nothing more about Pilate.
Outside the Bible, Josephus says that around AD 36 he attacked a crowd of Samaritans gathered at Mount Gerizim.
The Roman governor of Syria removed him and sent him to Rome.
What happened to him after that, we do not know.
Later legends give different endings, but none is reliable.
What does this mean for us today?.
Pilate shows how a person can know what is right and still do what is wrong.
He said Jesus was innocent three times.
He felt the pressure of the crowd, the priests, and his own career, and he gave in.
Washing his hands did not clear him.
Many of us will never face a decision as large as his, but we do face small moments when doing right costs us something.
The story asks what we will do when the crowd is loud.
It also shows something larger.
Pilate and the crowd thought they were in control, but Jesus told him, “You would have no authority over Me at all unless it had been given you from above.”
The Bible teaches that Jesus went to the cross willingly, to take the punishment for our sins.
Even the worst injustice in history became the way God saved the world.
